authors: Raj Chetty, John N. Friedman, Søren Leth-Petersen, Torben Heien Nielsen and Tore Olsen
title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark
summary: Uses the universe of Danish savings records to show that tax subsidies for retirement accounts mostly shift saving between accounts: each krone of subsidy raises total saving by about one øre. Automatic employer contributions, by contrast, raise total saving almost one for one, because roughly 85 percent of individuals are passive savers who do not re-optimise.
data: Income tax register with third-party reported earnings and pension contributions (IND)
Third-party reported wealth: end-of-year assets and liabilities in taxable accounts
Population register (BEF)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
variables: Outcome: contributions to employer and individual retirement accounts
Outcome: taxable saving (change in taxable assets), gross and net
Treatment: employer pension contribution changes at job switches (automatic contributions)
Treatment: 1999 reduction in tax subsidy for capital pensions for top-bracket taxpayers (price subsidy)
Treatment: government mandatory savings plan (SP) contributions
sample_size: approximately 41 million observations for 4 million individuals
sample: Danish population aged 18–60, excluding observations with self-employment income (unbalanced panel).

definitions.definition: Danish population 1995-2009 from merged income tax register, population register and IDA, excluding observations below age 18 or above 60 and observations with self-employment income (about 41 million observations on 4 million individuals).

Gross taxable saving = change in third-party reported end-of-year assets in taxable accounts; net saving = gross saving minus change in liabilities, where liabilities cover secured and unsecured debt except home mortgages. Saving measures and rates below the 1st or above the 99th percentile in the estimation sample are set to missing.

Annual employer and individual contributions to capital pension (lump-sum) and annuity pension accounts as reported by employers and pension funds; contributions above the 99th percentile are top-coded at the 99th percentile in each account and year.

Labor income = labor earnings before taxes excluding contributions to employer-administered pensions; total compensation = labor earnings plus employer and employee contributions to employer-administered accounts; taxable income = labor income plus other income (e.g., UI) affecting tax liability. Measured at the individual level, with joint-account balances split equally.

Individual switches firms in year t if he has earnings from two distinct firms in t and t-1 (primary job for multiple jobholders); switches where earnings fell by more than half or more than doubled are excluded; set missing in 2003, 2005 and 2007 when firm identifiers changed. Event studies require at least 4 years of data before and after.

From 1998 individuals with labor income at or above DKr 34,500 were required to contribute 1% of earnings (DKr 345 at the cutoff); RD on changes in pension contributions/saving from 1997 to 1998 for individuals within DKr 25,000 of the cutoff.

From 1999 the deduction for capital pension contributions fell from 59 to 45 cents per DKr for individuals in the top income tax bracket (cutoff DKr 251,200 in 1998); treatment group: taxable income DKr 25,000-75,000 above the top-tax cutoff; control: DKr 25,000-75,000 below.

authors: Henrik Jacobsen Kleven, Camille Landais, Emmanuel Saez and Esben Schultz
title: Migration and Wage Effects of Taxing Top Earners: Evidence from the Foreigners' Tax Scheme in Denmark
summary: The 1991 preferential tax scheme for high-earning foreigners roughly doubled the number of highly paid foreigners in Denmark. The implied elasticity of migration with respect to the net-of-tax rate is above one, far larger than domestic labour supply elasticities, and the scheme generated modest wage spillovers.
data: Administrative tax and payroll records for all residents (income tax register)
Civil registration (CPR) citizenship and migration records with dates of entry and exit
Foreigners' tax scheme beneficiary records (contract start and end dates)
Employer links at firm and establishment level with industry
variables: Treatment: eligibility for the preferential foreigners' tax scheme (earnings above threshold)
Outcome: number of foreigners above vs below the earnings threshold (migration response)
Outcome: earnings of scheme beneficiaries (wage effects / bunching at the threshold)
Outcome: spillovers on native top earners' employment and earnings
Key variable: citizenship and years of presence in Denmark
sample: All foreigners and natives resident in Denmark, focusing on foreigners with earnings around the scheme eligibility threshold (researchers excluded).

definitions.definition: Foreigners' scheme requires annual wage earnings with the requesting employer above a threshold that grows roughly with average earnings and lies between the 99.2th and 99.4th percentile of the Danish wage earnings distribution (DKK 765,600 in 2009); it must be met on an annualized basis (e.g. a 6-month contract needs half the annual threshold). For pre-1991 years the threshold is imputed by holding the threshold-to-average-earnings ratio at its 1991 value, with average earnings computed over all workers with positive earnings.

To be eligible the taxpayer must have been recruited abroad and not have been tax liable in Denmark in the 3 years before going on the scheme (applied to each scheme spell separately; prior scheme time not counted); citizenship plays no formal role, so Danish citizens tax-resident abroad for 3+ years qualify. Scheme lasts at most 36 months.
Earnings of part-year residents are annualized based on duration of stay in the year, with duration of stay measured from the migration database (daily dates of entry and exit from CPR records).

definitions.variable: Treatment and control groups of foreigners (migration DiD)
definitions.definition: Treatment: foreigners with (annualized) earnings above the eligibility threshold; controls: foreigners with earnings between 80% and 90% (control 1) and between 90% and 99.5% (control 2) of the threshold, series normalized to 1990. In the elasticity regressions controls are foreigners between 80% and 99% of the threshold; an alternative uses the 99.5-100th percentile vs the 95-97th and 97-99th percentiles of the full earnings distribution.

Nordic foreigners: citizens of Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden; English-speaking: Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, South Africa, UK, US. Expatriates are Danish citizens returning after a spell of at least three years abroad.

For year t, foreigners who arrived in Denmark in year t-1 and stayed the full calendar year t; earnings between 70-95% (below) and 105-400% (above) of the threshold, excluding 95-105% (bunchers) and above 400%; years 1991-1994 excluded because scheme earnings are not computerized.

definitions.variable: Top natives and top foreign employees (spillovers)
definitions.definition: Top natives: native workers with earnings above 75% of the scheme eligibility threshold (about the top 3% of native earnings). Top foreign employees: foreign employees with less than 3 years of presence in Denmark and annualized earnings above the threshold; industry scheme use = growth in top foreign employees between 1980-1990 and 1991-2000 divided by top native employees in 1980-1990.

authors: Katrine Jakobsen, Kristian Jakobsen, Henrik Kleven and Gabriel Zucman
title: Wealth Taxation and Wealth Accumulation: Theory and Evidence from Denmark
summary: Exploits the 1989 Danish wealth tax reform, which cut rates sharply for the wealthy, to estimate long-run effects of wealth taxes on wealth accumulation. Responses are sizable for the very wealthy (top one percent) and small for the moderately wealthy, with effects that keep growing over a decade.
data: Administrative wealth registry (third-party reported assets and debts, since 1980)
Income registers and socio-economic registers (occupation, family composition)
variables: Outcome: log taxable wealth and third-party reported wealth
Treatment: 1989 wealth tax cut (unbound vs bound by tax ceiling: ceiling DD)
Treatment: doubling of couples' exemption threshold (couples DD)
Running variable for bunching: taxable wealth around exemption threshold
Controls: pre-reform portfolio shares and income deciles
sample_size: 138,384 observations (ceiling DD) and 520,452 observations (couples DD, couples vs couples)
sample: Balanced panels of Danish households in the top 1% (ceiling DD) or married couples in the top 5% (couples DD) of the wealth distribution before the 1989 reform.

definitions.definition: Household id is the family id when the person's spouse id equals the cohabitation partner id and civil status is in the married range (up to 2007, from FAIN); from 2008 from BEF using spouse id = partner id and civil status G or P. Persons not so linked form their own household. Only persons aged 20+ are kept and wealth is summed within household.
definitions.codes: FAIN (<=2007): aegtefaelle_id == c_faelle_id, c_status 2-5, hhid = c_familie_id; BEF (>=2008): aegte_id == efalle, civst in {G, P}; alder >= 20

definitions.definition: Household net taxable wealth = sum over household members aged 20+ of the wealth variable FORM from the income-tax register (INDH); outcome is log(FORM). Portfolio shares use INDK components: equity share = listed stocks / total assets, housing share = (mortgage deeds + real estate value) / total assets.
definitions.codes: FORM (INDH); share_tx_equities = KURSAKT/QAKTIVF; share_tx_housing = (KURSPANT+KOEJD)/QAKTIVF; other INDK fields: FORMSK, LOFTFORM, QPASSIV, PRIGALD, KONTANT, KURSOBL, INDESTPI

definitions.variable: Wealth tax exemption threshold and marginal wealth tax
definitions.definition: Annual exemption threshold (allowance) by year; for couples it equals 2 x single allowance, except 1989-1992 when couples' allowance uses a separate married allowance x 2. Household marginal wealth tax rate tau_it = statutory rate if FORM exceeds the household allowance, else 0. Bunching analysis uses distance b = FORM - allowance, deflated, in DKK 20,000 bins from -540,000 to 540,000.

definitions.variable: Ceiling DD treatment (unbound by tax ceiling)
definitions.definition: X = wealth tax actually paid (FORMSK) / theoretical wealth tax ((FORM - allowance) x tax rate). Treatment: household in top 1% of the wealth distribution with X > 0.99 in every pre-reform year of the window (e.g. 1982-1988), i.e. not bound by the tax ceiling; control: top 1% with X < 0.80 (bound by ceiling). Households above the 99.99th percentile excluded. In the panel, status is re-coded post-reform using X, LOFTFORM > 0 and wealth relative to allowance.
definitions.codes: treatmt_2e_X80: X > .99 and top1 in 1982-1988; control_2e_X80: X < .80 and top1; drop form_pctile > .9999

definitions.definition: Treatment: married households with wealth between the (single) allowance and 2 x allowance in each pre-reform year (1988 and earlier years depending on window), which became exempt when the couples' threshold doubled in 1989; controls: (c1) singles with wealth in the same band, (c4) married couples in the top 5% with wealth below the allowance, or (c5) singles with wealth between allowance/2 and allowance.
definitions.codes: treatmt_c1*: married & allowance <= FORM <= 2*allowance; control_c1*: unmarried, same band; control_c4*: married & FORM < allowance & top5; control_c5*: unmarried & allowance/2 <= FORM <= allowance

definitions.definition: Households (persons 20+ aggregated by household id) observed with strictly positive aggregate wealth FORM in all 17 years 1980-1996.
definitions.codes: drop if form <= 0 | missing; keep if _N == 17 (balanced_1980_96)

definitions.definition: Household flagged as self-employed if business profit (NETOVSKUD_GL) is nonzero; a broader 'ext' flag also uses nonzero values of EGNKAPVK, UDLFKURS, UDLIND2 or UDLIND3 (foreign/business-related components).
definitions.codes: selv = netovskud_gl != 0; ext = netovskud_gl!=0 | egnkapvk!=0 | udlfkurs!=0 | udlind2!=0 | udlind3!=0

authors: Morten Bennedsen, Kasper Meisner Nielsen, Francisco Pérez-González and Daniel Wolfenzon
title: Inside the Family Firm: The Role of Families in Succession Decisions and Performance
summary: Uses the gender of a departing CEO's first-born child as an instrument for family succession in Danish firms. Family CEOs hurt performance: operating profitability falls by at least four percentage points relative to firms that hire outside CEOs, with the largest costs in fast-growing industries and large firms.
data: Købmandsstandens Oplysningsbureau (KOB) firm financial and management data (private, from annual reports)
Danish Civil Registration System (CPR) with family links
Danish Commerce and Companies Agency (Erhvervs- og Selskabsstyrelsen) management/board records with CPR numbers
Industry-level data from Statistics Denmark and OECD STAN
variables: Outcome: operating return on assets (OROA) around CEO transitions
Treatment: family CEO succession (incoming CEO related by blood or marriage)
Instrument: gender of the departing CEO's firstborn child
Heterogeneity: industry growth, skill intensity and firm size
sample_size: 5,334 successions
sample: CEO successions in Danish limited liability (public and private) firms between 1994 and 2002, first transition per firm.

definitions.definition: Ratio of earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to the book value of assets, from annual reports of limited liability firms (KOB). Performance change is the three-year average after succession minus the three-year average before, omitting the succession year.
definitions.source_location: Section II.B; footnote 13; Table IV notes

definitions.definition: OROA minus the equally weighted average OROA of all active firms (including non-event firms) in the same industry and year; four-digit NACE industries are used if they contain at least 20 non-event firms in a year, otherwise three- or two-digit groupings.
definitions.codes: NACE 4-digit, falling back to 3- or 2-digit; minimum 20 non-event firms

definitions.definition: OROA adjusted using as control firms in the same industry and the same industry-adjusted performance decile in the year before succession (Barber and Lyon, 1996).

Indicator equal to one if the incoming CEO is related by blood or marriage to the departing CEO according to family trees built from the Civil Registration System (parents, siblings, children, marital history), zero otherwise; family successions split into children and other relatives.
Indicator equal to one if the departing CEO's first child is male and zero if female; used as an instrument for family succession in a linear first stage.

CEO successions 1994-2002 in Danish limited liability firms, kept when the departing (incoming) CEO had been (stayed) in the position at least two years, CEO names were matched to CPR numbers via the ES dataset, matching KOB financial data existed around the transition and employment (where available) was non-zero; only the first transition per firm is kept (5,334 successions).

Sample split at the median of industry production growth, output volatility (value of production), labour compensation per employee and import penetration (Statistics Denmark), workers' schooling (authors' calculation from individual schooling and industry of employment), and R&D (industries reporting R&D expenses in OECD STAN).

definitions.variable: Return on capital employed and net income to assets
definitions.definition: ROCE is operating income divided by book equity plus book debt; net income to assets is after-tax profits over book value of assets; assets measured as log assets in 2000 DKK.

authors: Henrik Jacobsen Kleven, Martin B. Knudsen, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Pedersen and Emmanuel Saez
title: Unwilling or Unable to Cheat? Evidence from a Tax Audit Experiment in Denmark
summary: A randomised field experiment with the Danish tax authority on about 40,000 taxpayers. Evasion is close to zero for third-party reported income but substantial for self-reported income, and audit threat letters raise reported self-reported income. Information, not morality, is what makes modern tax systems work.
data: Randomized tax audit experiment implemented by the Danish tax authority (SKAT)
SKAT Business Object Database: third-party information reports, pre-populated returns, filed returns and after-audit returns, item by item
SKAT computer-generated audit flags
Basic socio-economic variables and employer industry/size from SKAT records
variables: Treatment: random assignment to 100% vs 0% unannounced audit group (2007 filing season)
Treatment: random threat-of-audit letters (100%, 50%, none) before the 2008 filing deadline
Outcome: detected tax evasion (audit adjustments to net income and tax)
Outcome: change in reported income in the following year
Heterogeneity: self-reported vs third-party reported income
sample_size: 25,020 employees and 17,764 self-employed
sample: Stratified random sample of Danish taxpayers (employees, including transfer recipients, and self-employed) selected by SKAT for the audit experiment.

definitions.definition: Stratified random sample of 25,020 employees and 17,764 self-employed (strata: employee/self-employed, light/heavy return complexity, 30 regional tax centres) randomly split into a 100% group subjected to unannounced comprehensive audits of returns filed in 2007 (2006 income) and a 0% group never audited; effects are intent-to-treat (actual audit rates 98.7% employees, 92% self-employed).

Employees in both audit groups randomly assigned (thirds) to receive a letter one month before the 1 May 2008 filing deadline stating that the return would certainly be audited (100% letter), that half of the group would be audited (50% letter), or no letter. Outcome is the probability of self-reported adjustments (upward/downward) relative to the latest return at the time the letter was received.

Net audit adjustment = after-audit return (A) minus filed return (F), split into under-reporting (upward adjustments raising tax liability) and over-reporting (downward adjustments), for net income, total tax and income components.
definitions.codes: Returns: information report (I), pre-populated (P), filed (F), after-audit (A)

definitions.variable: Third-party vs self-reported income and evasion
definitions.definition: Third-party income comes from information reports; self-reported income = total reported income minus third-party income. For always-positive line items, third-party under-reporting = A-F if F<A<I, = I-F if F<I<=A, zero otherwise; self-reported under-reporting is total upward adjustment net of third-party under-reporting. Third-party under-reporting is defined only for positive items.

Net income = personal income + capital income + stock income + self-employment income + foreign income - deductions. Personal income: earnings, pensions, alimony minus some retirement contributions; capital income: interest income, bond returns, net rents minus interest payments; stock income: dividends and realised capital gains on stocks; self-employment income: net profits of unincorporated businesses.
Presence and number of computer-generated audit flags, a deterministic function of the return characteristics that SKAT normally uses to select returns for examiner review.

authors: Rasmus Lentz and Dale T. Mortensen
title: An Empirical Model of Growth Through Product Innovation
summary: Estimates a Schumpeterian model of firm growth through product innovation on a Danish firm panel. Reallocation of labour from less to more innovative firms accounts for roughly half of aggregate productivity growth, with the remainder coming from innovation within firms.
data: Danish Business Statistics Register: annual panel of privately owned firms (value added, total wage bill, full-time equivalent employment)
variables: Firm value added (Y)
Total wage bill (W) used to build quality-adjusted employment
Full-time equivalent employment (N)
Labor productivity: value added per worker and per quality-adjusted worker
Moments: firm growth rates including exit, and productivity growth decomposition (within, between, cross, exit)
sample_size: unbalanced panel of 4,872 firms
sample: All privately owned Danish firms existing in 1992 with more than 20 workers, followed through 1997, excluding later entrants.

definitions.definition: Unbalanced annual panel 1992-1997 of privately owned firms from the Danish Business Statistics Register: all firms existing in 1992 with more than 20 workers, followed over time; entrants after 1992 excluded (about 4,872 firms).
definitions.source_location: Section 2 (Danish Firm Data); Section 5 (Danish Firm Data)

definitions.definition: N* of firm j equals its total wage bill W_j divided by the economy-wide average wage per worker (sum of W over sum of N); for firms observed in several years the implied labour quality is averaged over time.
definitions.codes: N*_j = W_j / w, w = sum_j W_j / sum_j N_j

definitions.definition: Value added per worker (Y/N) and value added per quality-adjusted worker (Y/N*), with Y in DKK.
Firm growth rate in value added (dY/Y) where an exiting firm contributes an observation of -1.

Growth in aggregate value added per worker decomposed following Foster, Haltiwanger and Krizan (2001) into within, between, cross, entry and exit terms, with firm employment shares as weights; no entry term because entrants are excluded.
definitions.codes: P_t = sum_e s_et p_et, p_et = Y_et/N_et, s_et = N_et/N_t

authors: Rasmus Lentz, Suphanit Piyapromdee and Jean-Marc Robin
title: The Anatomy of Sorting: Evidence from Danish Data
summary: Estimates a flexible model of worker and firm heterogeneity in wages and job mobility on Danish matched employer-employee data. Workers and firms sort positively, with sorting operating through both wages and non-wage amenities, and worker heterogeneity accounts for the bulk of wage dispersion.
data: Matched employer-employee register data (IDA) with annual wages
Weekly labour market spell/mobility data built from Statistics Denmark registers
variables: Outcome: log wage rate
Job-to-job mobility and transitions to and from non-employment (weekly)
Latent worker and firm types (finite mixture, classification EM)
Controls: gender, education, potential experience, tenure, calendar time
Sorting channels: job preferences, segmentation, layoffs, job finding
sample: Danish workers after completing education, employment spells starting before age 50, followed weekly across employers from 1987 to 2013 (read from the 2018 predecessor working paper).

definitions.definition: Annual total salary declared by the employer to the tax authorities divided by total hours worked by the worker in that year; assigned to the first week of the year or the first week of a new employment spell starting within the year. Hours are inferred by Statistics Denmark from mandatory pension contributions that depend on weekly hours.

Weekly employment and non-employment spells 1985-2013; spells with less than an average of 25 work hours per week are treated as non-employment spells (to keep only full-time workers). Non-employment is coded as firm ID 0.

Panel starts in 1987 (1985-1986 used to classify tenure of the 1987 stock of jobs); only employment spells starting after the individual finished the highest level of education are kept, and spells starting after age 50 are removed. Workers are drawn from the 1987 working-age population or enter in the first week of the year after their last year of schooling. About 4 million workers and 400,000 firms.
Based on normed years of education of the highest completed degree: low is below 12 years, medium is exactly 12 years, high is above 12 years.

Short tenure is less than 100 weeks of employment (26 weeks for non-employment spells). Potential experience is time since leaving school (age minus age upon leaving school), grouped as under 5, 5-10, 11-15 and over 15 years; calendar time in 3-year intervals (9 groups 1987-2013), giving 72 covariate cells.
Time-invariant firm characteristic indicating public or private status, used as observed firm covariate.

authors: Jesper Bagger, François Fontaine, Fabien Postel-Vinay and Jean-Marc Robin
title: Tenure, Experience, Human Capital, and Wages: A Tractable Equilibrium Search Model of Wage Dynamics
summary: Builds and estimates an equilibrium search model with on-the-job search and human capital accumulation using Danish career histories. Human capital accumulation drives most early-career wage growth, while job-to-job mobility and employer competition explain the later part of wage profiles.
data: Weekly labour market spell data built from administrative registers (employment, unemployment, non-participation, self-employment, retirement)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA): hourly wages, education, experience, ownership
ATP pension contributions used to measure actual experience since 1964
Firm accounts survey (Accounts Statistics) 1999–2003 with value added and hours
variables: Outcome: hourly wage of jobs active in the last week of November
Key variable: job tenure and actual labour market experience
Key variable: firm productivity measured by value added (accounting data)
Key variable: job-to-job, employment-to-unemployment transitions (spell data)
Stratification: three schooling levels (7–11, 12–14, 15–20 years)
sample_size: 168,649, 320,638 and 66,155 workers (2,534,203, 4,344,288 and 663,362 observations) in the three education groups
sample: Danish private-sector male workers born in 1948 or later, at least two years past graduation, with histories truncated at entry into retirement, self-employment, the public sector or industries lacking value-added data.

definitions.definition: Job spells defined at firm (not establishment) level; establishment-level IDA information aggregated to the firm, with firm industry and ownership taken from its largest establishment by remaining workers. Nonparticipation is a residual state: 47% of workers have at least one nonparticipation spell and 5.5% of last-week-of-November spells are nonparticipation.
IDA average hourly wage for jobs active in the last week of November, deflated to 2003 prices with Statistics Denmark's CPI.

Actual experience at end of calendar year constructed from mandatory ATP pension payments back to 1 January 1964; pre-1980 experience measured in years and post-1980 in 1/1000 of a year's full-time work. Workers dropped if pre-1980 experience changes over 1985-2003, if experience falls or rises by more than two years in a year, or exceeds age minus 15.

Statistics Denmark's accounting-data sampling scheme by firm size: theoretical sampling probability 0.10 (0-9 employees), 0.20 (10-19), 0.50 (20-49), 1.00 (>49); firms with revenue above DKK 100 million (DKK 200 million in wholesale) are also included; in practice 10% of firms with 5-9 employees and no firms with 0-4 employees are sampled (0-4 lumped with 5-9). Empirical sampling probabilities (pooled 1999-2003 last-week-of-November cross sections) of about 0.07-0.09, 0.29-0.30, 0.60-0.62 and 0.91-0.95 are used as weights.

Ownership code of the employing establishment in IDA identifies private-sector establishments; histories are truncated at entry into a public sector job, self-employment, retirement or an industry without accounting data. Firm industry and ownership taken from its largest establishment.

Years of education computed from type of highest completed education, grouped as 7-11 years (primary), 12-14 years (high school or vocational) and 15-20 years (bachelor or higher); workers enter two years after graduation and are dropped if ever observed in education afterwards or if years of education exceed age minus seven.
Men born on or after 1 January 1948 (so experience from 1964 is complete), 1985-2003, dropping firms with missing ID, ownership or industry and workers with gaps in observed histories.

authors: Jesper Bagger and Rasmus Lentz
title: An Empirical Model of Wage Dispersion with Sorting
summary: Estimates an equilibrium search model with endogenous search intensity and two-sided heterogeneity on Danish matched data. Finds positive assortative matching between worker and firm productivity, and quantifies how much of wage dispersion is due to sorting versus search frictions.
data: Weekly labour market spell data from administrative registers (jobs reported to tax authorities, public transfers, mandatory pension contributions)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA): education, hourly wages and firm sector
variables: Outcome: hourly wage (last week of November)
Key variable: job-to-job transitions and unemployment spells
Estimated: worker skill and firm productivity types (sorting)
Decomposition: log-wage variance into worker heterogeneity, firm heterogeneity, frictions and sorting
sample_size: 6,815,884 observations; 782,951 individuals; 1,698,990 job spells; 117,847 firms (NBER 2014 version)
sample: Danish workers up to age 55, after labour market entry, never observed in public-sector employment, self-employment, retirement or agriculture.

definitions.definition: Weekly spells 1985-2003 for the population aged 15-70 constructed from registers on public transfers, hourly wages, employer-reported job start/end dates and mandatory employer pension contributions; five states (employment, unemployment, retirement, self-employment, non-participation), with non-participation a residual state (neither employed, self-employed nor receiving a transfer classifying the person as unemployed or retired).

Non-participation recoded as unemployment; unemployment spells of 13 weeks or less followed by recall to the same employer are recoded as part of the original employment spell; unemployment spells of 2 weeks or less between employment spells with different employers are treated as a job-to-job transition.

IDA estimate of the average hourly wage for jobs active in the last week of November (no wage for spells not overlapping it); trimmed at 1st and 99th percentiles annually and trended to 2003 levels using implicit deflators.

1994-2003; histories truncated at age 55 and starting at graduation from highest completed education; workers ever observed in public-sector employment, self-employment, retirement or agriculture are discarded.

For each firm, the fraction of all hires over the 10-year window that come directly from other firms (job-to-job); measured only for firms with more than 15 hires and at least one hire from unemployment; used as a firm productivity rank.
Robustness estimation splits workers into less than 15 and more than 15 years of education.

authors: David Hummels, Rasmus Jørgensen, Jakob Munch and Chong Xiang
title: The Wage Effects of Offshoring: Evidence from Danish Matched Worker-Firm Data
summary: Links product-level firm imports and exports to worker wages. Offshoring raises wages of high-skilled workers and lowers wages of low-skilled workers within job spells, while exporting raises wages for all. Tasks that are routine or easily offshored lose the most.
data: Firm Statistics Register (FirmStat/FIRM)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Firm-worker link (FIDA)
Foreign Trade Statistics Register, Extrastat and Intrastat (UHDI)
UN COMTRADE world trade data for instruments
Firm accounts and other firm registers (Data Appendix)
variables: Outcome: log hourly wage of workers within job spells
Treatment: firm offshoring (imports of inputs)
Treatment: firm exports
Instruments: world export supply and world import demand shocks by product and country (COMTRADE) and transport costs
Heterogeneity: worker skill type (high vs low skilled)
Outcome: earnings losses of displaced workers
sample_size: about 1.95 million worker-firm-year and 9,800 firm-year observations
sample: Manufacturing workers in Danish firms that both import and export, excluding single-year job spells, workers changing skill level, and firms with fewer than 50 employees and less than 0.6 million DKK in imports.

definitions.definition: Wage rate uses annual hours from IDA (following Christensen et al. 2005); annual hours do not capture overtime. In a 2006 subsample with overtime data, a wage rate including overtime correlates 0.86 with the main wage rate.

Robustness split of low-skilled workers into medium-skilled (vocational education, defined as the final stage of secondary education preparing for labour market entry) and very-low-skilled (high school equivalent or less); results very similar. Workers whose skill level changes during the sample period are dropped.
Total value of imports by a given manufacturing firm in a given year, from the Foreign Trade Statistics Register (Extrastat and Intrastat), recorded at CN8 and aggregated to HS6.

Machinery imports (HS 84 and HS 85, 16.9% of imports) are included in broad offshoring for all firms; narrow offshoring excludes them except for firms that themselves produce machinery for sale. Within HS 84 the top 20 HS6 import products (59% of HS 84 imports) are all parts rather than machines.

definitions.variable: World export supply and world import demand instruments
definitions.definition: WES: country c's total supply of HS6 product k to the world market minus its supply to Denmark in year t; WID: country c's total purchases of product k from the world market less purchases from Denmark; both from COMTRADE and weighted by pre-sample firm input/output shares; plus exchange rates and transport costs fitted from US imports data.
definitions.source_location: Section III and Data Appendix section 2

definitions.definition: Start from 2.8 million manufacturing worker-firm-year observations after merging workers, firms and trade. Drop worker-firm-years whose job spell lasts a single year (~200,000 obs); drop workers whose skill level changes in the sample (~35,000 obs); drop firms with fewer than 50 employees and less than DKK 0.6 million in imports (about two manufacturing workers' average annual wages) (~600,000 obs).
definitions.codes: firm size < 50 employees and imports < DKK 0.6m dropped

definitions.definition: Firm identifier from 'Old Firm Statistics' (1995-1999) and 'General Firm Statistics' (1999-2006), combined in FirmStat to track firms across the 1999 break. Employees = number of full-time equivalent workers in the year (FirmStat). Capital stock = value of land, buildings, machines, equipment and inventory (Accounting Statistics register). Gross output (net of taxes) from the VAT register. Firm skill intensity = educational attainment of individual workers in IDA aggregated to the firm via FIDA.

IDA occupation uses the Danish version of ISCO-88, mapped to O*NET via the National Crosswalk Center crosswalk. Non-routine = principal component of O*NET 1.A.1.c.1 (mathematical reasoning), 1.A.2.b.3 (response orientation), 1.A.3.c.3 (gross body coordination), 2.A.1.e (mathematics), 4.A.2.b.2 (thinking creatively), 4.A.2.b.6 (organizing, planning, prioritizing). Routine = 1.A.2.a.2 (manual dexterity), 1.A.2.a.3 (finger dexterity), 1.A.2.b.2 (multilimb coordination), 4.A.2.a.2 (processing information), 4.A.2.a.3 (evaluating compliance with standards).

Displaced workers separate from firms where at least 30% of the initial-year workers are not employed by the firm the following year (gross flows). Offshorers are displaced from firms whose predicted offshoring (first stage) rose at least 10% between predisplacement and displacement year. Sample: manufacturing workers with at least six years tenure in some year 1997-2000, not dying, emigrating or turning 61 in 1995-2006, at firms importing at least DKK 600,000 with 50+ employees.
definitions.source_location: Section VI, footnotes 32-34, Data Appendix section 3

definitions.definition: Actual time in employment since 1964. Union membership and marital status also taken from IDA.

Foreign Trade Statistics Register = Extrastat (non-EU trade, near-complete customs coverage) + Intrastat (intra-EU trade, reported only above an annual value threshold). In 2002 the Intrastat thresholds were DKK 2.5 million for exports and DKK 1.5 million for imports.
definitions.codes: Intrastat threshold 2002: exports DKK 2.5m, imports DKK 1.5m

definitions.definition: Principal-component indices from O*NET: social sciences = 2.C.1 (all subitems), 2.C.6, 2.C.7, 2.C.8, 2.C.9, 2.C.4.e, 2.C.4.f; natural sciences = 2.C.2, 2.C.3, 2.C.5, 2.C.4.b, 2.C.4.c, 2.C.4.d, 2.C.4.g, 2.C.10, 2.A.1.f; communication and language = 4.A.4.a, 2.B.1, 1.A.1.a, 4.C.1.a.4, 4.C.1.b.1, 2.A.1.a-2.A.1.d; on-the-job hazards = 4.C.2.c, 4.C.2.b.1, 4.C.2.e.1.
definitions.codes: ISCO-88; O*NET item IDs as listed

definitions.definition: Ad-valorem shipping cost functions estimated on US data (US Imports of Merchandise for sea and air, 1995-2006; US Transborder Surface Freight data for truck and rail) as functions of weight/value, fuel prices (crude oil; jet fuel for air) and distance, then fitted for Danish firms' exporter-HS6 inputs using pre-sample trade shares and transport-mode shares (pre-sample Danish imports: 42% sea, 20% air, 37% truck, 1% rail).

authors: Søren Leth-Petersen
title: Intertemporal Consumption and Credit Constraints: Does Total Expenditure Respond to an Exogenous Shock to Credit?
summary: The 1992 reform that let Danish homeowners borrow against housing equity provides an exogenous credit shock. Total expenditure responded only modestly on average, with the response concentrated among young households with little liquid wealth, which indicates that credit constraints bind for a minority.
data: Income tax register: taxable income, transfers, final taxes
Wealth tax register: third-party reported assets and liabilities (housing, shares, mortgage deeds, cash, bonds, debt)
Administrative registers on family composition and dwelling characteristics
Danish Family Expenditure Survey (DES) 1994–1996, used to validate the expenditure imputation
variables: Outcome: total household expenditure imputed from income minus change in wealth
Treatment: 1992 credit market reform allowing home equity to be used as collateral for consumption loans
Treatment group: homeowners (renters as comparison/consistency check)
Credit-constraint proxy: low liquid (non-housing) assets in 1991 relative to monthly disposable income
sample_size: 38,486 households, of which 25,275 live in owner-occupied housing (working-paper version)
sample: Households from a 10% random sample of the Danish population, aged 18–75, not self-employed, non-movers observed in all years 1987–1996.

definitions.definition: Total expenditure imputed from tax registers as disposable income (taxable income plus some non-taxable components and transfers, minus final taxes) minus the change in net wealth from the end of one tax year to the end of the next, following Browning and Leth-Petersen (2003); capital gains are not netted out except for housing. Households with negative imputed expenditure are dropped.
definitions.codes: c_t = y_t - dW_t (equation 14), with allowance for housing capital gains

definitions.definition: Third-party reported assets in six pre-reform categories (housing assets at tax-assessed cash value, shares, deposited mortgage deeds, cash holdings, bonds, other assets incl. self-reported non-deposited bonds, ship shares and high-value objects) and total liabilities; mortgage debt is separately available only up to 1993, so only total liabilities are consistent across years. Employer pension funds are not observed.

Alternative splits used in robustness: low liquid assets = liquid assets of at most two months of disposable income in 1991; at most one month of disposable income in both 1990 and 1991; at most one month of disposable income in 1991 and subsequently experiencing an unemployment shock.

The 1992 mortgage reform allowed mortgage loans to finance non-housing purposes, up to 60% of the house value, and extended the maximum maturity from 20 to 30 years; homeowners are treated and renters serve as a consistency check.
Robustness subsamples: renters (separate analysis) and house owners holding no financial assets (no stocks or bonds).

Probit for low-liquid-asset status in 1991 uses: housing equity/house value and its square, ln(house value) and square (owners), ln(gross income) and square, age and square, single, UI membership, size of house and square, labour supply (male, female), self-employed (male, female), education short/medium/long, number of children dummies (1-4). Monetary values in DKK, 1990 prices. Matching with replacement; SEs per Abadie and Imbens (2006).
Highest level of education in the household, grouped into no/low vs medium/high for heterogeneity analysis.

authors: Thais Lærkholm Jensen and Niels Johannesen
title: The Consumption Effects of the 2007–2008 Financial Crisis: Evidence from Households in Denmark
summary: Customers of banks that were hit hard by the crisis cut consumption more than customers of healthier banks. The channel is reduced credit availability: exposed households borrowed less and spent less, which shows how bank distress transmits to the real economy through households.
data: Tax authority third-party reports of all individuals' loan and deposit account balances, linked to bank identity via branch numbers (Nets lists)
Bank balance sheet data from the Danish Central Bank (MFI statistics)
Administrative registers on demographics, education, labour market and income
Income and wealth registers (capital income, social transfers, stock portfolios, pension accounts)
Motor vehicle register and real estate register
variables: Treatment: primary bank's 2007 loan-to-deposit ratio (above vs below median exposure)
Outcome: individual borrowing (loan balances by account)
Outcome: imputed spending = disposable income minus change in net wealth
Outcome: car ownership (motor vehicle register)
Separate analysis: customers of banks that failed 2008–2011
sample_size: around 440,000 individuals, almost 3.5 million individual-years and more than 5.7 million individual-account-years
sample: 25% random sample of non-self-employed Danish residents aged 20–50 in 2007 whose primary bank did not fail during 2008–2011.

definitions.definition: Year-end loan and deposit account balances reported by financial institutions to the tax authorities; the first four digits of each account number identify the bank branch, mapped to bank identity using hand-collected Nets lists of branch id-numbers for each year 2003-2011.
definitions.codes: First four digits of account number = branch id

definitions.definition: If one bank relation in 2007, that bank; if multiple relations but a loan in only one, that bank; if loans in multiple banks, the bank with the largest loan balance; if no loans, the bank with the largest deposit balance. Always a bank, never a mortgage institution.
Individuals ordered by the 2007 loan-to-deposit ratio of their primary bank and split at the median individual: above-median primary bank = exposed (approximately equal numbers in each group).
registers: Danish Central Bank bank balance sheets

definitions.definition: Spending = disposable income minus change in net wealth. Disposable income = total realized income - taxes - interest payments + payments from private pension accounts (net of taxes) + imputed capital gains on stocks (start-of-period stock value times growth in stock price index). Net wealth = market value of securities + savings and checking accounts - mortgage loans - bank debt - other loans; real estate excluded (so spending includes real estate purchases). Main regressions exclude stock owners.
definitions.source_location: Online Appendix Table A1; WP Section 3.2

definitions.definition: Withdrawals (liquidations) from tax-favoured pension savings accounts, which carry a 60% penalty before pension age, used as an indicator of borrowing constraints.
Number of cars owned, indicators for owning at least one and at least two cars, and average car weight, from the auto register (weight and production year of each registered automobile).

Residents 2003-2011 aged 20-50 in 2007, excluding self-employed and individuals whose 2007 primary bank failed in 2008-2011 (analysed separately), 25% random sample (about 440,000 individuals); DKK variables winsorized at 1st and 99th percentiles.
Control: dummy for unemployment spells during 2006-2007; outcome: fraction of the year spent in unemployment.

authors: Steffen Andersen, John Y. Campbell, Kasper Meisner Nielsen and Tarun Ramadorai
title: Sources of Inaction in Household Finance: Evidence from the Danish Mortgage Market
summary: Many Danish households fail to refinance fixed-rate mortgages when it is clearly profitable. A model with inattention and psychological refinancing costs fits the data, and both frictions are stronger for households with less education, income and financial wealth.
data: Loan-level mortgage data for all Danish mortgages from Danmarks Nationalbank (via mortgage bank associations)
Civil Registration System / population register (CPR/BEF) for demographics and household links
Income and wealth data from the Danish Tax Authority (SKAT) (IND/formue)
Education register (UDDA)
variables: Outcome: refinancing of a fixed-rate mortgage in a quarter
Incentive: financial gain from refinancing given coupon and market rates
Structural parameters: probability of inattention and psychological refinancing cost
Household characteristics: age, education, income, housing and financial wealth
sample_size: 2,376,815 household observations (9,351,183 household-quarters); 378,421 refinancings
sample: Danish households holding a single fixed-rate mortgage observed in consecutive years, 2009–2017.

definitions.definition: A refinancing occurs when a household changes from one fixed-rate mortgage to another mortgage (fixed- or adjustable-rate) on the same property; terminations from moves, death or divorce are handled separately as mortgage termination. Annual loan data are expanded to quarters using mortgage issue dates.
A refinancing associated with an increase in mortgage principal of 10% or more.

Interest rate spread = coupon rate on old mortgage minus yield on a newly available mortgage of roughly the same maturity. Threshold from the Agarwal, Driscoll and Laibson (2013) closed form with baseline interest-rate volatility 0.0074 and discount rate 5%; incentive = spread minus threshold. Household-specific mortgage termination probability (from a probit on moves/death/divorce terminations) enters the threshold. Robustness: volatility 0.0037, discount rate 2.5%, constant 10% termination probability, Chen and Ling (1989) thresholds.

'Single' households have only one adult living at the address (~13% of sample); 'Married' households have two legally bound adults, including registered same-sex partnerships. 'Children in family' = children in household; 'Immigrant' = an immigrant in the household; 'Getting married' = change in marital status over the sample; 'Having children' = child born within the last 12 months.

All Danish households with an unchanging number of household members and a single fixed-rate mortgage at the beginning of each year 2010-2017; refinancing measured as a quarterly dummy. Robustness samples exclude cash-out and maturity-extension refinancings, exclude FRM-to-ARM refinancers, or restrict to mortgages over DKK 250,000 with horizon of at least 20 years.

'Financially literate' = a household member has a degree in finance or professional financial-industry training. 'Family financially literate' = non-resident parents, siblings, in-laws or children of the household are financially literate.

Ranks computed each year across all sample households, normalized to [-0.5, 0.5]: age = age of oldest household member; education = years needed to reach the highest education of any household member (12 = high school, 16 = Bachelor's, 18 = Master's, 20 = PhD); income = total taxable household income; financial wealth = cash, bonds, stocks and mutual funds less non-mortgage debt; housing assets = value of properties. Specifications add a nonlinear transform f(x) of each rank.

Probit of a monthly dummy for full prepayment/termination (moving, death, divorce, etc.) on household demographic dummies and rank variables (with nonlinear transforms), fitted on all households with unchanging membership and a fixed-rate mortgage 2010-2017; fitted values feed the ADL threshold.

authors: Annette Alstadsæter, Niels Johannesen and Gabriel Zucman
title: Tax Evasion and Inequality
summary: Matches leaked offshore account data (HSBC Switzerland, Panama Papers) and tax amnesty records to Scandinavian wealth registers. Tax evasion rises steeply with wealth: the top 0.01 percent evade about a quarter of their taxes, which materially raises measured top wealth shares.
data: Leaked HSBC Switzerland client list (Swiss Leaks, 2007) matched to tax records in Denmark, Norway and Sweden
Panama Papers / Mossack Fonseca leak matched to Norwegian and Swedish wealth data (not Denmark)
Tax amnesty voluntary disclosures in Norway and Sweden
Population-wide administrative wealth and income tax records for Norway, Sweden and Denmark
Danish stratified random tax audits by SKAT (tax years 2008, 2010, 2012)
National accounts household wealth totals
variables: Outcome: taxes evaded (share of taxes owed) by wealth group
Ranking variable: household net wealth including imputed pension wealth
Indicator: owning an undeclared HSBC account / Panama Papers shell / amnesty participation
Outcome (event study): reported wealth and income after amnesty
Random-audit detected evasion (domestic evasion)
period: HSBC leak 2006–2007; amnesties since 2006; Danish random audits for tax years 2008, 2010, 2012
sample_size: 520 HSBC households; 165 Panama Papers households; 1,422 amnesty taxpayers in Norway and 6,811 in Sweden; 18,985 randomly audited Danish taxpayers
sample: Scandinavian households appearing in offshore leaks or tax amnesties, ranked in the full population wealth distribution, combined with Danish random audits.

definitions.definition: A household is either a single person aged 20 or above or a married couple, in both cases with dependent children if any; fractiles are defined relative to the total number of households, including those not liable to wealth tax.

100% of national-accounts household wealth at market value distributed to households: all non-financial and financial assets minus debts, including funded pensions, excluding durables and valuables. Pension wealth imputed (40% to wage earners pro rata wage income, 60% to retirees pro rata pension income); unlisted equity imputed by capitalizing unlisted dividends and non-corporate business assets by capitalizing business income. Danish distribution taken from Jakobsen et al. (2018), based on individual wealth records.
definitions.source_location: Section 3.2; Online Appendix A and D

definitions.definition: Households who owned at least one account at HSBC Switzerland (including via shell companies with identified beneficial owners), declared themselves taxable in Scandinavia in 2006 and could be matched to a tax return (2006/2007 records); non-residents excluded; for Denmark all matched households are treated as evaders (about 95% of matched Danish accounts were undeclared).
registers: Leaked HSBC list (Danish tax authority version)

definitions.definition: SKAT stratified random audits for tax years 2008, 2010 and 2012 (18,985 taxpayers; self-employed and complex returns oversampled), every line item examined; main results include all errors; deliberate evaders are those rated 0-2 on SKAT's 0-6 compliance scale. Evasion rate = taxes evaded / (taxes paid + taxes evaded) by wealth group, weighted by audit weights.
definitions.source_location: Section 4 (Random Audit Data); Online Appendix H.1-H.2

authors: Itzik Fadlon and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Family Health Behaviors
summary: A severe health shock to one family member, such as a heart attack or stroke, makes spouses and adult children raise their own preventive behaviour: more check-ups, more preventive medication and lifestyle changes. Responses are sharp, immediate and persistent, and they reflect updating about one's own risk.
data: Prescription Drug Database (LMDB), 1995–2011
Health Insurance Registry (SSR, primary-care and specialist contacts), 1985–2011
National Patient Registry (LPR), inpatient 1980–2011 and outpatient 1994–2011
Cause of Death Registry (DAR)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) for demographics, education and coworker links
Family links (spouses, parents–children) from population registers
variables: Treatment: family member's first heart attack or stroke (non-fatal), or death (fatal shock)
Outcome: statin and other cardiovascular drug take-up
Outcome: preventive care such as GP visits and cholesterol testing
Control group: households experiencing the same shock five years later
Exposure groups: spouses, adult biological children, siblings, in-laws, coworkers
sample_size: Non-fatal shocks, spouses: 20,381 treated and 28,699 control (prime age 25–55), 37,828 treated and 36,392 control (older 55–85); biological children: 63,323 treated and 68,437 control (25–40), 39,783 treated and 32,926 control (40–65)
sample: Family members and close coworkers of all Danish individuals who had a first heart attack or stroke (or died) between 1985 and 2011.

definitions.definition: First-time heart attack or stroke (identified from the National Patient Registry, ICD diagnoses) between 1985 and 2011 where the individual survived the four-year analysis horizon (three years for stepchildren, children-in-law and coworker samples). Household matches based on period t = -1.
Death of a family member between 1985 and 2011, from the Cause of Death Registry (exact death dates and causes).

Treated = individuals whose family member (or peer) had a shock in a calendar year; controls = individuals from the same cohorts whose family member (or peer) had the same shock five years later (Delta=5). Non-fatal sample = households in which a member had a first heart attack or stroke and survived the four-year horizon; death sample = families with a member who died 1985-2011. Alternative control group: exact match cells within calendar year on predicted cardiovascular risk of family members and lagged outcome, controls weighted by representation in cell (about 94% of controls for prime-age spouses never affected).

Cholesterol (blood test) indicators are available only for residents of Greater Copenhagen; drug dosage information (e.g. opioid doses) is excluded for the adult-children sample under the data use agreement, so opioid dose outcomes are estimated only for spouses.
definitions.source_location: Appendix B; Appendix Table 2 and Table 7 notes

definitions.definition: Non-hospital contacts with on-call local doctors or nurses initiated outside regular working hours (8 am to 4 pm).

definitions.variable: Addiction treatment drugs and opioid doses
definitions.definition: Indicator for purchasing nicotine/alcohol dependence medication; prescription opioid consumption measured in WHO defined daily doses (DDD), i.e. prescription day equivalents (spouses only, dosage data excluded for adult children).

definitions.variable: Family circles (spouses, children, siblings, stepchildren, in-laws)
definitions.definition: Spouses = all married and cohabiting couples linked before the shock; adult children only for individuals born after 1960 (when parent links are available); children-in-law = spouses of the adult children of the shocked parent; 'nearby in-laws' = children-in-law living closer than the median distance to the parents-in-law; former spouses = linked by marriage or cohabitation in period -5 but not in period -1.
definitions.source_location: Appendix Table 1 notes; Appendix Tables 2, 10 notes

definitions.definition: Workplaces defined by physical establishment units in matched employer-employee data. Shocked individuals who in pre-shock periods t=-4 to t=-1 worked at workplaces with employment at or below the sample's 25th percentile (about 20 employees); their coworkers in a similar occupation class with an age gap of 5 years or less; coworkers who are also family members excluded. Robustness perturbs the 5-year age gap and the workplace-size cutoff.
definitions.codes: workplace size <= 25th percentile (~20 employees); age gap <= 5 years
definitions.source_location: Appendix Table 1 notes; Appendix Tables 9-10 notes

definitions.definition: Probit for the one-year probability of a first heart attack or stroke, estimated on the whole population aged 20-90 in 1994-2014, with age fixed effects, gender, hypertension and diabetes status (from lagged indicators of condition-specific medication), year fixed effects and education; lagged fitted probability used as individual risk.
Severity of the family shock measured by the number of hospitalization days (also split at the median).

authors: Anna Piil Damm and Christian Dustmann
title: Does Growing Up in a High Crime Neighborhood Affect Youth Criminal Behavior?
summary: Refugees arriving between 1986 and 1998 were allocated to municipalities quasi-randomly. Boys placed in neighbourhoods with a higher share of youth criminals were later more likely to be convicted, especially for violent crime, which identifies a causal neighbourhood effect on criminal behaviour.
data: Central Police Register: crime charges and convictions for the full population
Administrative registers: age, residence, parents' IDs, country of origin, immigrant status and date of immigration
Educational Institution Register and surveys
Municipality-level crime and socio-economic measures built from the registers
variables: Treatment: youth crime conviction rate (share of 15–25-year-olds convicted) in the municipality of assignment
Identification: quasi-random assignment of refugee families under the 1986–1998 spatial dispersal policy
Outcome: criminal conviction and charge between ages 15 and 21 (by crime type)
Longer-term outcomes: education and employment
Controls: family background, country of origin, municipality characteristics at assignment
sample_size: 4,425 children
sample: Refugee children from eight source countries who arrived in Denmark before age 15 with at least one refugee parent between 1986 and 1998 and are observed to age 21.

definitions.definition: Court ruling that the suspect is guilty of the charge, signalled by a sentence (fine, conditional withdrawal of charge, or suspended or unsuspended prison sentence); 'not guilty' if a not-guilty verdict was recorded or the indictment dropped. Convictions are linked to the start date of committing the offence; all charges and convictions are observed even after deletion from the criminal record.

Mapping of Central Police Register categories: (1) violence = all sexual assault convictions (rape, offence against decency, sexual offence against children under 12, other) and all violence convictions (violence against public authority, simple violence, threats, manslaughter, other); (2) property = document fraud, burglary in bank or shop, shoplifting etc., vandalism, fraud, other property offences; (3) drug crimes = sale of narcotics (penal code) and all Drugs Act offences; (4) other = perjury, privacy violation and defamation, negligent manslaughter (road accident), other penal code offences, Arms Act, tax acts and other special acts (gambling and trade laws, tax and duty law). Traffic Act offences (incl. drunk driving, speeding) excluded.
definitions.codes: Penal code, Traffic Act (excluded), Drugs Act, Arms Act, tax and other special acts

definitions.definition: Number of convictions for offences (except traffic offences) committed in age range a1-a2 (15-21, 15-17, 18-21); type-specific counts by category j.

definitions.variable: Youth crime conviction rate of municipality
definitions.definition: Share of individuals aged 15-25 living in the municipality convicted of an offence (except traffic) committed in that calendar year; overall crime conviction rate = same share among all residents; type-specific rates for j = violent, property, drugs, other. Computed for 1986-1998.

Individual who immigrated 1986-1998 from Lebanon, Iran, Iraq, Somalia, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Afghanistan or Ethiopia and, at the year of receiving a residence permit, was not married to someone from a non-refugee sending country or to a refugee-country immigrant who arrived at least one year earlier; former Yugoslavia excluded.

Full sample: children of immigrants from Iraq, Iran, Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Lebanon, Ethiopia, Afghanistan or Somalia who immigrated before age 15 in 1986-1998, at most one year after their refugee parent(s), and turn 21 in 1986-2006 (5,615 individuals). Balanced sample (4,425) excludes those who emigrated before 21 (975) and those living in Denmark at 21 but not observed annually in registers at ages 15-21 (215).
Relative poverty rate = share of adults in the municipality with equivalence-scaled disposable household income below 50% of the national median equivalence-scaled disposable household income.

Police officers per 1,000 inhabitants = detectives plus uniformed officers employed in the police district (annual police reports 1986-1999); crime detection rate = annual number of charges divided by annual number of reported crimes in the municipality or police district.

Reported crimes in a calendar year divided by inhabitants of the municipality (or police district); reported violent crimes per 10,000 inhabitants defined analogously. Source: 'Statistiske Efterretninger om Social Sikring og Retsvaesen' (1986-1998); inhabitants from Statistikbanken BEF1A.
Number of immigrants and descendants living in the municipality divided by inhabitants.

Pupils/teacher ratio = average number of pupils in a normal class in the municipality in a school year; weekly teacher wage hours per pupil. Sources: 'Folkeskolen i de enkelte kommuner' and 'Folkeskolen i tal' (Ministry of Education, 1989/90-1998/99).

Assignment year = first year of receipt of residence permit; source country dummies; nuclear family = living in a two-parent household; single parent = single-parent household; years of education before immigration constructed from the education code of the highest degree attained before immigration; number of persons in the household minus the number of parents living in it.

authors: Christian Dustmann, Kristine Vasiljeva and Anna Piil Damm
title: Refugee Migration and Electoral Outcomes
summary: Using the quasi-random refugee dispersal policy, refugee allocation raised vote shares for anti-immigration parties in rural municipalities and lowered them in the largest urban municipalities. Effects are strongest where refugees are few relative to natives and where crime rises after allocation.
data: Population register (BEF) to identify refugees and municipality of initial placement
Income, education, labour force and socio-economic registers for 1985 municipality characteristics
Statistics Denmark municipal and parliamentary election results
Danish National Election Survey (DNES) 1990–98
variables: Outcome: change in vote share of anti-immigration parties (Progress Party, Danish People's Party)
Treatment: cumulative share of allocated refugees in municipal population (1986 base)
Source of variation: Danish Spatial Dispersal Policy allocation of refugees 1986–98
Heterogeneity: urban vs rural municipality
Controls: 1985 municipality characteristics
period: Refugee allocation 1986–1998; parliamentary elections 1990–98 and municipal elections 1989–97
sample_size: 275 municipalities (550 observations for parliamentary elections); 76,673 refugees allocated 1986–98
sample: All 275 Danish municipalities observed across election cycles during the 1986–98 refugee dispersal policy.

definitions.definition: Refugees received in 1986-1998 who initially received a permanent residence permit, from Lebanon, Iran, Iraq, Somalia, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Ethiopia, or without citizenship; municipality of initial placement identified from the population register. Refugees from former Yugoslavia (special 1993 policy) and family-reunified spouses/children arriving more than 12 months after the refugee are excluded.

Cumulative number of refugees allocated to the municipality from 1986 until the year preceding each election, divided by the municipal population at the beginning of 1986; regressor is its change between consecutive election years (RS_it).

definitions.variable: Vote share changes by party group
definitions.definition: Percentage-point change in municipal vote shares between election years t-1 and t (1989-98: three parliamentary and three municipal elections) for anti-immigration parties (Progress Party and Danish People's Party), centre-right, centre-left and small centre parties; seat shares also computed.
Municipalities above the 95th percentile of municipal population size are labelled urban.

Share of adults whose disposable income as a household member is above 50% of the Danish median (one of several 1985 municipal characteristics with immigrant share, mean log gross earnings, crime rate, church-tax payers, unemployment rate, tertiary education share, immigrant welfare dependency).
registers: Population, education, labour force and socio-economic registers

definitions.definition: Being unemployed or not in the labour force at ages 18-65.

authors: Kristoffer B. Hvidberg, Claus T. Kreiner and Stefanie Stantcheva
title: Social Positions and Fairness Views on Inequality
summary: Links a large survey to income registers to compare perceived and actual positions in the income distribution and within reference groups (co-workers, neighbours, schoolmates). People misperceive their rank, fairness views depend on the perceived gap to others, and showing people their true position changes their views.
data: Custom online survey with randomised information treatment (February–March 2019), sent via Digital Post and linked on CPR
Income registers / tax returns (IND) for respondents and all reference group members
Population register (BEF) for cohort, municipality, neighbours and siblings
Education register (UDDA) incl. school attended at age 15 for schoolmates
Workplace links from employer-employee data (IDA) for co-workers and sector
Parents' income positions via family links
variables: Outcome: perceived own income position (rank) in each reference group
Outcome: perceived P50 and P95 incomes in reference groups
Outcome: fairness views on inequality within reference groups
Actual income rank computed from register data
Treatment: randomised information on actual income position
Events: unemployment, promotion and income shocks from income histories
sample_size: 9,415 respondents (from 50,100 invited)
sample: Danish-born people born 1969–1973 (aged 45–50), randomly drawn by Statistics Denmark, who completed the survey.

definitions.variable: Income concept for actual and perceived rank
definitions.definition: Income earned in 2017 as on the tax statement: wage income plus self-employment income plus taxable benefits and transfers (mainly UI benefits, disability benefits and social assistance); excludes capital income, deductions and taxes. Averages 96.0% of Statistics Denmark total income.
definitions.codes: inc_reg compared with perindkialt_13 (total personal income)

definitions.definition: Percentile rank of the respondent's register income within each reference group, computed from tax-return income of all members of the group.

Cohort: born the same year. Gender: same birth year and gender. Municipality: same birth year and current municipality. Education: same birth year and education level (basic, upper secondary, vocational, short-cycle higher, bachelor, master/PhD) using DISCED. Sector: same birth year and same sector (construction, real estate, business services, finance and insurance, trade and transport, manufacturing, information and communication, culture, agriculture, public work) based on DB07.
definitions.codes: DISCED (ISCED-based) education levels; DB07 sector codes

definitions.definition: For apartment dwellers, people aged 25-65 living in the same stairwell; for house dwellers, people aged 25-65 living on the same road. Neighbour links incl. road length were created by Statistics Denmark's GEO team; neighbour car and house value ranks use wealth registers.
People born the same year who attended the same school in the year they turned 15.
People working in the same workplace, defined as a single address entity (each location of a multi-location firm is a separate workplace).

Three or more months of unemployment in at least one year of the shock period 2012-2017, among respondents with no such shock in the pre-shock period 2008-2011 and in the workforce for the whole ten-year period.
Starting to receive disability insurance benefits, without having received them before, in one of the years 2012-2017 according to IDA.

At least one emergency room visit or hospital visit by GP referral in 2012-2017, excluding visits due to congenital diseases, pregnancy or routine checks; sample excludes those with such a shock in 2008-2011.
Switching from a job as a regular employee in the pre-shock period (2008-2011) to a management position in 2012-2017; in the code a manager is DISCO first digit 1.
Individuals born 1969-1973 invited via Digital Post; main analysis uses 9,415 respondents who completed the survey (Feb-Mar 2019), linked to registers on CPR.

authors: Henrik Kleven, Camille Landais and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Children and Gender Inequality: Evidence from Denmark
summary: Event studies around the birth of the first child show mothers' earnings fall about 20 percent relative to fathers' in the long run, through hours, participation and wage rates. These child penalties now account for most of the remaining gender earnings gap and are transmitted across generations through mothers' own upbringing.
data: Full-population Danish administrative registers linked by personal ID (earnings, labour supply, occupation, firm, education), 1980–2013
Family and generational links (population register)
ATP pension contributions as third-party measure of hours worked
Additional administrative data back to 1964 for intergenerational analysis
Matched employer-employee data (firm family-friendliness)
International Social Survey Program (ISSP) 2002 for gender attitudes
variables: Treatment/event: birth of first child (event time relative to first birth)
Outcome: earnings, labour force participation, hours worked (ATP), wage rates
Outcome: occupation rank, sector, firm family-friendliness
Child penalty: percentage drop of women's relative to men's earnings
Intergenerational: maternal grandparents' labour supply
period: 1980–2013 (with data back to 1964 for intergenerational transmission); first births 1985–2003
sample_size: around 470,000 births or 15,040,000 individual-year observations
sample: Danish parents with a first child born 1985–2003 who are observed alive and resident in Denmark from 5 years before to 10 years after the birth.

definitions.definition: For the OECD-comparable gender gap series, full-time workers aged 16-64 are identified using the ATP hours measure; earnings and participation gaps use the whole population aged 16-64, hours and wage gaps are conditional on participation.
Earnings divided by the ATP hours measure, for those who are working (conditional on participation).

Event study around year of first birth (t=0), event time -5 to +10 with t=-1 omitted, separately by gender with age and year dummies, estimated in levels; penalty P_t = (alpha_men_t - alpha_women_t) / E[counterfactual women's outcome | t], the percentage by which women fall behind men due to children.

Treatment = balanced panel of individuals with first child 1985-2003 observed in a 15-year window around the first birth; control = balanced panel of never-parents with a placebo birth in 1985-2003 observed in the same window.

definitions.variable: Never-parent control group with placebo births
definitions.definition: Separately by sex, a probit for zero lifetime fertility is estimated on non-truncated cohorts 1955-1973 with dummies for own-cohort income quartile, own-cohort wealth quartile, spouse-cohort wealth quartile, education length/degree (8 categories), decade of birth of maternal grandmother and of maternal grandfather, and region. For each cohort born after 1973, among those childless by 2013 the individuals with the highest predicted probability are designated never-parents so that their share equals the 1955-1973 average zero-fertility share. Placebo age at first child is drawn from a log-normal distribution fitted within birth cohort x education cells (for post-1973 cohorts the mean is extrapolated by a linear trend, variance held fixed).

Occupation ranked in five levels: unskilled labour, skilled labour, white-collar work (low level), white-collar work (high level) and top manager, an ordering consistent with average earnings or wage rates by occupation; separate indicator for being top manager.

Share of women with children below age 15 in the firm's workforce (excluding the woman's own first child when it arrives); outcome is the percentile rank in the distribution of firm family friendliness.
Indicator for working in the Danish public sector (no register code given).

Relative labour supply of (maternal or paternal) grandparents based on cumulated hours worked 1964-79 from ATP pension contributions, in quintiles. Robustness controls: grandparents' within-generation wealth-rank quintiles, region of residence, length and field of education of grandmother and grandfather (22 dummies), and parents' total number of children measured in 2014.
definitions.source_location: Figure A.IX-A.X notes; Table A.II notes

definitions.definition: Women with first child 1985-2003 and completed fertility of two or three when last observed in 2013; unbalanced panel with the longest available window (up to t=28 after first birth); event-time dummies around the third birth instrumented with the sex mix of the first two children.

authors: Mette Foged and Giovanni Peri
title: Immigrants' Effect on Native Workers: New Analysis on Longitudinal Data
summary: Refugee-country immigration into Danish municipalities from 1991 to 2008 pushed less-educated native workers toward more complex, less manual occupations. Native wages and employment rose rather than fell, and effects were positive even for low-skilled natives who moved across firms.
data: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Occupation codes linked to O*NET task intensities (manual, communication, cognitive)
Full population registers for municipality immigrant shares
Refugee spatial dispersal policy 1986–1998 (initial refugee allocation by municipality)
variables: Treatment: share of refugee-country immigrants in the municipality of work
Instrument: immigrant inflow predicted from the 1986–1998 refugee dispersal policy
Outcome: occupational complexity index (O*NET-based)
Outcome: log hourly wage (incl. mandatory pension contributions)
Outcome: fraction of year worked; occupational mobility
Controls: age, experience, tenure, education, marital status, region, industry
sample_size: 1,864,027 observations of employed low-skilled natives, 1995–2008, in the fixed-effects panel (20 percent random sample of natives); balanced-panel difference-in-differences regressions use 71,053 natives employed in 1994
sample: Danish-born individuals aged 18–65, not in school or permanently disabled, focusing on low-skilled (non-college) natives, across 97 municipalities.

definitions.definition: Immigrants (foreign-born) from eight refugee-sending countries that generated substantial refugee inflows 1994-2008: Yugoslavia, Somalia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Iran and Lebanon (Bosnia included in actual inflow but not in the instrument).

S_mt = F_mt / P_mt, the stock of employed refugee-country immigrants divided by total employment in municipality of work m in year t; computed on the full population (outcomes use a 20 percent random sample of natives).

For t > 1994, imputed working-age population from refugee country c in municipality m = s_cm x F_ct, where s_cm is the share of new immigrants from c first settling in m during 1986-1998 under the dispersal policy and F_ct is the national working-age population from c; summed over refugee countries and divided by municipality working-age population in 1988. Also used to define top and bottom quartile exposure municipalities for the difference-in-differences.

O*NET abilities merged to Danish registers at the four-digit ISCO-88 level via the National Crosswalk Center crosswalk. Following Ottaviano, Peri and Wright (2013), abilities are averaged into communication, cognitive (analytical) and manual intensity indices, each standardized to [0,1] as the occupation's centile in the 2000 ranking. Complexity = ln((Communication + Analytical)/Manual).

Occupations are reported by firms using the Danish version of ISCO-88. Missing or invalid ISCO-88 values are replaced by the next value within the worker-firm match if that value is also the most frequent ISCO-88 code within the match; authors note this (and weak incentives for firms to update codes) may understate within-firm job mobility.

Log hourly wage of native worker including mandatory pension contributions, deflated by the Danish CPI; since pension payments are available only from 1995, wages net of pension contributions are used when pre-1995 data are included. Observed only for those employed at end of November.
Equals one for a full-time employee throughout the year; for part-time and/or part-year employment, the share of the regular working year spent at work.

Event-study regressions use a strongly balanced panel of low-skilled (and separately high-skilled) natives employed in 1994; 'cohort' specifications fix controls and municipality at 1994 values (SEs clustered by 1994 municipality), 'area' specifications use actual values (SEs clustered by actual municipality).
97 municipalities identifiable consistently 1988-2008, merging Frederiksberg and Copenhagen; exposure measured by municipality of work (DiD exposure by 1994 municipality of residence).

Labour market experience = cumulative employment in years since first joining the labour force; tenure = time elapsed since hiring in the current establishment; low tenure = below sample average of 4.35 years in the establishment as of 1994.

authors: Itzik Fadlon and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Family Labor Supply Responses to Severe Health Shocks: Evidence from Danish Administrative Records
summary: Compares households hit by a fatal versus a non-fatal health shock at the same time. After a spouse's death the surviving spouse raises labour supply to self-insure, while after a non-fatal shock spouses reduce labour supply to care for the patient. Children of the household adjust less.
data: Cause of Death Registry
National Patient Registry (LPR) hospitalisation records with ICD diagnoses
Income and transfer registers (earnings, government transfers, pension and annuity payouts, capital income), 1980–2011
Third-party reported liquid wealth balances, 1984–2011
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), incl. ATP-based full-/part-time employment
Household linkages of spouses and cohabiting partners (population registers)
variables: Treatment: spousal death (fatal health shock) or first non-fatal heart attack/stroke
Control group: households experiencing the same shock a few years later
