title: Micro versus Macro Labor Supply Elasticities: The Role of Dynamic Returns to Effort
summary: Builds a model in which effort today raises earnings tomorrow, so responses to taxes are delayed and mediated by job switches. Danish administrative data confirm the model's life-cycle predictions for earnings and hours, and a quasi-experimental design based on job switchers finds a long-run earnings elasticity around 0.5, against a short-run elasticity of about 0.2.
data: Linked administrative registers on earnings, occupation (DISCO), firm and demographics, full population
Employer-employee matched data (firm x occupation job cells)
ATP pension contribution-based hours measure (1980–2018)
Monthly uncapped hours measure (from 2008)
Income tax records (2009 tax reform variation)
variables: Outcome: earnings (log earnings changes)
Treatment: 2009 tax reform change in marginal net-of-tax rate
Instrument: simulated net-of-tax rate change at baseline income
Mediator: job switches (firm x occupation cell), incl. mass-layoff switches
Outcome: hours worked
sample_size: N = 2,501,126 and 2,428,411 in the main elasticity regressions (Table 1)
sample: Full Danish population; tax-reform analysis uses taxpayers with baseline income between 250,000 and 1,000,000 DKK.

definitions.definition: Hours inferred from mandatory ATP pension contributions, which employers pay based on a binned measure of hours; for monthly-paid workers annual contributions depend on monthly hours in four bins, giving 37 annual hours bins. Capped at full time in all 12 months.
Uncapped hours worked for all workers at monthly level, available from 2008; used where precise hours variation is needed (aggregated to quarters in the promotion event study).

definitions.variable: Job (firm x occupation cell) and job switch
definitions.definition: Job is a firm x occupation cell; a switcher moves between firm x occupation cells after the reform. Occupations use DISCO-08 from 2010 (563 occupations), DISCO-88 1991-2009 (372) bridged with the Humlum (2021) crosswalk, and an older Danish classification before 1991 (299). Switches where more than 50% of an individual's coworkers move to the same job cell in the same year are dropped.
definitions.codes: DISCO-08; DISCO-88; pre-1991 Danish occupation codes

definitions.definition: Mass layoffs are layoffs in which firms with at least 20 employees reduce their workforce by at least 30% in a single year; switchers are workers who move firm following such a layoff. Used in an event study of log earnings vs a linear pre-layoff trend.
definitions.codes: firm size >= 20 employees; workforce reduction >= 30% within one year

definitions.definition: Total labour compensation, including contributions to employer-administered retirement savings plans; outcome is the log change between 2008 and 2010 (placebo 2006-2008).

definitions.variable: Reform treatment and simulated net-of-tax rate instrument
definitions.definition: Treatment assigned by pre-reform baseline taxable income (labour income, transfers, pensions, alimony and certain capital income) in bins relative to the 2009 reform threshold (around the 70th percentile). The instrument is the simulated log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate from tax code changes, holding income at baseline (Gruber-Saez). Baseline sample: taxpayers with baseline income 250,000-1,000,000 DKK.
Within-firm switch to an occupation cell whose median earnings are at least 10% higher (robustness 5% and 20%); promoted workers matched to unpromoted co-workers in the same firm.

definitions.variable: Occupational rank / top vs bottom occupations
definitions.definition: Occupation cells (6-digit occupation codes) ranked by mean wage earnings; for top/bottom occupations the ranking is computed among workers aged 45-50 (mean, P10 and P90 of wage earnings reported per cell). Occupational rank used in balance checks orders occupation cells by their mean earnings.
definitions.source_location: Online Appendix, Table A.1 and Figure A.6 notes

definitions.definition: Firm fixed effects from an AKM model log z_it = alpha_i + psi_J(i,t) + X_it beta + nu_it, with controls for year, age and tenure-in-current-firm dummies, estimated on pre-reform data 2002-2005 for firms with at least 10 employees; estimated firm effects merged onto the 2009 tax-reform sample to measure changes in firm premia for firm switchers.
definitions.source_location: Online Appendix, Section C and Figure A.9

definitions.definition: Validation measure of hours: actual, uncapped hours worked from the Danish component of the EU Labour Force Survey, compared with the administrative ATP pension-based hours measure; the survey measure is much noisier, especially at the top.
Count of job (firm x occupation cell) switches between ages 20 and 50 in a balanced panel of workers observed at every age 20-50, split by earnings percentile at age 50 (top 10%, top 1%, bottom 50%).
Robustness controls: dummies for age, gender, marital status and number of children, alone or combined with initial job-cell fixed effects (baseline uses job-cell fixed effects only).

authors: N. Meltem Daysal, Hui Ding, Maya Rossin-Slater and Hannes Schwandt
title: Germs in the Family: The Short- and Long-Term Consequences of Intrahousehold Disease Spread
summary: Shows that infant younger siblings are hospitalised for respiratory conditions two to three times as often as their older siblings were, because preschool-aged children bring disease home. Combining birth order with local variation in respiratory disease prevalence, early-life exposure lowers younger siblings' later earnings and education and worsens chronic respiratory and mental health.
data: National Patient Register (LPR)
Medical Birth Register (MFR)
Population register (BEF)
Register-Based Labour Force Statistics (RAS)
Income Statistics Register (IND)
Education Register (UDDA)
Academic Achievement Register (9th grade test scores)
Psychiatric Central Research Register (PCRR)
Health Insurance Register (Sygesikringsregisteret)
Childcare enrollment data
National Child Database (breastfeeding)
variables: Outcome: acute respiratory hospitalizations in the first year of life
Treatment: birth order (second-born vs first-born) interacted with municipality respiratory disease exposure index
Outcome: earnings, labour force participation and income rank at ages 18–32
Outcome: high school and college completion; 9th grade test scores
Outcome: chronic respiratory and mental healthcare use
sample_size: 1,230,180 children
sample: First- and second-born singleton siblings born in Denmark 1981–2017, at least 11 months apart, in 91 municipalities.

definitions.variable: Acute respiratory hospitalizations (first year of life)
definitions.definition: Number of inpatient hospitalizations in the first year of life (also split into first and second six months) with a primary diagnosis of an acute respiratory condition, from the National Patient Register (1981-2018).
definitions.codes: ICD-8 starting 46, 47, 48, 490, 079, 783; ICD-10 starting J (excluding J4) or B974

definitions.definition: Hospitalizations for respiratory syncytial virus, measurable only for cohorts born 1994 or later (ICD-10).
Inpatient visits with a primary diagnosis of a chronic respiratory condition (e.g. asthma, COPD), studied at ages 16-26.

Visits to psychiatric hospitals (inpatient, outpatient, ED from the Psychiatric Central Research Register) and to private psychiatric clinics (Health Insurance Register reimbursements, identified by physician specialty codes), at extensive and intensive margins, ages 16-26 (data 1997-2018).

Monthly number of acute respiratory hospitalizations per 100 children aged 13-71 months in the child's municipality of residence (2007 municipality structure, via crosswalk), excluding the child's own older sibling if aged 13-71 months, summed over the 12 months of the child's first year of life (also separate indices for months 1-6 and 7-12).
definitions.codes: Acute respiratory ICD codes as above

definitions.definition: From all 2,278,868 children born 1981-2017: drop one-child families; keep first- and second-born singletons only; require birth spacing of at least 11 months; require known municipality of birth in municipalities averaging at least 1,000 children aged 13-71 months (91 municipalities kept); drop missing parental controls and keep complete pairs. Final sample 1,230,180 children.

Indicator equal to 1 if in the labour force (employed or unemployed searching) and 0 if out of the labour force, based on tax-record labour market status as of November of the preceding year; ages 18-32.

definitions.variable: Wages, gross income and income rank
definitions.definition: Wages among the employed and gross personal income including government transfers, in 2010 USD, winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles; income rank is the percentile of gross personal income within the full Danish population of the same birth cohort and age; ages 18-32.

definitions.variable: Education attainment and 9th grade test scores
definitions.definition: Indicators for high school and college graduation by ages 18-32 from highest completed schooling; 9th grade Danish (reading) and mathematics scores (2001-2019) standardized within subject and test year.

authors: Katrine Jakobsen, Thomas H. Jørgensen and Hamish Low
title: Fertility and Family Labor Supply
summary: Uses the 2009 Danish tax reform to show that higher net-of-tax wages for women reduce fertility while higher wages for men raise it. A life-cycle model of couples choosing the timing and number of children, estimated on register data, implies that allowing fertility to adjust raises women's labour supply responsiveness substantially and that human capital depreciation around births drives much of the long-run gender wage gap.
data: Monthly payroll records (BFL/eIndkomst)
Annual income tax data (IND)
Population and family register (BEF), family definitions and parent links
Education register (UDDA)
Labour market experience from ATP payments
Parental leave spell register (OF)
variables: Outcome: fertility (births)
Treatment: 2009–2018 tax reform changes in marginal net-of-tax wage rate
Outcome: labour market participation, part-time and full-time work from pay-slip hours
Outcome: annual labour income
Control: education (high vs less skilled), labour market experience
sample_size: 10,851,444 individual-year observations (estimation sample); 2,531,181 (tax sample)
sample: Danish individuals aged 25–60 with an opposite-sex partner, not students, self-employed, retired or on disability pension; tax sample restricted to cohabiting or married women aged 25–40.

definitions.variable: Labour market participation, part-time and full-time work
definitions.definition: Participation means at least 481 annual hours (e.g. 37 hours for 13 weeks) on BFL pay slips together with annual income of at least 50,000 DKK; part time is 481-1,664 annual hours; full time is more than 1,664 hours. Monthly hours and income are scaled down by the share of the month registered on parental leave in the OF register.

12-month sum of monthly labour income from BFL pay slips, by calendar year for age profiles and centred on the birth month for event-study moments (e.g. income from January-February before a March birth counts as year -1); excludes income registered while on parental leave; deflated by CPI, in 1000 DKK. Estimation sample 2010-2018.
Personal income from annual tax data: labour income from wage work, profits from own firms and labour market transfers; deflated by CPI.

Partners follow Statistics Denmark's family definition, including married and cohabiting couples; cohabitants are two adults at the same address registered as parents to a child, or two opposite-sex adults with an age difference under 15 years at the same address. Constructed from EFALLE in BEF; couple age is the woman's age. Estimation sample keeps couples with at most five years age difference.
High skilled if at least 180 months of education (at least a bachelor's degree), measured as the highest degree earned in the sample period; less skilled otherwise.
Statistics Denmark's experience measure based on accumulated mandatory ATP pension payments, which depend on hours worked; part-time employment counts as 2/3 of full time.
Individuals aged 25-60 with an opposite-sex partner; observations dropped if mainly student, self-employed, retired or on disability pension, based on main activity at end of November.

Four-year mechanical change log(1 - tau_{t+4}(z_t)) - log(1 - tau_t(z_t)) in the marginal net-of-tax rate, holding income and characteristics at year-t values, computed with a Danish tax simulator; used to instrument own and partner net-of-tax rate changes and virtual income. Restricted to couples where both have personal income of 50,000-600,000 DKK in the base year. Outcome is the 4-year difference in number of children born.
Bank deposits, bonds, stocks and property net of loans and mortgages at end of year; registered property values raised by 10% (following Leth-Petersen 2010); deflated by CPI, in 1000 DKK.

definitions.variable: Child linkage and age of children
definitions.definition: Children and their ages are linked to parents through the parent identifiers in BEF; almost all children can be linked to a mother.

Two samples: the BFL estimation sample of all individuals aged 25-60 with partners, 2010-2018; and the tax sample of women aged 25-40 with partners, 2004-2018 (used with personal income PERINDKP). Both split by less skilled vs high skilled.

authors: Christian Dustmann and Rasmus Landersø
title: Child's Gender, Young Fathers' Crime, and Spillover Effects in Criminal Behavior
summary: Uses the gender of a first-born child as a natural experiment for young fathers in Denmark. Having a son rather than a daughter lowers the father's subsequent criminal behaviour, and the reduction spills over to the father's peers and later to the child, which identifies both a direct parenting response and network effects in crime.
data: Birth register (child's gender, parent links)
Population register (BEF) for demographics and family links
Central Police Register crime data (charges and convictions)
Victim register (from 2001)
Income, education and occupation registers
Residential register with neighbourhood classification
variables: Outcome: young father's crime convictions and charges
Treatment: first child is a son vs a daughter
Spillover outcome: crime of male peers in the father's neighbourhood
Peer group: males within ±3 years of father's age in the same neighbourhood
Outcome: neighbourhood crime victimisation
sample_size: 2,803 first-time fathers aged 20 or younger; 101,132 male peers in 2,114 neighbourhoods
sample: Danish men who fathered their first child at age 20 or younger between 1991 and 2004, plus male peers in their neighbourhoods.

definitions.definition: Charges or convictions for offences against the criminal code from the Central Police Register, excluding traffic offences; convictions (court rulings of guilt) are the preferred measure. Charges and convictions are dated by the date the crime was committed (exact crime dates available from 1990); records are observed even after deletion from the individual's criminal record.

Property crime: theft, fencing, aggravated vandalism, fraud, burglary, forgery, economic crimes. Violent crime: simple violence (assault), severe or life-threatening violence, threats, violence against or obstructing a public servant, failure to help a person in danger, coercion, attempted murder or homicide. Other crime: drug possession and sale, possession of weapons/explosives, false testimony, sexual crimes.
definitions.source_location: Footnote 8; online Table A1 (code breakdown, not read)

definitions.definition: Males who father their first child at age 20 or younger, children born 1991-2004 (birth and demographic registers), with information on both parents from the birth for up to 5 subsequent years, matched uniquely to a neighbourhood; treatment is the first child being a son. Fathers in neighbourhoods with more than one young father having a first child in the same year are excluded.

Neighbourhoods follow the classification documented in Damm and Schultz-Nielsen (2008), constructed in 2004, linked to individuals through anonymised home address identifiers in the residential register; the largest and smallest 5% of neighbourhoods are excluded from most analyses.

Peers are all males within +/-3 years of the focal father's age living in the father's neighbourhood on January 1 of the year the child is born (alternatively all males aged 14-25 at the birth), regardless of later moves; the father and his family members are excluded. Peer crime is their convictions/charges.

Based on individuals who report having been the victim of a crime (register available from 2001); victim sample includes all individuals living in the father's neighbourhood at the time of the birth, counting the number of victims in each neighbourhood.

authors: Christopher Taber and Rune Vejlin
title: Estimation of a Roy/Search/Compensating Differential Model of the Labor Market
summary: Combines a Roy model, search frictions, compensating differentials and on-the-job human capital accumulation in one framework, establishes what is non-parametrically identified, and estimates it on Danish matched data. Pre-market skills account for most wage variation, while preferences for non-wage job attributes and search frictions matter greatly for turnover and for which jobs workers choose.
data: Weekly labour market spell data built from Statistics Denmark registers (all individuals aged 15–74)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) with hourly wage measure
Danish Work Environment Cohort Study surveys (1995 and 2000) on reasons for job separation
variables: Outcome: log hourly wage (detrended)
Job-to-job transitions between establishments (revealed preference)
Employment and non-employment spell durations
Worker skill/education group and labour market experience
Decomposition of wage variance into skill, search, compensating differential and human capital components
sample_size: 2,969,454 workers, 25,630,532 spells and 467,983 establishments (estimation sample)
sample: Danish workers after labour market entry and up to age 55, followed in weekly spell data across establishments, 1985–2003.

definitions.definition: Weekly spell data 1985-2003 for all individuals aged 15-74 with states employed, unemployed, self-employed, retired and non-participation. Unemployment = receiving unemployment insurance benefits or social assistance; non-participation is the residual (not observed in any register). Unemployment and non-participation are aggregated into non-employment.
registers: Weekly spell data (built from Statistics Denmark registers)

definitions.definition: Hourly wage measure of Lund and Vejlin (2015), which improves on IDA's annual average hourly wage for the job held in the last week of November; log wages are detrended by gender-education groups conditional on experience.

Job types are establishments (not firms). Statistics Denmark's establishment identifier is the same across years if one of three criteria is met: same owner and industry; same owner and workforce; or same workforce and either same address or same industry. A job is an employment spell within an establishment.

Transition between two establishments with a very short intermediate non-employment spell: non-employment spells of 2 weeks or less are allocated to the first employment spell; non-employment spells of 12 weeks or less between jobs at the same establishment are overwritten as employment (recalls). Transitions to/from establishments with missing ID and from closing or mass-layoff establishments are ignored.
Mass layoff: establishment has more than 15 workers in year t and less than 30 percent of them left in year t+1. Closing: establishment no longer observed in the data.

From the Danish Work Environment Cohort Study (1995 and 2000), whether the job spell in November 5 years earlier ended due to the employer or the employee; matched to register data to form a moment identifying the probability of an immediate offer after job destruction.

Workers censored after age 55 and when entering retirement or self-employment; spells before labour market entry (time of highest completed education, not observed in education later, or age 19) dropped; workers with errors in education information or gaps in spell histories (e.g. missing IDA year) dropped.

authors: Benjamin U. Friedrich and Martin B. Hackmann
title: The Returns to Nursing: Evidence from a Parental-Leave Program
summary: A Danish parental-leave programme offering up to a year off per child aged 0 to 8 induced a nurse shortage that hospitals and nursing homes could not replace. Nurse employment fell by 15 percent in hospitals and 10 percent in nursing homes, 30-day readmissions of heart attack patients rose, and nursing home mortality increased sharply.
data: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) for health workers, plants and industries
Population register (BEF) for children's ages, residence and household characteristics
Social benefits records of parental leave spells (from 1995)
National Patient Register (LPR), inpatient hospitalisations 1990–2000
Register of Causes of Death (DAR), 1991–2000
variables: Treatment: 1994 parental leave programme; exposure = share of nurses eligible times estimated take-up, by health sector and county
Outcome: nurse employment in hospitals and nursing homes
Outcome: 30-day hospital readmission rates and other quality-of-care measures
Outcome: nursing home (elderly) mortality
Eligibility: having a youngest child aged 8 or younger
sample: Danish nurses, nursing assistants and doctors, and hospital patients and nursing home residents, aggregated to health sector by county, 1990–2000.

definitions.variable: Skilled nurse / unskilled nurse / doctor (by education)
definitions.definition: Health workers are classified by vocational education code in IDAP: skilled nurses (general nurse BSc, specialist nurse training, midwife BSc, nurse MSc); unskilled nurses (health and care workers); medical doctors (MD, PhD; medical BSc 7172 excluded). Doctors' first 7 years of experience are treated as residency and not counted as doctors.
definitions.codes: ERHAUDD (or HFAUDD in SAS extract): skilled nurse 5166-5173, 5175, 5180, 5181, 8634; unskilled nurse 5146-5150, 5152; doctor 7170, 7180

definitions.definition: Workplace industry from IDAS (BRANCHE1, else BRANCHE03, else BRANCHE07) merged by establishment (LBNR) and year. Hospitals = industry 851100; nursing homes = 853140 or 853150. Missing codes are filled backwards within establishment and, for nursing homes, backwards by person within the same firm (CVRNR); other employed = other sectors; no workplace type = unemployment/nonparticipation. New freelancers (missing LBNR) among unskilled nurses keep their previous sector.
Indicator that the age of the youngest child in the family is 8 or younger, from the family register (C_ALDYNGST, else ALDYNGST).

Leave = worker with an establishment in t-1 has none in t, or is on maternity leave at end of November (SHSS maternity benefit months: November value 30, or positive in both November and December). Individual take-up is estimated by regressing leave on age-of-youngest-child dummies interacted with 1995 vs 1993; predicted take-up is assigned to workers based on prior-year child age, and county-sector exposure = summed expected take-up / number of active workers of that type in 1993.
definitions.codes: SHSS: BEL_BAR, VARMMSF11, VARMMSF12; child-care leave VAR_ORL_BP, VARMMO1-12

definitions.definition: County assigned from workplace municipality (AKOM) for employed workers, otherwise residence municipality, using pre-2007 municipality code ranges mapped to 15 counties.

Among inpatient (patient type 0) stays of 100 days or less, a readmission occurs if the next admission (or scheduled referral date) of the same person is within 30 days after discharge, starting at least one day after discharge; same-day readmission counts only if referred by a GP to the same hospital. Set to missing if the patient died before discharge.
definitions.codes: C_PATTYPE == 0; D_INDDTO, D_UDDTO, D_HENDTO, C_UDM == 1, C_SGH

definitions.definition: Patients aged 65+ with primary diagnosis acute myocardial infarction; index admissions exclude those with an ischemic heart admission in the preceding 365 days. 30-day mortality = death within 30 days of admission (DAR).
definitions.codes: AMI: ICD-8 4109, 41099; ICD-10 DI21, DI22. Ischemic: ICD-8 410-414; ICD-10 DI20-DI25

definitions.definition: Nursing home addresses are identified from deaths registered in a nursing home (place-of-death institution code 2) 1990-2000, using the first 14 characters of the address code (BOPIKOM) within municipality, keeping addresses where no children live; residents aged 60+ living at those addresses are nursing home residents, and their mortality is the outcome.

authors: Andrew Caplin, Victoria Gregory, Eungik Lee, Søren Leth-Petersen and Johan Sæverud
title: Subjective Earnings Risk
summary: Introduces a survey instrument for earnings risk that allows for quitting and being fired, fielded to Danish workers and linked to their register earnings histories. Job transitions drive subjective risk, which is many times smaller than traditional register-based estimates even after conditioning on demographics and job history, and helps explain why many hold few liquid assets.
data: Copenhagen Life Panel (CLP) survey, January 2021 wave, linked on CPR number
Income-tax register earnings (IND)
Monthly employer-employee match and earnings data (BFL/eIndkomst)
Demographic, education, household composition and household wealth registers
variables: Survey: subjective probabilities of staying, quitting and being laid off
Survey: subjective earnings distributions conditional on each job transition
Benchmark: realized job transitions, time out of work and earnings growth in 2021 (administrative)
Weights: population weights from a survey-participation model on 2020 administrative data
sample_size: 10,942 employed respondents (gross sample 14,683 respondents aged 20–65)
sample: Copenhagen Life Panel respondents aged 20–65 who were employed at the time of the January 2021 survey.

definitions.definition: From monthly eIndkomst job records (BFL), each person-month is assigned the job with the most paid hours (AJO_LOENTIMER) as the primary employer; its CVR number, wage and hours are kept. Month and year come from the job start date field AJO_JOB_START_DATO.
definitions.codes: AJO_CVR_NR_FRA_PROD_JOB, AJO_SMALT_LOENBELOEB, AJO_LOENTIMER, AJO_JOB_START_DATO; primary job = max(AJO_LOENTIMER) within pnr-year-month

definitions.definition: Among workers with an employer and monthly wage above 2,000 DKK in December 2020, stay=1 if the main employer in December 2021 is the same as in December 2020, else 0. Sample restricted to ages 20-65 and 2020 annual BFL earnings of at least 24,000 DKK.
definitions.codes: wage>2000 in Dec 2020; employer_g == F12.employer_g; sum_earnings>=24000

definitions.variable: Months out of work after separation
definitions.definition: A separation is a month in which the worker has a main employer with monthly wage above 2,000 DKK and next month's employer differs; only the first separation per person is used. Time out of work = months until a different non-missing employer appears (capped at 24) minus one, so job-to-job moves count as 0 and returns to the same employer are not reemployment. The paper describes separations in 2020; the posted do-file's window (date<=24 from Dec 2018) covers Dec 2018-Dec 2019.
definitions.codes: jan_sep = employer_g != F1employer_g; reemp = first k with F`k'employer_g != employer_g & non-missing; gap = reemp-1; cap 24
definitions.source_location: script/analysis/fig4/preprocess_fig4b.do; paper Section 3.2 and Figure 4 note

definitions.definition: Annual earnings are wage income LOENMV_13 from the income register (IND); self-employment income is NETOVSKUD_13 kept separately. Realized earnings growth 2020-2021 is ln(earnings_2021*100/102) - ln(earnings_2020), dropping observations with earnings below 24,000 DKK in either year and trimming at the 1st/99th percentile.
definitions.codes: LOENMV_13 (earnings), NETOVSKUD_13 (self-employment income); threshold 24,000 DKK; deflator 100/102; winsor2 trim 1/99

definitions.definition: Net wealth = (KOEJD + BANKAKT + KURSAKT + OBLAKT + PANTAKT) - (BANKGAELD + GAELD_TIL_OFF + OBLGAELD + PANTGAELD), missing public debt set to 0. Liquid wealth = BANKAKT + KURSAKT + OBLAKT + PANTAKT. Pension wealth is the sum of PF_FORMUE across contracts in PENSFORM.
definitions.codes: KOEJD, BANKAKT, KURSAKT, OBLAKT, PANTAKT, BANKGAELD, GAELD_TIL_OFF, OBLGAELD, PANTGAELD; PF_FORMUE

definitions.variable: Monthly UI, cash benefits and retirement transfers
definitions.definition: From ILME monthly non-employee e-income records, amounts across A/B income fields are summed per person-month and classified by the income-type code of the largest payment: UI if VMO_INDK_ART codes 2,5,8,16,104; cash benefits if type code 6 or art codes 40,41,43,84,87; retirement if art codes 6,9,10,13,20,24,25,44,45,74,83,86,113,115.
definitions.codes: VMO_INDKOMST_ART_KODE UI: 2,5,8,16,104; CB: VMO_INDKOMST_TYPE_KODE 6 or ART 40,41,43,84,87; Retirement ART: 6,9,10,13,20,24,25,44,45,74,83,86,113,115

definitions.definition: Main job (highest LOENTIMER in IDAN per year) is public if ARB_SEKTORKODE is non-missing and not 99, and recoded private if ARB_SEKTORKODE is in 18, 28, 89, 81, 58, 48, 42, 52. Industry groups come from DB07 ranges of ARB_HOVED_BRA_DB07 (e.g. >=840000 public services, 850000 teaching, 860000 health).

Main job's DISCO_KODE first digit mapped to 9 groups (1 management, 2 high knowledge, 3 medium knowledge, 4 office, 5 sales/services, 6 farming, 7 craft, 8 skilled, 9 unskilled); military (DISCO below 100000) dropped. Tenure = year - ANSAAR.
definitions.codes: DISCO_KODE first digit 1-9; DISCO_KODE<100000 excluded; ANSAAR

definitions.definition: Highest completed education HFAUDD (latest available year) mapped through the audd format's H1 level: 10 elementary; 20, 25 high school; 30, 35 vocational; 40, 50, 60 bachelor; 65, 70 master.
Inverse predicted propensity scores from a probability model of survey participation estimated on 2020 administrative data on the demographics of Danes active in the labour market.

authors: Dmitry Taubinsky, Luigi Butera, Matteo Saccarola and Chen Lian
title: Beliefs About the Economy Are Excessively Sensitive to Household-Level Shocks: Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
summary: Links Statistics Denmark's consumer expectations survey to the registers to show that people's inflation forecasts and backcasts move strongly, and negatively, with their own recent and expected income changes, far more than actual inflation does. The pattern departs from Bayesian rational expectations and is consistent with affect-cued recall, where bad personal events cue pessimistic recollections.
data: Danish Consumer Expectations Survey (Statistics Denmark Omnibus), linked on CPR
Tax registers from SKAT: income, liquid assets, net wealth, taxes (IND, formue)
Civil Registration System / Population register (CPR/BEF)
Education register (UDDA)
National Patient Register (LPR), emergency room visits 1994–2018
variables: Outcome: inflation forecasts and backcasts (qualitative and quantitative)
Explanatory: recent change in household log nominal income (t-1 vs t-2)
Explanatory: future household income change and expected household financial situation
Shock: family emergency room visit in the survey month
Benchmark: realized inflation
sample_size: 35050 usable responses (from 55171 survey respondents aged 25–60)
sample: Danish Consumer Expectations Survey respondents aged 25–60 in 2012–2019 without substantial self-employment income and with complete answers, linked to administrative data.

definitions.definition: Yearly total income before taxes and labour market contributions, including labour income, public transfers, property income and most other taxable income attributable to the individual (excludes imputed rental value, pension contributions to employer schemes and lottery winnings). Household value is the average of the two spouses' values if a spouse is present in CPR, otherwise the individual value.
definitions.source_location: code_dstserver/code_epinion/2_build_registries.do; NBER WP w32664 Section 1.2 and footnote 6

definitions.definition: Total taxable wage income, benefits, bonuses, severance pay and value of stock options, averaged across spouses as for total income.

definitions.variable: Recent and future household income change
definitions.definition: For a respondent interviewed in any month of year t, recent change = log nominal household income in t-1 minus t-2; future change = log income in t+1 minus t-1. Changes are trimmed at the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles.

Liquid assets follow Andersen et al. (2020): total value of bank deposits, stocks and bonds reported by financial institutions to SKAT. Net wealth is SKAT's tax-purpose measure of net household assets excluding non-deposited cash and foreign assets, with real estate at tax-assessed values; both averaged across spouses and used as asinh changes.
Exclude respondents if self-employment income exceeds one fourth of household income (in absolute value) in any year from t-4 to t+1 around the interview.

Monthly survey respondents 2012-2019 (backcast analyses 2013-2019) aged 25-60, excluding high self-employment income, missing key survey answers (Do not know, refused or forecast >100 pp) and missing registry variables, after trimming income changes and inflation answers at 2.5/97.5 percentiles.

definitions.variable: Family emergency room visit in survey month
definitions.definition: Indicator equal to one if any household member (household identifier from BEF) visited the emergency room in the calendar month of the interview. An ER visit is an acute outpatient hospital contact in the NPR (recorded as patient type ER before 2014, acute outpatient from 2014). Respondents with more than 7 family ER visits over 2008-2018 are dropped.
definitions.source_location: code_dstserver/analysis/A9_healthregs.do; NBER WP Online Appendix A.1 (Emergency Room Visits Data) and ER table notes

definitions.definition: HFAUDD from UDDA mapped via an ISCED crosswalk to single-digit ISCED 2011 levels 1-6; code 9 (not known) set to missing.

authors: Asger Lau Andersen, Kilian Huber, Niels Johannesen, Ludwig Straub and Emil Toft Vestergaard
title: Disaggregated Economic Accounts
summary: Builds a system of national accounts broken down into bilateral money flows between region-by-industry consumer cells, producer cells, the government and the rest of the world, and implements it for Denmark using bank transaction data and registers. Spending is locally and urban biased, and fiscal transfers raise GDP more when targeted at cells whose spending reaches cells with high unemployment.
data: Danske Bank geo-coded transaction-level data (about 20% of Danish adult consumers), 2018–2019
Government tax and income registers (labour compensation, mixed income, interest, dividends, transfers)
Employment registers linking adults to industry of main employment and region
Danish national accounts (SNA positions, input-output tables), 2018
CrediWire producer-to-producer transactions (about 5 million)
Firm-level export and import data for manufacturing firms
variables: Outcome: bilateral cell-to-cell flows (consumer spending, labour and profit income, taxes, transfers, intermediates trade)
Unit: consumer cells (industry of main employment x region of residence)
Unit: producer cells (industry x region of establishments)
Derived: domestic spending share, gravity, urban bias and spending intensity measures
sample_size: approx. 2,700 consumer cells and approx. 2,600 producer cells; around 43 million entries
sample: All Danish adults and production establishments grouped into region-by-industry cells, with consumer spending measured from Danske Bank customers.

definitions.variable: Consumer cell (region x industry of main employment)
definitions.definition: Every adult is assigned to a region by home address at the start of 2018 (BEF), one per each of 98 municipalities, and to an industry by the NACE code of the establishment responsible for the largest part of 2018 labour income (AKM), mapped from six-digit NACE to 24 work industries. Cells with fewer than 3 individuals or establishments are censored.
definitions.codes: six-digit NACE mapped to 24 DEA work industries (Table A.I); 98 municipalities

definitions.definition: Adults without labour income are assigned to 'retired' if older than 65, 'students' if they receive a government stipend, 'long-term unemployed' if they receive unemployment or cash benefits (fully benefit-dependent with no labour income all year), and otherwise 'out of workforce'.

Firm establishments are assigned to 2,646 producer cells by region and production industry using the employment registers; 24 work industries plus 3 housing industries without employees (private landlords, owner-occupied housing, government-owned housing).

Total annual labour compensation per individual including employer pension contributions, from IND and INPI, aggregated to consumer x producer cells and scaled by 1.01 to SNA D.1. Compensation from foreign producers (IND) scaled by 1.47; payments by Danish producers in BFL to persons not in BEF are treated as foreign employees and scaled by 1.14.

definitions.variable: Mixed income, dividends and owner-occupied housing surplus
definitions.definition: Mixed income links sole-proprietorship establishments in IDAN (including municipality) to owners' mixed income. Dividends (SNA D.42) are allocated to consumer cells in proportion to stock dividend income in IND and to producer cells in proportion to accounting income. Owner-occupied housing surplus (B.2G) = imputed rental values in IND scaled by 0.67.

Social benefits (SNA D.62) = all government income transfers plus private pension payouts from IND, scaled by 1.03. Other current transfers (D.7) allocated by BEF population shares; pension entitlement adjustment (D.8) from IND and INPI contributions net of payouts.

Danske Bank customers (main account at Danske Bank and at least one spending transaction per month in 2018-2019) assigned home region monthly from bank address records and industry from the employer paying the largest share of annual income. Merchant region from geocoded transaction-string addresses and industry from an MCC-to-ISIC/NACE crosswalk; cash withdrawals allocated in proportion to in-person card payments.

definitions.variable: Manual labour share and cell characteristics
definitions.definition: Individual does manual labour if main occupation (AKM) is manual trades, operator and assembly, transportation, other manual labour or military. Cell averages also of university degree (UDDA), total debt, liquid financial assets (deposits, stocks, bonds, fund shares) and illiquid assets (FORMGELD).

Firm output is distributed across a firm's establishments using within-firm labour compensation shares, then aggregated to 173 subindustries combining the 117-industry national IO table and DEA industries; intermediate flows are split proportional to output shares.

authors: Ole Agersnap, Amalie Sofie Jensen and Henrik Kleven
title: The Welfare Magnet Hypothesis: Evidence from an Immigrant Welfare Scheme in Denmark
summary: The 2002 cut in benefits for non-EU immigrants, its repeal and its reintroduction provide repeated quasi-experiments on the welfare magnet hypothesis. The cut reduced net immigration by about 5,000 people a year and the repeal reversed it almost exactly, implying a migration elasticity with respect to benefits of 1.3.
data: Danish administrative registers on the full population 1980–2017 (immigrant status, country of origin, demographics, family links)
Residence permit data by permit type (asylum, family, work/study; available from 1997)
Central Person Register (CPR) migration records
National statistics bureaus of other Nordic countries and OECD International Migration Database (1991–2017)
variables: Treatment: maximum monthly welfare benefit for non-EU immigrants (2002 introduction, 2012 repeal, 2015 reintroduction of the immigrant welfare scheme)
Outcome: net immigration flow by welfare benefit group, scaled by pre-scheme stock
Outcome: gross inflow by residence permit type
Comparison: EU vs non-EU immigrants; Denmark vs other Nordic countries
sample_size: 444 group-year observations (12 welfare benefit groups)
sample: Immigrant flows to Denmark aged at least 30 (baseline), collapsed into 12 benefit-eligibility groups by EU/non-EU origin, marital status and number of children.

definitions.definition: First-generation immigrants from outside the EU and the four EFTA countries (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland), who are subject to the immigrant welfare scheme. 'Inside the EU' is defined by member countries in the pre-scheme year 2001, to avoid confounding from later EU enlargements.

Year-to-year change in the stock of first-generation immigrants residing in Denmark according to the Central Person Register, by group, scaled by the group's pre-scheme (2001) immigrant stock and residualized on a linear group-specific trend estimated on 1980-2001.

Immigration flows by type of residence permit granted (asylum, family, work, study; available from 1997). Asylum and family permit holders are treated as potentially welfare-eligible; work/study permit holders as untreated. Asylum applications are used as a supplementary measure.

definitions.variable: Welfare benefit groups and maximum monthly benefit
definitions.definition: Maximum monthly cash benefits (2018 USD) for non-employed households at age 40 out of work for three months; with children, the first child is aged 10 and the second aged 8. Danish scheme benefits from STAR (Danish Agency for Labour Market and Recruitment) website; other benefits computed with the OECD tax-benefit calculator. Only cash welfare, excluding UI and in-kind benefits such as housing support.

Main within-country specification restricts to immigrants at least 30 years old, to avoid confounding from the 2002 '24-Year Rule' requiring both spouses to be at least 24 for marriage-based residency. The cross-country analysis has no age restriction.

Weighted average of Finland (0.468), Norway (0.361) and Sweden (0.171), chosen to match 1991-2001 non-EU/EFTA net immigration flows normalized by each country's 2001 non-EU/EFTA immigrant stock. Immigrants from the former Yugoslavia are dropped throughout to remove the Bosnia shock.
definitions.source_location: Section 3 (cross-country strategy), footnote 18; Appendix Figure A.IV notes

definitions.definition: Official Statistics Denmark definitions: a first-generation immigrant is born outside Denmark with neither parent being both a Danish citizen and born in Denmark; a second-generation immigrant (descendant) is born in Denmark with neither parent being both a Danish citizen and born in Denmark.

Asylum applications to Denmark from outside the EU at annual and quarterly frequency: applications submitted (available from 2000), applications registered for administrative review, and residence permits granted to asylum seekers; asylum seekers from Bosnia dropped. An inflow measure without a control group, used to validate timing of responses.
definitions.source_location: Online Appendix, Section B and Figures A.IV-A.V

authors: Henrik Kleven, Camille Landais and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Does Biology Drive Child Penalties? Evidence from Biological and Adoptive Families
summary: Compares event-study child penalties for biological and adoptive mothers using almost 40 years of Danish adoption data. Short-run penalties are slightly larger for biological mothers, but long-run penalties are virtually identical, so biology is not a key driver of child-related gender gaps.
data: Statistics Denmark administrative registers covering the full population 1980–2017, linked with family identifiers
Adoption registry of Statistics Denmark (1988–2009), augmented with foreign adoptions identified via country of origin and Central Person Register immigration records
Earnings and labour-supply registers incl. hours from the ATP mandated pension scheme
Education registers
variables: Event: arrival of first child (by birth or adoption)
Outcome: annual earnings (wages, salaries, self-employment)
Outcome: labour force participation, hours worked, wage rates
Comparison group: biological vs adoptive families (biological sample reweighted to match adoptive families)
sample_size: around 527,000 first births (biological sample) and around 4,600 first arrivals (adoptive sample)
sample: Danish parents whose first child arrived by birth or foreign adoption (before age 5) between 1985 and 2007, with both parents known, alive and resident in Denmark from 5 years before to 10 years after.

definitions.definition: Children who (1) were born in a non-western country, (2) have two known parents born in a western country, (3) whose parents both had a legal address in Denmark with no emigration record at the time of birth, and (4) have a recorded entry (immigration record) into the Central Person Register after the date of birth. Validated against Statistics Denmark official adoption records (1988-2009), with virtually no type I or type II errors; about 16,260 foreign adoptees 1980-2017, mostly from Asia (South Korea, India, China), Latin America (Colombia) and Africa.
definitions.source_location: Online Appendix, Figure A.I notes and Table A.I

definitions.definition: Stepwise restrictions: children with known parents born 1980-2017 (16,260 adoptive / 2,454,200 biological); born 1985-2007; first-born only; siblings all of the same type (biological or adoptive); adoptees arrived before age 5; parents balanced on event time (final 4,580 adoptive / 527,000 biological).
Annual income from wages, salaries and self-employment.

Hours worked from administrative, third-party-reported data on contributions to the mandated ATP (Arbejdsmarkedets Tillaegspension) pension scheme, which employers pay based on employees' individual hours worked. The wage rate is earnings divided by hours worked.

Baseline reweighting of the biological sample on pre-birth variables (year of first child, mother's age at first child, mother's pre-child education and pre-child earnings) plus subsequent-children variables (years to second child, total number of children); alternatives use no reweighting or pre-birth variables only.

Baseline measured just before the arrival of the first child (event time -1), splitting women at the median. Forward-looking (potentially endogenous) alternatives measure it 10 years after first child arrival, after 15 years of experience, or at age 45.

authors: Asger Lau Andersen, Niels Johannesen and Adam Sheridan
title: Dynamic Spending Responses to Wealth Shocks: Evidence from Quasi Lotteries on the Stock Market
summary: Uses lottery-like variation in stock market gains across investors with similar portfolios, observed in granular bank data, to trace spending responses. Responses are immediate and persistent, cumulating to a marginal propensity to consume of 4.4 percent over one year and 16 percent over three, consistent with the permanent income hypothesis with some inattention.
data: Danske Bank customer records: transaction-level spending, securities portfolios and online logins (2009–2016)

Liquid assets (deposits, stocks and other securities) at the beginning of the month relative to average monthly income; household-months are ranked within month and split into terciles.

authors: Niels Johannesen, Johan Sæverud and Emmanuel Saez
title: Taxing the Wealth of the Poor: Evidence from the Danish Old-Age Support Asset Test
summary: The asset test for Danish old-age support creates diffuse but large excess mass in liquid assets just below the threshold among the eligible, relative to comparable ineligible groups. Danske Bank customer data: monthly spending, cash withdrawals and account balances (2014–2016)

Outcome: bunching / excess mass of liquid wealth below the threshold
Outcome: year-end spending and cash withdrawals (bank data)
Eligibility: age 65+ and low income

definitions.definition: Third-party-reported year-end value of current accounts, savings accounts and securities accounts (bank deposits and listed securities); excludes durables, real estate and pension accounts and does not net out debt. Available for the full population; mirrors the 'default wealth' the authorities use for the old-age check asset test.

The variable available to the authors does not capture corrections made close to year-end.

Age-eligible = aged 65 or older (statutory retirement age in the sample period). Low-income (income-eligible) = income, net of social security and before self-reported corrections, below the threshold at which the old-age check is fully phased out (disregard DKK 42,000, phase-out rate 34% for singles in 2020). Asset test: check lost entirely when liquid wealth at end of t-1 exceeds DKK 90,000 (2020 value; threshold raised 15% in 2010). For the 2001-2007 reform analysis the 2003 income threshold is applied throughout.
definitions.source_location: Section I.A; Figure 1 and 2 notes; Supplemental Appendix Figure A.4 notes

definitions.variable: Treatment and control groups for bunching
definitions.definition: Treated: low-income singles aged 65+. Old-age check (created 2003) parameters expressed in 2020 values by inflating with the index used to adjust tax and transfer parameters (tied to average wage earnings per worker; $1 = 6.53 DKK in 2020). Maximum check raised above indexation in 2005, 2007, 2009 and 2013; asset-test threshold raised about 15% above indexation in 2010; income test (phase-out start and end thresholds) very strict initially but unchanged in real terms since 2005 except a small increase in 2019.

authors: Itzik Fadlon, Astrid Sophie Fugleholm and Torben Heien Nielsen
title: Survivors' Mental Health and the Protective Role of Income Stability
summary: Documents the immediate, large and lingering rise in mental health medication after a spouse's death across the universe of Danish households. A large share of the spike is explained by the income loss the death imposes, so safety-net liquidity protects survivors' mental health.
data: Population Registry (BEF) with family linkages
Death Registry
National Patient Registry (LPR)
Income Registry (earnings, transfers, pension payouts, capital income)
Education Registry
Pharmaceutical Database / prescription register (LMDB)
Health Insurance Registry (psychiatrist visits)
variables: Treatment: spouse's fatal heart attack or stroke (death within 12 months), treated vs later-event control group
Outcome: take-up of mental health medication (ATC N05, N06)
Mechanism: household income loss from spousal death (instrumented by deceased spouse's earnings share)
Heterogeneity: baseline income, net wealth and insurance (DI/OAP, sick pay)
sample_size: 12,637 treatment and 15,212 control households
sample: Danish couples aged 45–80 in which one spouse had a heart attack or stroke between 1999 and 2018 and died within 12 months, excluding the self-employed, balanced four years before and after.

definitions.variable: Fatal heart attack or stroke (death event)

Indicator for redeeming a prescription for psychotropic drugs classified as psycholeptics (ATC N05) or psychoanaleptics (ATC N06) by the surviving spouse, measured at monthly and annual frequency (extensive margin).

Household income decomposed into seven sources for each spouse: earnings, sick pay, DI + old-age pension (OAP), other government benefits, private pensions, capital income and other income, compared between the year before (period -1) and the year after (period 1) the index event. In 2SLS the household income loss is normalized at the treatment-group mean and winsorized at the top and bottom 1 percent.

Household income loss is instrumented with an indicator for whether the deceased spouse had earnings and a quadratic in the share of household income earned by the deceased spouse in the year before the event; 2SLS uses observations for years -1 and 0 with household FE, calendar-year FE and a quadratic in the survivor's age; SEs clustered by household.

Households where one spouse has a health event 1999-2018 and dies within 12 months; treatment = event in 1999-2013, control = similar event in 2004-2018 with placebo event assigned five years earlier; both spouses aged 45-80 at baseline; balanced from four years before to four years after. Specifications include household FE, calendar-year FE and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. For Delta = 3-7 robustness the calendar interval of treated spousal deaths is held fixed so only the control group changes. Variables are measured in the year before the actual or placebo event.

Accumulated number of hospital diagnoses related to alcohol following Browning and Heinesen (2012): alcohol poisoning, addiction syndrome, delirious abstinence, alcohol psychosis, oesophageal varices, alcoholic liver disease, alcoholic pancreatic disease.

summary: The dismantling of Multi-Fibre Arrangement quotas on Chinese textiles at WTO accession exposed Danish textile firms to low-wage competition. Within firms, employment, value added and intangible assets fell and the workforce shifted toward skilled workers, while firms refocused away from products where China's advantage grew.
data: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Firm accounting statistics (Regnskabsdata / FIRE)

Firm fixed effects, year effects

Assets intended for long-term ownership or use, including licences, trademarks, copyrights, exclusive distribution rights, software and goodwill, from the accounting statistics; outcomes are log intangible assets and the logit of intangibles over total assets. Textile/clothing production training (clothing operator, fashion craft, hand stitcher, cutter, tailor, knitting/textile operator) = hffsp 355880 and 355890. ICD-8: diabetes 249, 250; cardiovascular disease 390-458; heart disease 410-414. ICD-10: diabetes DE10-DE14; cardiovascular disease DI00-DI99; heart disease DI20-DI25.

Groups (ICD-10; ICD-8): 1 infection A00-B99, 000-136; 2 cancer C00-C97, 140-209; 3 other cancer D00-D48, 210-239; 4 blood D50-D89, 280-289; 5 endocrine/metabolic E00-E90, 240-246, 250-279; 6 mental F03-F99, 290-315; 7 nervous system G00-G31, 320-389; 8 heart disease G35-H95, I00-I25, I27, I30-I51, 390-398, 400-404, 410-414, 420-429; 9 other cardiovascular I26, I28, I60-I99, 430-438, 440-448, 450-458; 10 respiratory J00-J99, 460-474, 480-486, 490-493, 500-519; 11 digestive K00-K92, 520-577; 12-13 skin/musculoskeletal L00-L99, M00-M99, 680-738; 14 genitourinary N00-N98, 580-629; 15 pregnancy O00-O99, 630-678; 16 perinatal P00-P96, 760-779; 17 congenital Q00-Q99, 746-759; 18 symptoms R00-R98, R99, 780-793, 795-796; 19 accidents V01-X59, Y40-Y86, Y88, E80-E94; 20 suicide/murder/legal interventions X60-X99, Y00-Y36, Y89, R99, E95-E99 (as printed).
registers: Danish Register of Causes of Death

definitions.definition: From the Statistical Commune Data Archive: party vote shares in three elections, population and urbanization in 1935, percent female 1930, percent workers in agriculture/industry 1930, percent on public aid 1936, percent income/property taxpayers 1936, aggregate taxable income and assessed property value 1936; plus 1936 infant mortality and enteritis deaths per 1,000 births by medical district (Medical Reports) and distance to Copenhagen; used as controls interacted with cohort and for propensity-score matching (caliper 0.05, one control without replacement).
registers: Medical Reports for the Kingdom of Denmark
definitions.source_location: Section III.A; Section II matching, footnote 26

authors: Maya Rossin-Slater and Miriam Wüst
title: What Is the Added Value of Preschool for Poor Children? Long-Term and Intergenerational Impacts and Interactions with an Infant Health Intervention
summary: Access to preschool targeted at low-income children between 1933 and 1960 raised adult education, earnings and survival past 65, and the children of exposed women obtained more education by 25. Exposure to the nurse home visiting programme in infancy reduces preschool's added value, so the two programmes are partial substitutes.
data: Archival data on all approved Danish preschools 1933–1960 (establishment and approval year, slots)
Nurse Home Visiting program implementation dates by municipality
Statistical Commune Data Archive (elections and censuses) for municipality controls
Municipal live births and infant deaths
DigDag historical administrative geography (parish-municipality mapping)
Administrative population register data 1980–2012 (education, earnings, survival, hospital admissions, diagnoses)
Mother-child links (Danish Civil Registration System)
variables: Treatment: approved preschool in municipality of birth at age 3
Interaction: exposure to the infant Nurse Home Visiting program
Outcome: education and earnings around age 50
Outcome: survival past age 65, hospital admissions, diagnoses
Intergenerational outcome: oldest child's educational attainment by age 25
Controls: municipality and birth-year fixed effects, county-by-year trends, municipality characteristics
sample_size: 1,640,214 observations (Danish-born with valid parish codes); 880,708 observations in municipalities with an approved preschool by 1960, collapsed to 3,862 municipality × birth-year cells
sample: Danish-born individuals born 1930–1957 with a valid parish of birth who are observed after 1980, focusing on the 138 municipalities that ever had an approved preschool.

definitions.definition: Indicator equal to one for birth cohorts that had at least one government-approved preschool in their municipality of birth at age 3, using the year of government approval from archival lists of all approved preschools (Skjernbaek, nine editions 1921-1960); municipality of birth is assumed to be the early-childhood municipality.

definitions.variable: Nurse Home Visiting (NHV) exposure in birth year
definitions.definition: Indicator for an approved NHV program in the municipality in the birth year, based on DNBH approval dates 1937-1949 from the Danish National Archives (approval required sufficient nurse coverage). For 28 municipalities without an NHV program by 1949, treatment year is assigned from Skjernbaek lists (year of previous publication if listed, otherwise never treated).
registers: Danish National Board of Health (DNBH) archival records

definitions.variable: Municipality of birth from parish of birth
definitions.definition: Births are registered at parish level; parish of birth is mapped to 1930-1960 municipalities using DigDag. Individuals with invalid or undocumented parish codes, post-1970 municipality coding, registration by religious minorities, or hospital births are dropped (about 90 percent of Danish-born have a valid parish of birth).
definitions.source_location: Section 2, Sample construction and selection, footnote 15

definitions.variable: Years of schooling and more than compulsory schooling at age 50
definitions.definition: Years of schooling at age 50 adding up schooling across educational programs, and an indicator for having more than nine years of compulsory schooling at age 50.
Natural log of average wage income (in 2012 prices) over all ages between 30 and 60 observable in the 1980-2012 register data.

Equally weighted average of years of schooling at 50, more-than-compulsory indicator and log average wage income 30-60, each standardized by the mean and SD of the control group (municipality-by-cohort cells without an approved preschool by age 3 in the 138 ever-implementing municipalities).

Indicator for surviving past age 65, with data left-censored so that all individuals enter the risk period at age 50 (outcome data start in 1980). Supplementary outcomes include hospital care utilization (e.g. nights in hospital ages 55-64) and diagnoses of cardiovascular disease, heart disease, diabetes and cancer; specific diagnosis codes are not given in the main text.
Main second-generation analysis uses firstborn children of mothers born 1935-1957; robustness uses all children of these mothers; cells by mother's municipality x birth year.
registers: Population register parent links; education register

definitions.definition: Robustness income outcomes (municipality x birth-year cells): average age 30-60 wage income in levels; log present discounted value of age 30-60 wage income (following Chetty et al. 2011); log average age 30-60 total income; log average age 49-51 wage income; indicator for any positive wage income at ages 49-51.
Number of nights spent in hospital over age ranges 45-54 and 55-64 (first generation), analysed at municipality x birth-year cell level.
Indicators for diagnoses of cardiovascular disease, heart disease, diabetes and cancer (first generation); code lists not given in this appendix (follows Hjort, Solvsten and Wust 2017).

For females born 1935-1957 in the 138 municipalities with an approved preschool by 1960: no children, number of children, age at first birth, and father ever missing in child's birth record ('Dad Ever Miss.').

Share of children aged 3-7 enrolled in preschool: enrollment counts per preschool from the nine years of preschool book publications, interpolated to every year and aggregated to municipality x year, divided by number of survivors past age four; urban municipalities, 1940-1950 (1940 first year all living 7-year-olds observed, since birth data start 1933). (Table A11 title says aged 3-6; its notes say 3-7.)
registers: Archival preschool records; municipal births and infant deaths

definitions.definition: 138 municipalities that ever had an approved preschool by 1960; individuals born 1935-1957; robustness drops cohorts born 1950-1957 in 28 municipalities lacking precise NHV initiation information, and drops NHV-treated observations in the bottom 1st percentile of the human capital index.

authors: Anne Sofie Tegner Anker, Jennifer L. Doleac and Rasmus Landersø
title: The Effects of DNA Databases on the Deterrence and Detection of Offenders
summary: A large expansion of Denmark's DNA database cut recidivism within a year by up to 42 percent and raised the chance that re-offenders are caught, implying that a 1 percent higher detection probability lowers crime by more than 2 percent. Registered offenders also became more likely to work, study and live in stable families.
data: Central Charge Register (crime date, charge date, crime type)
Danish Central DNA Database person-specific section (DNA registration records)
Conviction records (crime registers)
Full-population registers on demographics, labour market and family links
variables: Treatment: offender registered in the DNA database
Instrument: charged after the May 2005 DNA database expansion (donut RD, excluding June–September 2005)
Running variable: months before May / after October 2005
Outcome: convictions within one, two and three years after the charge (all crime and by type)
Detection vs. deterrence: split by charges filed more vs. less than three weeks after the crime
Secondary outcomes: employment, education, marriage
period: Charges June 2003–September 2007 (excluding June–September 2005), with follow-up outcomes
sample_size: 38,674 individuals with 66,911 charge observations
sample: Danish-resident males aged 18–30 charged with Penal Code or Weapons Act offenses who had at most 10 previous charges.

definitions.definition: Indicator that the charged offender appears in the person-specific section of the Central DNA Database, merged to the charge register via personal identification and record numbers.

definitions.variable: Post-reform charge instrument and donut window
definitions.definition: Sampling window +/-24 months around the 2005 reform, excluding June-September of the reform year; placebo samples shift the reform to e.g. 2002. Robustness caps on number of prior charges at max 5, 10 or 15.
definitions.source_location: Table A-2 and placebo table notes

definitions.definition: Charges for offenses against the Penal Code or Weapons Act (excluding traffic offenses, small-scale drug possession, Health Code and Tax Law violations) against Danish-resident males aged 18-30 at the charge with at most 10 previous charges; one charge per person per day; unit of observation is the charge.

Convictions for crimes committed after the sample charge, counted from the day after the charge, within one, two and three years; coded as a binary (at least one conviction) and as a count top-coded at 10 convictions per follow-up year. Measured for all crime and separately for violence, property, sexual, other penal (incl. serious drug offenses) and Weapons Act violations.

definitions.variable: Fast vs. slow charges (deterrence vs. detection)
definitions.definition: Solved fast = time from crime date to charge < 3 weeks; solved slowly = >= 3 weeks. Clearance rates computed from all charges and all reported crimes in 2005, excluding heavily reported but rarely solved types such as bicycle theft (charged <10% of the time). Robustness uses a 2-week cutoff (share of crimes solved within 2 weeks: 0.572 overall, 0.520 property, 0.670 violent).
registers: Central Crime Register; National Police reported crime
definitions.source_location: Table A-13 notes; Table A-15 notes (2-week cutoff)

definitions.definition: Mapping of charge types to analysis categories. Sexual (Penal Code): incest, rape, pedophilia, voyeurism/flashing, other sexual violations. Violence: violence against public servant, disturbance of public peace, murder/manslaughter (incl. attempted), simple violence, major violence, threats, other violent assaults. Property: fraud, arson, theft, burglary, robbery, vandalism, other property crime. Other (penal): crimes against/as a public servant, drug smuggling or sales, obstruction of justice, restraining orders, other penal code crimes. Weapon: Weapons/Arms Act violations (explosives, firearms, knives). Not categorized: Traffic Act violations (accidents and speeding, traffic accidents with alcohol, drunk driving, other traffic), Drug Act possession/sales, other special acts (smuggling, construction, health, social fraud).
Cumulated time in employment, education/training and unemployment over years 1-4 after the initial charge.
Married; same partner; living with child and the child's mother, measured 1, 2 and 3 years after charge.

Age, immigrant background, has children, single, years of education, gross income, employment status, number of prior charges, crime type dummies and month fixed effects; standard errors clustered by personal identification number.

authors: Asger Lau Andersen, Amalie Sofie Jensen, Niels Johannesen, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen and Adam Sheridan
title: How Do Households Respond to Job Loss? Lessons from Multiple High-Frequency Datasets
summary: Combines bank transaction data with government registers to measure every margin of self-insurance after job loss. Over two years households cut spending by 30 percent of the income loss and cover about half of it by running down liquid balances; spousal labour supply, private transfers, home equity extraction and consumer credit contribute less.
data: Danske Bank customer transaction and account records (spending, income inflows, balances, loans)
Monthly payroll and income transfer records (BFL/eIndkomst) from the Danish Tax Agency
Population register (BEF) household structure and spouse links
End-of-year account-level bank loan and deposit records from the Danish Tax Agency
Loan-level mortgage data from mortgage banks (via Statistics Denmark)
Mass layoff notifications to the Danish Agency for Labour Market and Recruitment
Annual income and wealth, education, home ownership and occupation registers
variables: Treatment: job loss event (main employer wage payments cease, followed by unemployment benefits)
Outcome: household spending (card, mobile, bills, ATM withdrawals)
Outcome: net saving in liquid assets, non-mortgage debt repayment, mortgage refinancing and equity extraction
Outcome: spousal labour income, private transfers, government transfers
Design: monthly event study from 18 months before to 24 months after job loss
Subsample: involuntary job loss from mass layoffs
sample_size: 10,002 individuals (baseline sample of active bank customers); gross sample of 66,844 job losers
sample: Danish individuals born 1950–1979 who lost their job between July 2010 and December 2015 after at least 18 months of stable earnings, in stable households that are active customers of Danske Bank.

definitions.definition: Month in which wage payments from the individual's main employer cease and total gross wage income drops below DKr 1,000; the individual must receive unemployment benefits or social insurance in months -1 to 3 and no early retirement, sickness or parental leave benefits then, must have had gross wage income of at least DKr 10,000 for at least 18 consecutive months before, and must not return to the same employer within three months.
registers: Monthly payroll and income transfer records (Danish Tax Agency, via Statistics Denmark)

definitions.definition: Baseline sample of active customers: at least five outgoing spending transactions in each month of the event window, with the partner (if any) meeting the same criterion. Exclusive-customer subsample: active customers (and partners) with no deposits or loans at other retail banks. Characteristics measured in month -6 relative to job loss (annual income over the calendar year containing month -6; shares held at other banks and mortgage debt at end of previous calendar year).
registers: Danske Bank; tax records; mortgage data

definitions.definition: Mass layoff notifications from the Ministry of Employment (firms with >20 employees must report planned large-scale layoffs; 'large scale' ranges from 10 workers for firms with 20-100 employees to 30 workers for firms with >300 employees), linked by firm ID to Tax Agency payroll data; individuals whose employer's report date falls in months -7 to -1 relative to the observed layoff month; 1,156 individuals.
registers: Ministry of Employment mass layoff notifications; BFL/eIndkomst

definitions.variable: Household disposable income (bank inflows) and components
definitions.definition: Disposable income = sum of monthly incoming direct deposits, person-to-person transfers from outside the household and cash deposits into Danske Bank accounts owned by the affected person and/or spouse (excluding transfers between own accounts). Wage income: inflow coded as wage if sender's bank registration number (4-digit Danish bank code) is the one mapped to the recipient's employer in that month (mapping = registration number from which the highest share of the employer's payroll employees, per Tax Agency payroll data, received payments; second-ranked used if top is the central-government number and employer is not central government), or if transaction type code is e.g. 'salary transfers'. Joint-account wage payments go to the spouse if from the spouse's employer, otherwise to the affected person. Government transfers: sender registration number linked to a paying agency per payroll data, or the central-government registration number when person does not work for central government. Private transfers and other income = residual.
registers: Danske Bank transactions; BFL/eIndkomst monthly payroll and transfer records
definitions.source_location: Appendix A (Income variables) and Appendix C

definitions.definition: Sum of outgoing card payments (incl. mobile-phone payments), bill payments and cash withdrawals from the household's bank accounts, excluding outflows identified via recipient MCC as tax or debt payments; excludes bank fees, securities purchases and uncategorized transfers. Bank aggregates raw transactions to daily totals per account x transaction type x recipient category. Household = affected person + spouse; joint-account outflows split evenly between owners.

Utilities: MCC 4900, 4812, 4814, 4821, 4899 or bill-payment label utilities/elec/gas/water/heating/internet/cable TV/telephone/TV license. Restaurants and bars: MCC 5813, 5462, 5811, 5812, 5814. Groceries: MCC 5411, 5422, 5441, 5499, 5921 or bill-payment label groceries.
Change in end-of-month balances on Danske Bank deposit accounts owned by the affected person or spouse plus outflows minus inflows of transactions with type code 'securities trade'.
Change in end-of-month balances on loan accounts (amounts owed coded as negative balances) owned by the affected person or spouse.

definitions.variable: Mortgage equity extraction and loan types (monthly)
definitions.definition: Monthly mortgage portfolio reconstructed from annual end-of-year loan-level snapshots: loans tracked by unique loan ID; loans appearing/disappearing dated by origination of new loans, and, if ambiguous, termination month inferred by comparing interest implied by rate and balance with mortgage interest reported in annual tax returns. Adjustable-rate and interest-only indicators from loan type; average monthly payment imputed from remaining balance, time to maturity, interest rate and amortization profile; mortgage repayments = sum of average monthly payments over loans held at end of month.
registers: Mortgage bank loan-level data (end-of-year); tax returns (interest)

authors: Christian Dustmann, Rasmus Landersø and Lars Højsgaard Andersen
title: Unintended Consequences of Welfare Cuts on Children and Adolescents
summary: The 2002 benefit cut for newly arrived refugees reduced family disposable income by 30 percent over five years. Children exposed at preschool or school age obtained lower grades, less education and lower adult earnings, and teenagers at exposure saw large increases in convictions for violent and property crime.
data: Danish Immigration Service residence permit records
Historical Migrations database
Income register from tax authority records
Register on Completed Education
Daycare register
9th-grade exam grades, 6th-grade national language test scores and school well-being survey (Ministry of Education)
Crime registers: police and court records
variables: Treatment: parents granted residency after the 2002 Start Aid welfare cut
Running variable: residency date relative to the reform
Outcome: 9th-grade GPA, 6th-grade language test scores, completed education
Outcome: adult earnings and employment
Outcome: criminal convictions
period: Residency granted January 2001–December 2003; income data through 2019
sample_size: 6,888 individuals (3,406 adults aged 18–45 with children and 3,482 children aged 0–18)
sample: Refugee families with children granted residency in Denmark within 18 months of the 2002 reform, excluding Afghans, former Yugoslavs and emigrants.

definitions.variable: Refugee family sample and age at exposure
definitions.definition: Danish Immigration Service residence permits granted 1997-2006 (252,795 permits; 67,375 to refugees: 44,232 new refugees, 23,143 family reunification), merged with the Historical Migrations database (residency date, origin, emigration); base sample = refugees granted residency within 18 months of the 2002 Start Aid reform, families with children at residence; refugees from Afghanistan and the former Yugoslavia excluded due to concurrent processing changes. Child age groups at residency 0-7, 8-14 (7-14 in some tables) and 14-18. 'Refugee permit status' = 1 if granted on asylum grounds, 0 if family-reunified spouse/child of a refugee. Standard errors clustered by residency month.
registers: Danish Immigration Service residence permits; Historical Migrations database

definitions.definition: Average grade over all 9th-grade exams, standardized to mean 0, SD 1 in the total population; also rank in the total population GPA distribution and quartile indicators; exams 2002-2019.
Compulsory national Danish test in grade 6 (from 2009 implementation), composite of language comprehension, decoding and reading comprehension; standardized following Beuchert and Nandrup (2018).

Average of Likert-scored responses (Very often/Often/Sometimes/Rarely/Never) to: 'How often can you solve problems if you only try hard enough?', 'How often can you succeed in what you set out to do?', 'How often does your stomach hurt?'; standardized to mean 0, SD 1 in the full population.

Years of completed schooling from the 2020 Register on Completed Education (status on October 1); levels collapsed into (i) lower secondary (max ten years of schooling), (ii) academic high school, (iii) vocational degrees (vocational high school and short vocational college degrees), (iv) all college and university degrees.
Preschool enrollment measured from annual daycare register data.

Earnings = pre-tax wage earnings + self-employment income + business profits; disposable income = pre-tax earnings + public transfers - taxes; employment = positive earnings; measured from first year after residency; 2020 PPP-adjusted USD.

Convictions for offences against the criminal code (court ruling of guilt resulting in a fine, suspended sentence or imprisonment), dated by exact offence date; e.g. 'crime in year 1' = offence committed within the first 365 days after residency.
For children aged 7-14 at exposure: average annual earnings at 17-18 in bins $0-1,499, $1,500-2,999, $3,000-4,499, $4,500+; working (earnings > 0) crossed with studying.

authors: Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen and Alan Manning
title: Background Matters, but Not Whether Parents Are Immigrants: Outcomes of Children Born in Denmark
summary: Children born in Denmark to immigrant parents have lower earnings, more unemployment, less education, more transfers and more convictions than children of Danish-born parents. Conditional on parental socioeconomic characteristics, however, they do as well or slightly better, so the gaps reflect deprived backgrounds rather than immigrant parentage.
data: Danish register data linking children to parents (Statistics Denmark, 1980–2017)
Income and earnings registers (annual labour income incl. self-employment, transfers)
Monthly employment register (hours, hourly wages, from 2008)
Education registers (incl. survey-based registration of foreign education of immigrants)
Criminal justice registers (convictions, prison sentences, dropped charges / not-guilty verdicts)
Occupation codes (ISCO88)
variables: Group: number of parents born outside Denmark (0, 1, 2; Greenland/Faroe Islands)
Outcome: earnings and unemployment at age 30
Outcome: public transfers, completed education by age 30
Outcome: criminal convictions, prison sentences, dropped charges
Controls: parental income, unemployment years, occupation and education during childhood
sample_size: 396,417 children (Table 1 total); 362,460 with two Danish-born parents, 10,399 with two immigrant parents, 20,908 with one immigrant parent, 2,650 with a parent from Greenland/Faroe Islands
sample: All children born in Denmark 1980–1987 with both parents known, followed to age 30.

definitions.definition: Everyone born in Denmark 1980-1987 with both parents known in BEF and known parental origin. Observed in the year they turn 30, kept only if fully liable to pay taxes in Denmark (AKM register) and resident in Denmark (BEF).
