definitions.definition: Enrolment: indicator for ever having been enrolled in a STEM study at college level or higher. Completion: field of the highest obtained degree is STEM. STEM = ISCED fields Natural Sciences, Mathematics and Statistics (05), ICT (06), and Engineering, Manufacturing and Construction (07); split into subfields Biology, Math and Physics, ICT and Engineering, and a fourth group.
definitions.codes: ISCED-F 2013 fields 05, 06, 07; comparison fields ISCED 091 (health), 01 (education), 02 (arts/humanities), 031 (social sciences), 04 (business/law)
definitions.source_location: Section II.D outcome description and footnote 21

definitions.definition: Share of female students in the student's high school math-track cohort at high school entry, constructed at the cohort-school-track level and excluding the student (leave-one-out).

All students entering the math track of general (academic) high school 1980-1994; excludes students missing gender/age, students not aged 14-19 at entry, schools where under 95 percent of a cohort is aged 14-19, school-cohorts with fewer than 10 students, and schools not admitting students for at least four consecutive years.
Indicator for working in a high-skilled STEM occupation for at least half the years observed in 11-15 and 16-20 years after high school entry.

Average of the individual's annual labour earnings percentile over a five-year period (11-15 and 16-20 years after high school entry), with percentiles computed by year of birth and age using the entire Danish population as reference; earnings in 2015 DKK.
Number of children by age 36, and timing of first child.

authors: Claudio Labanca and Dario Pozzoli
title: Constraints on Hours within the Firm
summary: Uses Danish linked employer-employee data with hours and tax-rate variation from the 2010 Danish tax reform. Employees in firms with tight constraints on working hours do not adjust their hours when their taxes change, while employees in more flexible firms respond both directly and through spillovers from their coworkers.
data: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Wage statistics with annual regular and overtime hours (Lønstatistikken, LON)
Firm Statistics Register (Firmstat)
Danish Foreign Trade Statistics Register
Firm-Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (FIDA)
Danish Tax Register (income tax records)
O*NET occupational data
variables: Outcome: annual hours worked (regular plus overtime)
Treatment: change in simulated marginal tax rate from the 2010 Danish tax reform (2008–2011 interval)
Moderator: firm-level hours constraints/coordination measured by within-firm dispersion of hours
Hourly wage: annual earnings over total hours
Spillovers: tax changes of coworkers
sample_size: more than 400,000 employees and approximately 8,300 firms (787,683 individual-year observations)
sample: Full-time employees aged 15–65 in private firms where hours are reported for at least 95% of the workforce, 2003–2011 (working-paper version 'Coordination of Hours within the Firm', IZA DP 12062).

definitions.definition: Annual hours of regular plus overtime work from Lønstatistikken (LON), reported by employers whose pension contributions depend on hours. Only firms where hours are observed for at least 95 percent of the workforce are kept; for spells in week 48 shorter than a year, hours and earnings are annualized.
Annual earnings divided by the sum of regular and overtime hours.

Each employee is matched to the highest-paying employer in the employment spell of week 48 (FIDA). Sample: full-time employees aged 15-65 in 2003-2011, full-time defined (official definition) as working more than an average of 26 weekly hours over a year, in private firms covered by Firmstat.

definitions.variable: Hours coordination (dispersion of hours across skill groups)
definitions.definition: Standard deviation across skill groups in a firm-year of the average annual (regular plus overtime) hours of each skill group; firm measure is its average over 2003-2011. Lower dispersion means greater coordination. Skill groups are deciles of the sum of the fixed and time-varying individual components of an AKM hourly-wage model; alternative: education (primary/secondary/tertiary) x occupation (manager/middle manager/blue collar) cells.

Marginal tax rate on labour income simulated from the Danish Tax Register with an extension of the Kleven-Schultz (2014) tax simulator to 2006-2011: increase in tax liability from raising labour income by 100 DKK, holding other income components fixed. Changes are taken over the 2008-2011 interval.

Post-reform (2011) marginal tax rate simulated using pre-reform (2008) income adjusted for inflation; the log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate from this mechanical rate instruments the observed change. For spillovers, the firm average of mechanical changes among high-income workers instruments the change in their average hours.

Low-income: tax-exempt or in the bottom tax bracket in 2008. High-income: in the middle or top bracket in 2008, excluding a residual group in the top bracket in 2008 predicted (from 2008 real income and the post-reform schedule) to fall into the bottom bracket in 2011.

Value added per employee and TFP from Firmstat accounting data; in some specifications value added per employee is instrumented with TFP. Construction details are in an online appendix not included in the WP.

authors: Emma von Essen and Nina Smith
title: Network Connections and Board Seats: Are Female Networks Less Valuable?
summary: Uses Danish employer-employee data from 1995 to 2011 to study how professional networks affect first appointments to supervisory boards. Larger networks raise the chance of a board seat, more so for men, because men's networks connect them more often to larger and listed firms and to other men.
data: Matched employer-employee data for the Danish labour market
variables: Outcome: first-time appointment to a supervisory board
Explanatory: size of professional network
Heterogeneity: gender
Network composition: connections to large/listed firms, to men, and to incumbent directors
sample: Danish workers observed in employer-employee data 1995–2011, studied for first-time supervisory board appointments.

authors: Anne Toft Hansen, Ulrik Hvidman and Hans Henrik Sievertsen
title: Grades and Employer Learning
summary: Uses a nationwide rescaling of Danish university grades to identify the return to GPA that is unrelated to ability. A reform-induced higher GPA raises earnings right after graduation, especially for graduates with fewer other signals, but the effect fades within a few years, consistent with employers learning quickly about productivity.
data: University student records (Aarhus University and University of Copenhagen) with grades before and after the 2007 recoding
Administrative registers from Statistics Denmark (background, parental income and education, earnings)
variables: Outcome: log total gross earnings in each of the first five calendar years after graduation
Treatment: reform-induced change in GPA from the 1 August 2007 recoding to the new grading scale
Outcome: indicator for positive earnings
Controls: gender, age at graduation, high school GPA, parental income, employment and education
period: Students enrolled on 1 August 2007 who graduated before 2011; earnings for the first five years after graduation
sample_size: 3,813 students
sample: Master's students at Aarhus University or University of Copenhagen enrolled on 1 August 2007 with at most 40 ECTS remaining who graduated before 2011.

definitions.definition: Deviation of a student's recoded (post-1 August 2007, 7-point scale) GPA from a cubic fit of post-recoding GPA on pre-recoding (13-scale) GPA; grades were recoded per the Ministry of Education mapping. Final GPA is a weighted average of recoded grades and grades from exams after the recoding.
registers: University student records (Aarhus University, University of Copenhagen)

definitions.definition: Students enrolled in a master's program on 1 August 2007 at Aarhus University (incl. Aarhus School of Business) or University of Copenhagen with at most 40 ECTS points remaining on the recoding date, who graduated before 2011 (3,813 students).

definitions.variable: Log total gross earnings after graduation
definitions.definition: Log total gross earnings in each of the first five calendar years after graduation; individuals with zero earnings excluded. A separate extensive-margin outcome is an indicator for positive earnings. Monetary values in 2015 prices (CPI).

Log disposable income (after transfers and taxes), unemployment, public-sector employment, job changes, annual earnings growth, and earnings growth with the same employer, in each of the first five years after graduation.

Parental income (mean total disposable income across observed parents, calendar year before graduation/reform), parental unemployment (mean annual unemployment), indicator for at least one parent with a university degree, and parental origin (non-Western vs Western per Statistics Denmark); missing values set to zero with missing dummies.
Low earnings while studying used as a proxy for little relevant labour-market experience; Aarhus University attendance used as a further proxy.

authors: Jonas Fluchtmann, Anita M. Glenny, Nikolaj A. Harmon and Jonas Maibom
title: Unemployed Job Search across People and over Time: Evidence from Applied-For Jobs
summary: Uses the logs of job applications made by Danish unemployment insurance recipients to document how the jobs people apply for differ across job seekers and change over an unemployment spell, and what these patterns imply for models of directed search.
data: Joblog applied-for job records (Danish Agency for Labour Market and Recruitment)
DREAM event-history register of public transfers
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Employment statistics for employees with hours and earnings (BFL)
Firm purchases data (FIKS)
Auxiliary survey of UI recipients on application coverage
O*NET Related Occupation Matrix
variables: Outcome: predicted log wage of applied-for jobs (occupation and AKM firm effect)
Outcome: share of applied-for jobs that are full-time
Outcome: scope of search index (commute time, related occupation, related industry)
Outcome: share of applications to publicly posted vacancies
Time variable: month of unemployment spell
sample_size: 127,695 individuals (spells) and over 4 million applied-for jobs
sample: Individuals of Danish origin starting UI spells between September 2015 and September 2017, eligible for the full two years of benefits, with spells of at least 8 weeks and at least one registered application.

definitions.definition: New UI spell: at least 4 consecutive weeks of UI benefit payments with no UI payout in the 4 weeks before spell start (DREAM). Spell ends with 4 consecutive weeks without UI paid out; followed for a year or until exit.

Individuals of Danish origin (immigrants excluded) starting UI spells September 2015-September 2017 with full two-year UI eligibility; spell lasts at least 8 weeks; applications in the last 4 weeks of a spell dropped; at least one Joblog application registered; first spell only. 127,695 spells.

Log wage predicted for each applied-for job from re-employment wages of new hires: post-LASSO OLS (Rigorous-LASSO selects 233 of 10,407 regressors) on 1-, 2- and 3-digit industry and occupation dummies, an AKM-availability dummy, the within-industry-demeaned AKM firm effect, and all pairwise interactions; averaged per recipient-month. Robustness uses the AKM firm effect directly.
definitions.codes: DISCO-08 and NACE Rev. 2 at 1-3 digits

definitions.definition: Firm fixed effects from an AKM log-wage model estimated on BFL matched employer-employee data 2008-2015 (290,108 connected firms) with year-month fixed effects; worker-weighted industry means removed after estimation.
Share of a recipient's applied-for jobs in a month reported as full-time by the UI recipient in Joblog (full-time in Denmark is 37 hours per week).

Standardized combination of average commute time to applied-for jobs (Google Maps driving times from residence municipality to firm address, Harmon 2013), share in an occupation unrelated to the previous job (not among the O*NET top-10 related occupations, mapped to 3-digit DISCO), and share in an unrelated industry (not among the 10 most skill-related 3-digit NACE Rev. 2 industries, Neffke and Henning 2013); restandardized by first-month mean and SD.

definitions.variable: Share of applications to publicly posted vacancies
definitions.definition: Monthly share of applied-for jobs that the job seeker reports in Joblog as found via a publicly posted vacancy (other channels: network, contacted by firm/headhunter, cold contact).
Firm purchases from FIKS, built from mandatory VAT reports; firm employment computed from BFL.

authors: Anne Ardila Brenøe, Serena Canaan, Nikolaj A. Harmon and Heather N. Royer
title: Is Parental Leave Costly for Firms and Coworkers?
summary: Compares small Danish firms where a female employee is about to give birth with similar firms without an impending birth. There is little evidence of negative effects on firm output or coworkers: most firms cover the absence by hiring temporary workers and raising other employees' hours, and only firms unable to reallocate work show losses.
data: Central Person Registry with parent-child links (CPR/BEF)
Parental leave benefit payouts and employer leave reimbursements
Central education register (UDDA)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Annual employer wage payment records (CON and RAS)
Mandatory pension contributions for approximate hours (ATP)
Value-added tax (VAT) firm sales and purchases data
variables: Treatment: a female employee at a small private firm giving birth (event year)
Outcome: firm employment, FTE hours, wage bill (total and excluding leave), sales, gross profit proxy, survival
Outcome: coworker hours, earnings, employment and sick days
Mechanism: parental leave days at the firm
Design: dynamic difference-in-differences with matched control events
sample_size: 24,829 treatment events (births) and 162,151 control events covering 45,940 unique firms; 9,934 treatment events in 16,080 firms after trimming
sample: Births to prime-age (21–35) women employed in small private-sector Danish firms, compared with matched control firms without such births.

definitions.definition: Potential event = a woman's main job at a firm in a baseline year; event year = baseline + 2. Treatment event: woman gives birth in the event year but not in the year before or after; control event: no birth in the event year, the year before or the year after. Woman aged 19-33 at baseline, at least one year tenure at the baseline firm and not a student.

Private-sector firm (CVR) with 3-30 employees in November of the baseline year and fewer than 60 employment relationships during the baseline year; active at baseline (hours at least one FTE, positive sales and wage payments in baseline, positive sales or wages the year before); sales per employee 10,000 DKK-100 million DKK and wages per worker 10,000 DKK-1 million DKK.

Standard IDA main November employment relationship: worker counted at the firm if their main job was there in the last week of November; includes workers on leave. Main job = job with most hours, ties broken by highest earnings.

Approximate yearly hours from mandatory ATP pension contributions (step schedule for 0-9, 9-17, 18-26 and 27+ weekly hours, topping out at full time, 37 hours), scaled to full-time equivalents (Lund and Vejlin 2016); share of year on paid parental leave subtracted since ATP continues during paid leave. Misses overtime.

definitions.variable: Wage bill and wage bill ex. leave
definitions.definition: Total wage bill = sum of all pre-tax payments to workers in the year (from CON and RAS), including payments to workers on paid leave. Wage bill ex. leave: each worker's wage = payments / ATP hours incl. paid leave, multiplied by hours excluding paid leave; the gap (paid leave covered by the firm) is subtracted from the total wage bill.

definitions.variable: Sales, gross profit proxy and survival
definitions.definition: Total sales and purchases from VAT data (corrected to include exports; negative values recoded to zero). Gross profit proxy = sales minus purchases minus wage bill ex. leave (purchases include capital equipment). Total variable costs = purchases + wage bill ex. leave. Exiting firms kept with zero employees/hours/sales; shutdown proxied by zero sales.

Total days of paid and unpaid leave from payouts of parental leave benefits to individuals and leave reimbursements to firms, incl. pregnancy-related extensions; prenatal and postnatal days allocated around the birth; truncated at 38 weeks any prenatal, 6 weeks paid prenatal, 52 weeks paid postnatal, 104 weeks any postnatal.

Male and female coworkers of event women in the baseline year whose job at the baseline firm is their main labour market attachment, with hours at least half an FTE and earnings above 75,000 DKK in the baseline year; followed even if they leave the firm.
Take-up of publicly paid sick days (any sick days); eligibility for public sickness funds starts after two weeks of sickness, so the measure captures longer sickness spells.

authors: Mette Foged, Linea Hasager and Giovanni Peri
title: Comparing the Effects of Policies for the Labor Market Integration of Refugees
summary: Uses quasi-experimental variation from several Danish reforms to compare, in a common framework, the long-run employment and earnings effects of language training, active labour market programmes and benefit cuts for refugees, and ranks the policies by their effects and costs.
data: Admission Register (OPHG)
Migration register (VNDS)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Income register (IND)
Population register (BEF)
Education register (UDDA)
Family register (FAM)
variables: Outcome: employment (any employment in the year)
Outcome: annual gross labour earnings (2015 USD)
Policy 1: initial dispersal across municipalities (conditional random assignment)
Policy 2: 1999 language training reform (RD at 1 January 1999 admission)
Policy 3: Start Aid welfare benefit cut (RD at 1 July 2002 admission)
Policy 4: 'Industry Packages' ALMP rolled out across municipalities 2015–2018
period: 1986–2008 refugee arrivals (outcomes followed up to 15 years; ALMP analysis January 2008–April 2019)
sample_size: 56,192 adult refugees
sample: Refugees and family-reunified refugees aged 18–55 on arrival who settled in a Danish municipality 1986–2008, split into policy-specific arrival cohorts.

definitions.definition: Refugees and family members reunified with refugees identified from admission category in the Admission Register (OPHG) from 1997 onward; refugee status before 1997 imputed from year of arrival and country of origin. Date of first settlement in Denmark and later out-migration from the migration register (VNDS); refugees followed from first settlement in a municipality (within two months of being granted status), 1986-2008 arrivals.

Indicator equal to one if the individual was employed at some point in the year (IDA). Appendix alternative: employment as a fraction of a full working year. For the ALMP analysis, monthly any-employment.

Annual gross labour market income from the income register (IND), converted to US dollars at 2015 prices; short/medium/long-run outcomes are individual averages over years 1-5, 6-10 and 11-15 since asylum. Monthly version (ALMP) multiplied by 12.

definitions.variable: Initial placement: municipal labour market strength and co-nationals
definitions.definition: For the conditionally random dispersal (refugees granted status 1987-1998): employment rate of non-Western immigrants in the municipality of first placement in the placement year, and share of co-nationals in that municipality's population; both divided by their SD.

Refugees granted status 1997-2000 (Somalis excluded); treatment = recognized after 1 January 1999, giving eligibility to 430 additional hours of language training in the first 3 years. RD on days between grant date and cutoff, triangular kernel, 548-day bandwidth.

Refugees arriving 2001-2003 (Bosnians and Afghans omitted); treatment = admitted after 1 July 2002, when Start Aid reduced welfare benefits (cut reversed in 2012). RD with triangular kernel and 548-day bandwidth around the admission-date cutoff.

Exposure = share of a refugee's first year in the municipality during which the Industry Packages program was available; monthly refugee-arrival cohorts January 2008-April 2019 observed one year after placement; Vejle implemented August 2013, other municipalities 2015 to early 2018.
Linguistically far = refugees from countries with non-Latin-based languages; close = Latin-based (country-based because mother tongue is only available around 1999).

authors: Jacob Nielsen Arendt, Christian Dustmann and Hyejin Ku
title: Permanent Residency and Refugee Immigrants' Skill Investment
summary: A Danish reform tightened the employment and language requirements refugees must meet to obtain permanent residency. Rather than encouraging investment, it lowered overall employment and barely moved language proficiency, because refugees with weak pre-reform prospects reduced effort when the requirements looked out of reach.
data: Population, income, education and immigration registers linked via the Central Person Registry
Danish language test results
Employment in annual full-time equivalents (register data)
variables: Outcome: annual employment in full-time equivalents
Outcome: passing the Danish language test at intermediate or higher level
Treatment: temporary residency in Jan–Oct 2004 (exposed to the 2007 permanent-residency reform) vs Jan–Oct 2003
Heterogeneity: pre-reform employment or language performance type
Time: years since temporary residency (YSR 1–7)
period: Residency cohorts 2003–2004, followed seven years since temporary residency (to 2011)
sample_size: 767 unique individuals; 5,122 person-year observations
sample: Refugees aged 18–64 who applied for asylum after 28 February 2002 and received temporary residency in Jan–Oct 2003 (control) or Jan–Oct 2004 (treatment).

definitions.definition: Employment in annual full-time equivalents (FTE = 1 for a full year of work), from a register variable recording cumulative employment in a calendar year, observed for everyone in Denmark on 1 January. For YSR = 1 only, FTE can exceed 1 because the cumulative variable includes work in the year residency was granted.
definitions.source_location: Section 5 'Data on Refugee Immigrants' and footnote 17

definitions.definition: Indicator for having passed the standard Danish language test at the intermediate or higher level (test levels: basic, intermediate, high); observed from YSR = 1; passing is treated as absorbing, so the person counts as proficient at that level in all later periods.

Refugees who applied for asylum after 28 February 2002 and were aged 18-64 when granted temporary residency; treatment = temporary residency granted January-October 2004 (exposed to the 1 May 2007 permanent-residency reform), control = January-October 2003.
For persons granted temporary residency during year y, YSR = 1 is year y+1 (first full calendar year with employment observed as of 1 January), followed for seven years (YSR 1-7).
HIGH if cumulative employment by YSR = 2 is above 0.75 FTE, otherwise LOW (20% HIGH, 80% LOW). The reform's requirement is 2.5 FTE of cumulative employment.
HIGH if the person had passed the Danish language test at the intermediate level or higher by YSR = 2 (about 16%), otherwise LOW; combined with employment type into LOW/LOW, LOW/HIGH, etc.

Danish natives selected by propensity-score matching to treated (control) refugees on YSR = 1 employment (2005 for treated, 2004 for control), age, gender, being single, having any children and county of residence (initial assignment county for refugees), used in a triple-difference check for the 2009 recession.

authors: Sadegh Eshaghnia, James J. Heckman and Rasmus Landersø
title: The Impact of the Level and Timing of Parental Resources on Child Development and Intergenerational Mobility
summary: Uses Danish registers covering parents' full income histories to separate the level of parents' lifetime resources from their timing during childhood. Lifetime resources matter far more than when income arrives, and conventional intergenerational elasticities based on short income windows give a misleading picture of mobility.
data: Population register with family links (BEF)
Education register (UDDA)
Income, assets and transfers register (IND)
Sentencing register (KRAF)
Incarceration register (KRIN)
Danish Household Expenditure Survey
Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (DALSC)
9th-grade national leaving exam scores
variables: Outcome: child income at ages 30–35 (IGE)
Outcome: years of education by age 35
Outcome: any criminal conviction by age 35
Outcome: math test score at age 16 and language test at age 11
Explanatory: level and timing of parental income/resources by child age (lifetime vs snapshot)
sample_size: around 100,000 children and their families (105,953 individuals; 98,686 in the IGE log-log sample)
sample: Children born in 1981 and 1982 linked to their parents, non-migrants with non-migrant parents; plus the 1995–1997 birth cohorts for exam scores and DALSC children born 1995.

definitions.definition: Pre-tax taxable wage earnings plus other wage-type income such as fringe benefits and stock options; parental resources are the sum of mother's and father's amounts irrespective of marital status, measured at each age of the child.

Total personal income (wage income, business and self-employment income, capital income, public transfer income, property income and other non-classifiable personal income) plus the rental value of own home for owner-occupiers, minus taxes and interest expenses. Spouses' or cohabitees' resources pooled where appropriate.

Expected present value at age t of future disposable income (adjusted for unrealized housing capital gains) discounted with a subjective stochastic discount factor (beta = 0.96), where expectations condition on an estimated information set (gender, education level, employment status, cohabitation, number of children, quartiles of mean income, mean consumption, consumption growth and consumption SD, homeownership, and interactions).

Household consumption predicted from register disposable income and assets and liabilities in t and t-1 by a random forest (number of trees by 5-fold cross-validation) trained on the Danish Household Expenditure Survey (1997+); adult-equivalent using the OECD equivalence scale.
Minimum number of years it takes to complete the highest degree obtained by age 35.

Indicator for appearing in the crime registers (criminal convictions from the sentencing register KRAF) by age 35, regardless of offence type. Appendix D.2 splits into violent, property (e.g. forgery, arson, burglary, theft, shoplifting, embezzlement, fraud, extortion, robbery, tax fraud, vandalism) and other crimes (all except violent, property and traffic), measured by ages 20, 25 and 30.
definitions.source_location: Section 3.1, footnote 17; Appendix A.1; Appendix D.2

definitions.definition: Mathematics grade at the 9th-grade national leaving exam for all children born 1995-1997, standardised to mean 0 and SD 1.
Language development test at age 11 from the Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (children born 15 Sept-31 Oct 1995, 2007 wave), standardised to mean 0 and SD 1.

Children born 1981-1982 linked to parents, with neither child nor parents having migrated (105,953); child resources averaged over ages 30-35; for log-log IGE, zero/negative average income and incomes more than 4 SD from the mean dropped (100,344) and children with fewer than three observations dropped (98,686).

authors: Eskil Heinesen, Christian Hvid, Lars Kirkebøen, Edwin Leuven and Magne Mogstad
title: Instrumental Variables with Unordered Treatments: Theory and Evidence from Returns to Fields of Study
summary: Shows that the assumptions needed to identify returns to unordered treatments, such as fields of study, have testable implications, and characterises the bias when they fail. Using admission cut-offs and applicants' ranked choices in Denmark and Norway, payoffs to fields are strongly correlated across the two countries once fields violating the assumptions are dropped.
data: Danish administrative data on all applications to post-secondary education 1994–2002 (coordinated admission system)
Population register and other registers (background, completed field of study, annual earnings)
Norwegian post-secondary application data 1998–2004 linked to registers (comparison country)
variables: Outcome: annual earnings eight years after application (wages, self-employment and income-replacing transfers)
Treatment: completed field of study (nine broad fields)
Instrument: application score just above vs below the admission cutoff of the preferred field
Preferred and next-best field from applicants' rankings
period: Applications 1994–2002 (Denmark), outcomes eight years after application
sample: First-time applicants to Danish post-secondary education without a prior post-secondary degree who applied to at least two broad fields, with the preferred field having an admission cutoff, and who completed a field within eight years (paralleled with Norwegian applicants).

definitions.variable: Annual earnings eight years after application
definitions.definition: Annual earnings eight years after the first observed application: wage income, self-employment income and transfers replacing such income (short-term sickness pay, paid parental leave), excluding unemployment benefits; deflated by CPI (base 2011) and converted to 1,000s of USD at 2010-2016 average rates (5.9 DKK per USD).

definitions.variable: Completed field of study (nine broad fields)
definitions.definition: Field of the post-secondary degree completed within eight years of application, aggregating detailed fields into nine broad fields (Medicine, Law, Technology, Other Health, Humanities, Teaching, Social Science, Business, Science) following Kirkeboen et al. (2016), except that Technology covers integrated, vocational/professional short- and long-cycle degrees (mostly computer science and engineering) and Science covers open-ended bachelor programmes in sciences plus agriculture, forestry and aquaculture.

z = 1[GPA > Q1] + 1[Std <= GPA <= Q1] x Offer, where Q1 and Std are the Quota 1 and standby GPA thresholds of the preferred field; at GPA exactly equal to a threshold the offer is treated as random conditional on age (and on applying for standby). Applicants rank up to 8 programmes; where several programmes in the preferred broad field are listed, the lowest cutoff is used.

Defined from the local ranking on the application list around the admission cutoff: the preferred field is the one ranked just above the next-best field, where the applicant's score is near the preferred field's cutoff; fixed effects for preferred-field x next-best-field combinations are included.

All applications to post-secondary education 1994-2002 (Denmark; Norway 1998-2004); first observed application kept; those already holding a post-secondary degree excluded; restricted to those who completed a field within eight years and who applied to at least two broad fields with the most-preferred field having an admission cutoff.

High-school GPA over all subjects of the study programme, recorded to one decimal on the 13-point scale (0-13, omitting 1, 2, 4, 12); used as the running variable, controlled linearly on each side of the cutoff.

authors: Anders Frederiksen, Takao Kato and Nina Smith
title: Working Hours, Top Management Appointments, and Gender: Evidence from Linked Employer-Employee Data
summary: Links the Danish Labour Force Survey's detailed hours to register career histories. Long hours, hours relative to peers and nonstandard hours raise the odds of a top management appointment within the firm, and the gender gap in hours, driven mainly by supply-side factors, is a major contributor to the gender gap in reaching top management.
data: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Danish Labour Force Survey (DLFS/AKU) linked on person identifier
Organizational hierarchy codes (occupation-based) from registers
variables: Outcome: appointment to a top management position between year t and t+1
Explanatory: weekly working hours from the Labour Force Survey in year t
Heterogeneity: gender (gender gap in hours and promotions)
Hierarchy level: top manager, manager, white-collar, blue/grey-collar
Controls: experience, tenure, education, children, marital status
sample_size: 168,499 employees
sample: Danish employees randomly sampled in the Labour Force Survey 1994–2010, merged with IDA register data (IZA DP 11675 working-paper version).

definitions.definition: Job level from the RAS socioeconomic job code: 131 = top manager, 132 = (function) manager, 133 = white-collar, 134 or 135 = blue/grey-collar. Only persons with job_socio_kode 131-135 are extracted from RAS (from 1994 on).
definitions.codes: RAS job_socio_kode 131 (top manager), 132 (function manager), 133 (white collar), 134-135 (blue/grey collar)
definitions.source_location: 3 Produce regression data.do, section 'INFORMATION ABOUT JOBLEVEL FROM RAS'; 1 Produce IDA project data.sas (RAS extract)

definitions.definition: prom1 = 1 if the person is a function manager (pos = 2, RAS code 132) in year t and a top manager (pos = 1, RAS code 131) in year t+1 (lead of position in the person-year panel). Logit models for prom1 are estimated on managers (pos = 2) only; in the multinomial version, promotions are split into internal (same workplace lbnr in t+1) and external (new workplace).
definitions.source_location: 3 Produce regression data.do ('promotion categories'); 4 Tables and figures.do (Table 6 mlogit)

definitions.definition: Actual and usual weekly hours from the Labour Force Survey (AKU), harmonised across file versions (hwactual/timuf/b7timuf/v51; hwusual/...); values >= 97 set to missing; only the first AKU observation per person (by year and reference week) is kept, years 1996-2018, and observations with zero or missing hours are dropped. Regressions use hours/100 and interval dummies (<37, 37, 38-47, >=48 hours).
definitions.codes: h_actual, h_usual; missing if >= 97; dummies ha0_36, ha37, ha38_47, hagt48
definitions.source_location: 2 Produce AKU data.do; 3 Produce regression data.do (interval dummies)

definitions.definition: Indicators from AKU for evening, night, Saturday, Sunday and shift work (value 9 = missing). d_frequent = 1 if evening, night, Saturday or Sunday work equals 1 (frequently); d_sometimes = 1 if any equals 2 (sometimes).
definitions.codes: AKU evenwk/omaften/v205, nightwk/omnat/v206, satwk/loerdage/v207, sunwk/soendage/v208, shiftwk/skifteho/v204; 9 = missing
definitions.source_location: 2 Produce AKU data.do; 3 Produce regression data.do ('work flexibility')

definitions.definition: Accumulated labour market experience from IDAP: erhverv_akk/1000 plus erhverv_1979/1000 (pre-1979 experience, set to 0 if missing), rounded to whole years.

Primary job from IDAN (job_type = 'H', workplace lbnr != 0); tenure = year minus ansaar (hiring year), set to missing if > 50 or < 0. Workplace size = number of IDAN primary-job employees per lbnr and year.
definitions.source_location: 3 Produce regression data.do, 'TENURE AND WORKPLACE ID FROM IDAN'

definitions.definition: Highest completed education from UDDA HFAUDD grouped: 1000-1999 high school or less; 2000-3999 vocational (IVU/erhvervsfaglig); 4000-4999 short cycle (KVU); 5000-5999 and 8500-8999 medium (MVU, 'Master'); 6000-8499 long (LVU); >=9000 or missing other. HFAUDD = 1 dropped; 3-digit codes multiplied by 10.
private = 1 if RAS job function code (1996-2007) is 32, 42, 52, 80 or 90, or RAS sector code (2008-2016) is 18, 28, 32, 38, 42, 48, 52, 58, 62 or 81; 0 otherwise; job_funktion_kode 99 dropped.
definitions.codes: JOB_FUNKTION_KODE in 32,42,52,80,90; JOB_SEKTOR_KODE in 18,28,32,38,42,48,52,58,62,81; drop JOB_FUNKTION_KODE 99

definitions.definition: Workplace industry from IDAS: 6-digit DB77/93 code (DB03 after 2003) and DB07 code, mapped to about 12 groups (primary, manufacturing, utilities, construction, trade, transport, finance, real estate/business services, public administration, education, health/social, other) by code ranges, e.g. DB07 840000-849999 public administration, 850000-859999 education, 860000-899999 health and social.
definitions.codes: ARB_BRANCHE_DB7793 / ARB_BRANCHE_DB03 / ARB_BRANCHE_DB07 ranges as in do-file

definitions.definition: Firm sales (oms_firm) and total exports (eksport_ialt) from the IDA firm file; exporter = 1 if exports > 0. Merged by CVR number.
definitions.source_location: 3 Produce regression data.do, 'EXPORT AND SALES FROM FIRM'

definitions.definition: Partner = 1 if civil status CIVST is 'G' (married) or 'P' (registered partnership); number of children and age of youngest/oldest child from the IDA family file (c_antboernf, c_aldyngst, c_aldaeldst), with dummies for youngest/oldest child aged 0-2, 3-4, 5+.
definitions.codes: CIVST in G, P; c_antboernf, c_aldyngst, c_aldaeldst
definitions.source_location: 3 Produce regression data.do, PERSONER and FAMILIE sections

authors: Frederik Almar, Benjamin Friedrich, Ana Reynoso, Bastian Schulz and Rune Vejlin
title: Educational Ambition, Marital Sorting, and Inequality
summary: Classifies detailed Danish education programmes into ambition types by their graduates' starting wages and wage growth. Assortative matching by educational ambition has risen sharply even though sorting by conventional education levels looks flat, and the marriage market accounts for more than 40 percent of the rise in household income inequality since 1980.
data: Population register with partner links (BEF)
Education register with four-digit ISCED programme codes (UDDA)
Employment register with hourly wages (IDAN)
Income register (IND)
Danish Labour Force Survey (LFS/AKU), 2000–2018
Employment register for hours, part-time/full-time (RAS)
variables: Classification: educational 'ambition types' from programme-level starting wages and wage growth (about 1,800 programmes)
Outcome: marital sorting by ambition type (assortative matching)
Outcome: household labour income inequality
Wage measure: residualised log hourly wages by programme
LFS job attributes: hours, evening/weekend/home work
sample_size: on average 3,031,511 individuals per year aged 19–60; 1,800,866 individuals in couples per year
sample: All individuals living in Denmark aged 19–60 in 1980–2018, with couples defined as married or cohabiting opposite-sex partners.

definitions.definition: Hourly wage in the primary job held in the last week of November (IDAN), ranking job types H, 3, A, S, M and keeping the highest; variable TIMELON before 2008 and SMAL_TIMELOEN from 2008. Log hourly wages are regressed on year dummies (base 2000) and education-specific experience profiles, and the year coefficients are subtracted. Hours underlying the wage are contractual (pre-2008 in four bins).
definitions.codes: TIMELON (<2008), SMAL_TIMELOEN (>=2008); JOB_TYPE rank H,3,A,S,M; reg log_wage ib2000.aar i.educ_eika#c.erhverv_akk_new
definitions.source_location: Data/Gen_sample1_new/Make analysis sample 1.do; IZA DP 17814 Online Appendix A.1 fn. 35 and A.2

definitions.definition: Highest completed education (HFAUDD, four-digit Danish ISCED/audd code, about 1,800 programmes) measured at age 35, or at the oldest observed age if the person is not observed at 35; graduation year from HF_VFRA. Grades 7-9 pooled as 9th grade; 9th grade (1109) and 10th grade (1110) split into 5 sub-programmes by region of graduation (regions 81-85); old pre-1980 high-school code mapped to the new one.
definitions.codes: HFAUDD, HF_VFRA; 1109 and 1110 split by region 81-85; 1097 mapped to 1198
definitions.source_location: Make analysis sample 1.do ('final education'); kmeans ambition types.do; Online Appendix A.2 'Education', 'Educational programs'

definitions.variable: Programme starting wage (w0) and wage growth (g)
definitions.definition: For each individual graduating in 1980 or later: w0 = mean residualised log hourly wage in years 1-5 after graduation; w1 = mean in years 9-11. Programme-level values average across graduates observed in both windows, excluding those with individual wage growth exp(w1-w0)-1 at or above the 99th percentile; programme growth g = exp(mean w1 - mean w0) - 1.
definitions.source_location: Make analysis sample 1.do ('peer wage growth'); Online Appendix A.2 'Starting wages and growth'

definitions.definition: Programmes are clustered by k-means on (programme starting wage, programme wage growth), with k = 3, 4 or 5 (seed 1234), both in raw and standardised versions; the four-type classification gives the (low/high w0) x (low/high g) ambition types.
definitions.codes: cluster kmeans wage_start_mean_ambition wage_growth_ambition, k(4) s(kr(1234))

definitions.definition: Relationship = married (CIVST = 'G') or with a cohabitation partner id (FAELLE_NR non-missing); couple id is the man's PNR, linked through AEGTE_NR (spouse) or FAELLE_NR (cohabitant). Only couples where both partners are observed and both are aged 19-60 are kept.
definitions.source_location: kmeans ambition types.do, 'Define marital status' and 'Make couple ID'

definitions.definition: All persons living in Denmark at end of year 1980-2018 aged 19-60, irrespective of marital status (about 3.0 million per year); persons with missing education (2.6%) excluded.
definitions.source_location: Make analysis sample 1.do; paper Section 2 (IZA DP 17814)

definitions.definition: Residence municipality (BOPAEL_KOM_KODE) mapped from pre-2007 to post-2007 municipalities using each person's modal 2005-to-2006 transition, then grouped into the five regions 81-85 by municipality code lists; region in the graduation year (or first observed year) is used.
definitions.codes: BOPAEL_KOM_KODE; region 81 (Nordjylland) ... 85 (Sjaelland) via inlist() of municipality codes

definitions.definition: Full-time from RAS: at least 32 hours per week (threshold 30 hours in 1980-1992 and 27 hours in 1993-2007). Part-time penalty = ratio of w1 (wage in years 9-11 after graduation) of full-time workers to that of part-time workers, by programme.

From LFS (AKU, 2000-2018): sft = 1 if usual weekly hours >= 38, or = 37 combined with evening, night, Saturday, Sunday or home work (answer 1 or 2) or overtime as reason (hourreas = 16); evening/night/weekend defined only when shiftwk = 3. Programme averages use yfactor weights for programmes with >= 50 (or 100) LFS observations; hwactual = 99 dropped.

Sum over 30 years after graduation of deflated log annual earned income ERHVERVSINDK_13 (employment plus self-employment income), year effects (base 2000) removed, for graduates observed for all 30 years; averaged by programme.
definitions.source_location: Data/Gen_life_earnings_ambition_final/Get life-time earnings.do; Online Appendix A.2 'Income measure'

definitions.definition: Average net wealth at age 50 by programme, excluding pension assets, deflated to 2000 prices.
Fraction of a programme's graduates who reach a managerial position, i.e. hold a corresponding occupational code for at least two consecutive years.

authors: Michael Svarer, Michael Rosholm and Jakob Roland Munch
title: Rent Control and Unemployment Duration
summary: Uses Danish register data on unemployment spells and housing to study whether living in rent-controlled housing affects job finding. Unemployed workers in rent-controlled dwellings have lower exit rates from unemployment, consistent with rent control reducing geographic mobility.
data: 10% random sample of the Danish adult population from administrative registers (Statistics Denmark)
Housing unit characteristics for dwellings occupied by the sample
Weekly labour market event histories
Danish Tax Authorities 1999 hedonic model for owner-occupied housing (to predict uncontrolled rent)
variables: Outcome: unemployment duration in weeks (exit to job in local vs national labour market)
Explanatory: rent control benefit decile (predicted uncontrolled rent minus actual rent), time-varying
Mobility: job finding with move to another of 51 commuting areas
Tenure type: private rental housing vs other
sample_size: 14,645 persons contributing 31,966 unemployment spells
sample: Inflow sample of unemployment spells 1997–2000 from a 10% random sample of the Danish adult population (IZA DP 842 working-paper version).

definitions.definition: Flow sample of unemployment spells starting 1997-2000, from weekly labour-market event histories; duration measured in weeks, with destination employment recorded. Temporary layoffs (return to the previous employer, about 40% of spells) are treated as right-censored, as are exits to states outside the labour market.
registers: 10% sample of Danish adult population (Statistics Denmark registers)

definitions.definition: Local labour markets are groups of municipalities between which the internal migration rate is 50% higher than the external migration rate (Andersen 2000), giving 51 commuting areas in Denmark.

An unemployed worker is geographically mobile if he or she gets a job and moves to another commuting area within the window from 8 weeks before to 52 weeks after the start of the job spell; otherwise a job exit is local.

definitions.variable: Rent control benefit and decile of rent control degree
definitions.definition: Rent control benefit = predicted uncontrolled rent minus actual rent; uncontrolled rent from the Danish Tax Authorities' 1999 hedonic model for owner-occupied housing (sales 1996-1999, dwelling traits, more than 50,000 geographic areas) times an estimate of user cost; missing actual rents (about 50% of units) imputed by Heckman two-step. The regressor is the decile of the rent control degree (benefit / uncontrolled rent), using 1999 decile limits applied to 1997, 1998 and 2000; time-varying across housing units via moving dates.
Ratio of UI benefits received to the most recent wage.

Housing market split into owner-occupied (51%), co-operative (6%), public rental (19%) and private rental (18%); analysis concerns private rental units, where rents are regulated except in dwellings built after 1991.
definitions.source_location: Section 3 'The Danish private rental housing market'

authors: Paul Bingley and Gauthier Lanot
title: Public Pension Programmes and the Retirement of Married Couples in Denmark
summary: Estimates a dynamic discrete choice model of couples' joint retirement and saving on a 1 percent register sample of Danish couples, using the introduction and reforms of the early retirement programme (efterløn) for identification. Retirement responds asymmetrically for men and women to their own and their spouse's income flows.
data: 1% sample of Danish couples of potential retirement age from an administrative register
variables: Outcome: retirement decisions of husband and wife (joint retirement)
Identifying variation: introduction and subsequent reforms of the publicly financed early retirement programme (efterløn)
Explanatory: own and spouse's income flows
Model: dynamic discrete choice model with saving
sample: A 1% register sample of Danish married couples of potential retirement age.

authors: Brian Krogh Graversen and Jan C. van Ours
title: How to Help Unemployed Find Jobs Quickly: Experimental Evidence from a Mandatory Activation Program
summary: A randomised experiment in two Danish counties assigned newly unemployed workers to an intensive activation programme with early job search courses, frequent meetings and mandatory activation. Treated workers found jobs substantially faster, with the threat of mandatory activation an important part of the effect.
data: Public Employment Service (PES) administrative registers (treatment status, demographics, meetings with caseworkers)
DREAM weekly register of public income transfers (Danish National Labour Market Authority)
variables: Outcome: unemployment duration in weeks / job finding rate
Treatment: random assignment to mandatory activation programme by birth date (born 1st–15th of month)
Mechanism: meetings with caseworkers, job search programmes, training programmes
Exit states: employment, other benefits, right-censoring
sample_size: 4,520 unemployment spells (2,229 treatment, 2,291 control)
sample: Newly unemployed UI benefit recipients registering at the PES in Storstrøm and South Jutland counties between November 2005 and February 2006, first spell only.

definitions.definition: From weekly DREAM transfer data: the spell starts in the week the person became unemployed and continues until the person has not received UI benefits (or participated in ALMPs) for four consecutive weeks; switching to sickness benefits counts as still unemployed. Only the first spell is used; data run to mid-September 2006, so spells are censored after 26-43 weeks depending on assignment week.

definitions.variable: Exit to employment and other exit states
definitions.definition: A worker is assumed to find a job as soon as he or she no longer receives benefit payments (after the 4-week rule); other exit states (e.g. early retirement pay, other benefits) and right-censoring are distinguished using the DREAM event history.
definitions.source_location: Section 2.3 footnote 11; Appendix A Table A2

definitions.definition: Newly unemployed UI benefit recipients (clean seniority record, i.e. eligible for the full 4-year UI period) registering at the PES in Storstrom and South Jutland counties between week 43 of 2005 and week 8 of 2006 and still unemployed on the Friday of the registration week; treatment if born on the 1st-15th of a month, control if born on the 16th or later. Bad-weather and work-sharing unemployment excluded.

From 5,180 assigned: drop 27 incorrectly assigned by birth date, 43 bad-weather/work-sharing cases, 37 who died or moved abroad, and 553 who did not receive UI benefits within 6 weeks of PES registration, leaving 4,520 (2,229 treatment, 2,291 control).

definitions.variable: Treatment programme components (meetings, job search and training programmes)
definitions.definition: Meetings with caseworkers (type and date, from PES registers, including private contractors); job search programmes (2-week courses); training programmes grouping short work experience (up to 4 weeks), employment subsidy and training/education programmes.
Occupational classification based on the name of the UI fund that pays the individual's UI benefits.

authors: Nabanita Datta Gupta and Marianne Simonsen
title: Non-cognitive Child Outcomes and Universal High Quality Child Care
summary: Links the Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children to the registers to compare non-cognitive outcomes at age seven for children in universal preschool, family day care and home care at age three. Attending high-quality preschool does not harm non-cognitive outcomes relative to home care, while long hours in family day care are associated with worse outcomes for some groups.
data: Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (DALSC), waves 1996, 1999, 2003
Administrative registers on parents' education, labour market status, hours, wages and income (1994–2003)
Day Care Register (Statistics Denmark), used descriptively
variables: Outcome: Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) index at age 7½
Treatment: mode of care at age 3½ (preschool, family day care, home care)
Instrument/pseudo-experiment: municipality differences in childcare take-up and provision
Heterogeneity: child gender and mother's education
Hours in non-parental care
sample_size: 4,343 observations (children) in the main OLS estimates
sample: About 6,000 Danish children born between 15 September and 31 October 1995 surveyed in DALSC, linked to parental register data.

definitions.definition: Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire total index (0-40, 0 = no behavioural problems) built from emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity/inattention and peer-relationship items (25 items answered not true/somewhat true/certainly true), reported by the primary parent in the 2003 DALSC wave at child age 7.5.

Dummies from the 1999 DALSC wave (age 3.5): home care (parents or grandparents), municipality family day care, municipality preschool, municipality-provided programme (either), private care, other care.
definitions.source_location: Appendix Table A3 'Child Care at age three'

definitions.definition: Binary indicator that the child's municipality guarantees all children a (center-based) preschool slot within the municipality, used as the instrument for preschool take-up; information on child care guarantees supplied by Bureau 2000. Bornholm excluded.
definitions.source_location: Section 2.1 'Guaranteed access to preschool (GAPS)'; acknowledgements; Appendix (instrument)

definitions.definition: Number of hours per week in non-parental care (DALSC), grouped into six categories: 10 hours or less, 10-20, 20-30, 30-40, 40-50 and above 50 hours, analysed within family day care and within preschool.
definitions.source_location: Section 5 'Effects of hours in care'; Appendix Table A3

definitions.definition: Mother's highest education from Statistics Denmark registers: high school or below; vocational degree; short tertiary (13-14 years); medium tertiary (15-16 years); long tertiary (17 years or more).

definitions.variable: Mother's degree of employment after birth
definitions.definition: Fraction of the year employed in 1996, 1997 and 1998 (one to three years after the 1995 birth), plus labour market experience before birth (1995, in years) and 1995 hourly wage and job level (senior/higher management, medium, lower, lowest level).

definitions.variable: Early public care enrolment (nursery / family day care 1997-1998)
definitions.definition: Dummies for enrolment in nursery and in family day care in 1997 and 1998, from the Statistics Denmark Day Care Register; also arranged care at six months and being on a municipal waiting list at six months (DALSC).
About 6,000 children born 15 September-31 October 1995 (DALSC); care mode measured in 1999 (age 3.5), outcome in 2003 (age 7.5); merged to parents' register data 1994-2003.

authors: Daniel le Maire and Bertel Schjerning
title: Tax Bunching, Income Shifting and Self-Employment
summary: Self-employed Danes bunch sharply at the top tax kink, but much of the bunching reflects intertemporal shifting of income through retained earnings in the business rather than real changes in effort. Accounting for shifting implies a much smaller elasticity of real income.
data: Tax records of Danish self-employed individuals (taxable income, retained earnings)
variables: Outcome: bunching of taxable income at kinks of the tax schedule
Mechanism: intertemporal income shifting via retained earnings in the business tax schemes
Estimate: taxable income elasticity (0.43–0.53 ignoring shifting; structural 0.14–0.20)
sample: Danish self-employed taxpayers.

definitions.definition: Persons whose primary occupation is self-employment, classified with the Statistics Denmark occupation variables pstill2 (primary) and sstill2 (secondary); narrower than Chetty et al. (2011), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation.

Entire population panel 1994-2009, aged 25-59, main occupation self-employment; restricted to self-employed whose spouse's primary or secondary occupation is not self-employment (because transfers to assisting spouses are only observed 1994-2001).
Sum of wage earnings, declared firm profits (net of retained earnings), remunerations, provisions, alimony etc. minus deductions; interest income is capital income and not part of personal income.

definitions.variable: Taxable income relative to the effective kink
definitions.definition: For each individual, the difference between actual taxable income and the taxable income needed to reach the middle or top tax bracket, computed with the authors' own tax simulator accounting for special deductions and joint taxation of couples (simulated tax within +/-5 DKK of actual for 95% of the sample); distributions plotted in 1,000 DKK bins.

Piecewise-linear personal income tax with five brackets before 1996 and four from 1996; e.g. 2001: about 8% below 33,400 DKK, about 44% up to 179,900 DKK (bottom tax), 49% above (middle tax) and 63% above 279,900 DKK (top tax). Top-tax base is mainly individual; middle-tax base depends on household income; middle cutoff raised to the top cutoff in 2009.

definitions.variable: Business tax scheme and retained earnings
definitions.definition: Self-employed choose the personal income tax scheme, the capital returns scheme (from 1993) or the firm tax scheme (from 1987); the latter two are treated as one and allow retaining profits in the firm, taxed provisionally at the firm tax rate (34% in 1994 falling to 25% in 2009), with withdrawals taxed as personal income. Retained earnings = profits retained under these schemes.
definitions.source_location: Section 2.1 'Three Tax Schemes for the Self-employed'; Table 2

definitions.definition: Income before shifting: personal income plus retained earnings plus income shifted along other margins such as pension contributions and transfers to assisting spouses; used (adjusted for income shocks) to estimate the real bunching response.

Excess mass at the tax cutoff estimated following Saez (2010) within a bandwidth around the kink, applied to taxable income and to adjusted earned income; the dynamic extension separates bunching from intertemporal shifting via retained earnings.

authors: Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Jakob Roland Munch and Hans Jørgen Whitta-Jacobsen
title: Taxation and the Long Run Allocation of Labor: Theory and Danish Evidence
summary: Estimates a search model with non-linear taxation, in which workers keep looking for better-paid jobs, on employer-employee register data for all Danish workers and workplaces in 2004 to 2006. Danish taxes reduce total income by about 12 percent through the allocation of labour across jobs, and moving to low-tax OECD levels would recover four fifths of the loss.
data: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Wage Statistics Register (Lønstatistikken) for hours-adjusted wages (robustness)
Empirical effective marginal tax rate schedule for 2006 from Kleven and Kreiner (2006)
variables: Workplace average hourly wage rate (annual labour income / annual hours)
Workplace size, number of stayers and new hires (job-to-job flows)
New hires from non-employment
Effective marginal tax rates by income level (used to estimate structural search model and efficiency loss)
sample_size: 126,400 workplaces employing 1.4 million workers
sample: Full population of private-sector workplaces in Denmark in 2005 and their workers aged 18–65, with wages between DKK 90 and DKK 714 per hour.

definitions.definition: Workers aged 18-65 employed in private-sector workplaces in 2005, drawn from IDA for 2004-2006; employment at each workplace is observed in a specific week in each year. Workers with hourly wage rates in the top percentile (above DKK 714) or below DKK 90 are excluded.
A workplace is an IDA establishment defined by a geographical location; most firms have one workplace but some larger firms have several.

Annual labour income (including mandatory pension fund payments) divided by annual hours; annual hours are based on the mandatory ATP pension contributions, so overtime is not counted and part-time hours are imprecise.
Each worker is assigned the average hourly wage rate of employees at his/her workplace in 2005 (following Christensen et al. 2005), after trimming wages below DKK 90 and above DKK 714.
Size is the number of employees at the workplace in 2005; stayers are workers employed at the workplace in 2005 who are still employed there in 2006.

definitions.variable: New hires / new hires from non-employment
definitions.definition: New hires are workers employed at the workplace in 2005 who were not employed there in 2004; new hires from non-employment are workers employed at the workplace in 2005 who were not employed at any workplace in 2004 (non-employment or non-participation).
Distribution of firm-specific average wages for persons entering firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighting each firm's wage by its share of all hires from non-employment.

Effective marginal tax rates by annual labour income from the Kleven and Kreiner (2006) empirical tax function for 2006 (income taxes, indirect taxes and benefit claw-back), deflated to 2005 by average labour income growth; hourly wages are converted to annual income using median annual hours of 1,660. The participation tax rate m0 is 0.59 at baseline (0.82 in a robustness check).

Robustness check: the employer-reported hourly wage from the Wage Statistics Register (Lønstatistikken) is regressed on the IDA wage rate after dropping the top and bottom 1% and IDA wages flagged as low quality by Statistics Denmark. The fitted relationship is then used to impute an overtime- and part-time-adjusted wage for all workers.

authors: Juanna Schrøter Joensen and Helena Skyt Nielsen
title: Spillovers in Education Choice
summary: Exploits the Danish high school pilot that made advanced mathematics cheaper to take for some cohorts. An older sibling's advanced maths choice raises the probability that the younger sibling also chooses advanced maths, with spillovers that depend on the siblings' gender composition.
data: Danish administrative registers on high school enrolment, course packages and completion (Statistics Denmark education registers)
Parent and sibling links from population registers
Parental education and income registers
Earnings registers (younger siblings' earnings at ages 30–35)
variables: Outcome: younger sibling chooses advanced math-science course package in high school
Endogenous regressor: older sibling's advanced math-science choice
Instrument: older sibling enrolled in a high school that unexpectedly introduced the pilot scheme (PilotIntro)
Outcomes: younger sibling's college/STEM education at age 30 and log earnings at ages 30–35
Controls: parental education and income, county and entry-cohort fixed effects
period: High school entry cohorts 1984–1987 (older siblings) and 1988–1991 (younger siblings, main sample); register data from 1980 onwards
sample_size: 7,786 sibling pairs (main closely spaced sample); 17,691 sibling pairs in the wider sample with age gap < 10 years
sample: Older siblings entering academic high school 1984–1987 who graduated in three years, paired with younger siblings entering high school 1988–1991 with an age gap of at most 4 years.

definitions.definition: Indicator that the student chose a high-school course package combining advanced math and advanced science. In traditional schools the only such package was advanced math, advanced physics and intermediate chemistry; pilot schools also offered advanced math, advanced chemistry and intermediate physics. The choice is made at the end of the first high-school year.

PilotIntro = 1 if the (older sibling) enrolled in a high school that unexpectedly introduced the pilot scheme after the student's enrolment but before the advanced-course choice (cohorts entering 1984-87). PilotSchool = 1 if the school had adopted the pilot before the student's enrolment.

Older siblings entering academic high school 1984-87 who graduated in three years, paired with a younger sibling who entered after 1987 and graduated in three years. The main sample has younger-sibling cohorts 1988-91 and an age gap of at most 4 years; the wider sample has cohorts 1988-97 and a gap of at most 10 years.
registers: Statistics Denmark population and education registers

definitions.definition: Mutually exclusive indicators for the mother's and father's highest completed education, plus their gross income as observed at the end of the year before the child started high school (when the child was 15).

Indicator that the highest completed education is in a STEM field, following the National Science Foundation definition (math, engineering, natural and technical sciences, and some social and life sciences). It is used for parents and for younger siblings' education at age 30.
Indicator that the younger sibling's highest completed education at age 30 is more than a 4-year college degree (also interacted with STEM field).
Log annual earnings of the younger sibling at ages 30-35, in real 1989 DKK.
definitions.source_location: Section 5 (Table 7); Appendix A Figure A1 note

authors: Maya Rossin-Slater and Miriam Wüst
title: Parental Responses to Child Support Obligations: Evidence from Administrative Data
summary: Uses discontinuities in the Danish child support schedule by fathers' income to estimate how higher obligations affect separated parents. The paper documents responses in fathers' income, subsequent family formation and the parents' living arrangements.
data: Danish administrative registers on children born 1985–2008 linked to parents and siblings (population/family registers)
Income and tax records including tax-deductible child support payments
Labour market registers (employment, earnings, disability insurance, early retirement)
Birth records (fertility through 2010)
Education registers
Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (DALSC) and Children and Youth in Denmark (CYD) survey (descriptive, supplementary)
variables: Treatment: father's average child support obligation (from Danish child support guideline schedule)
Identifying variation: income thresholds in the child support guidelines (simulated instrument)
Outcome: father's annual child support payment
Outcome: father–child co-residence (physical custody)
Outcomes: post-separation fertility and labour supply of both parents
sample_size: 73,303 fathers (71,575 unique mothers)
sample: Fathers observed every year 1998–2010 who separated from their oldest child's mother (or had a first child while not cohabiting) in 1999–2008, with one or two children under 18 and separation-year income near the first three guideline thresholds.

definitions.definition: The year in which the father no longer resides with his oldest child's mother, or the year he has a first child while not living with the child's mother. The sample is restricted to separation years 1999-2008.

Fathers observed in the registers every year 1998-2010 who either were married to or cohabiting with their oldest child's mother at childbirth (or in 1998 for children born earlier), or had a first child 1999-2008 while not married to or cohabiting with the mother. Also required: separation in 1999-2008, one or two children under 18 at separation, and separation-year income in a 100,000 DKK window around the first three schedule thresholds (175,000-505,000 DKK). The result is 73,303 fathers, one observation each.

The father's annual obligation from the Danish child support guideline (normal amount plus extra amount per child, plus a supplement of 25-300% of the normal amount above income thresholds). It is a step function of current gross income and the number of biological children under 18, including new children. It is averaged over all post-separation years and expressed in thousands of real 2000 DKK.

Instrument: the obligation in each post-separation year computed from the father's separation-year gross income and his 'original' children still under 18, so children ageing out are counted but new children and post-separation income changes are ignored. It is averaged over the post-separation period.

Tax-deductible annual child support payments by non-custodial fathers as reported to the tax authorities, so only payments above the non-deductible extra amount are observed. Formal and voluntary payments cannot be distinguished.

Indicator that the father shares a residence address with the child in any year after separation, based on one address per person per year. It captures sole-father and some joint physical custody but understates joint custody.
Whether the mother or father has an additional child after separation, measured from the universe of birth records through 2010 and split by birth within or outside a new partnership.

Fraction of post-separation years in which the father has any positive labour income, and the proportion of years not in the labour force. NILF is split by disability leave (Social Disability Pension), retirement including early retirement (Post-Employment Wage program, ages 60-64), and means-tested welfare.

authors: Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Labor Supply and Optimization Frictions: Evidence from the Danish Student Labor Market
summary: Danish students lose part of their study grant when annual earnings exceed a threshold. Register data show bunching below the threshold that grows as students gain experience with the rule, so optimisation frictions hide a structural elasticity well above the observed response.
data: Danish administrative registers for the full population (education, earnings, benefits, demographics)
Annual income tax returns
Monthly student benefit (SU) take-up records from the Student Benefit Administration
Monthly payroll records of earnings and hours (BFL/eIndkomst), from 2008
variables: Outcome: annual labour earnings relative to the student benefit income limit (bunching)
Incentive: kink/notch from phase-out (payback) of student grants above the individual income limit
Simulated individual marginal tax and phase-out rates
Monthly earnings and benefit take-up (timing of adjustment)
sample_size: around 75,000 observations per year (core sample 75,500 individuals per year on average)
sample: Individuals aged 18–35 enrolled in tertiary education, fully eligible for student benefits and with positive labour earnings (above DKK 8,000 per year).

definitions.definition: Individuals aged 18-35 enrolled in tertiary education, fully eligible for student benefits (SU), and with positive labour earnings, defined as earned income above DKK 8,000 per year. This gives about 75,500 observations per year, 2006-2011.

definitions.variable: Income counted against the SU income limit
definitions.definition: Labour income (net of labour market contribution), transfers other than student benefits, and capital income, except certain types of stock income. All amounts are scaled to 2018 levels using the official wage indexation of student benefits.

The baseline income limit is 12 times the monthly basic amount (DKK 7,700, 2018 levels; about DKK 93,000 annually) and rises by DKK 11,600 for each month of benefits not taken up. It is computed from monthly benefit take-up records of the Student Benefit Administration.

Marginal income tax of 42% above a personal allowance of DKK 49,900. Benefits are phased out at 50% for the first DKK 11,600 above the individual income limit and at 100% beyond that, so the effective marginal rate jumps from 42% to 72% at the baseline limit under optimal take-up. If the payback exceeds DKK 9,200, the whole payback rises by 7% (a notch). The 2009 reform raised the baseline limit by 24% and the phase-out rate from 52% to 62%.

Total earned income from tax records minus the individual income limit; positive amounts translate into payback of benefits. Predicted end-of-year benefits (initial payout minus predicted payback) match reported benefits within DKK 2 for 97.9% of the core sample.
All jobs not in wholesale (NACE 46), retail (47), postal service (53), hotels and restaurants (55, 56), cleaning (81), elderly, social and childcare (87, 88), or sports and amusement facilities (93).
Monthly records of earnings and hours worked for all wage earners, available from 2008 and used for average weekly hours and the within-person variability of monthly earnings.
Number of years enrolled in tertiary education between 2004 and 2007 (that is, over the previous four years).
definitions.source_location: Table 3 note a; Appendix Figure A.VI

authors: N. Meltem Daysal, Michael Lovenheim, Nikolaj Siersbæk and David N. Wasser
title: Home Prices, Fertility, and Early-Life Health Outcomes
summary: For Danish homeowners aged 20 to 44, a 100,000 kroner rise in home prices raises the probability of giving birth by about 2.35 percent. Birth outcomes improve too, but mostly because of who gives birth, and there is no effect on children's health in the first five years.
data: Medical Birth Register (MFR)
National Patient Register (LPR)
State's Sales and Valuation Registry (public property valuations and sales prices)
Population register (BEF) and other registers for demographics, education, household income and partner status
variables: Treatment: once-lagged one-year change in estimated home value (public valuation adjusted by local sale-price ratio)
Outcome: indicator for giving birth
Outcomes: birth weight, low birth weight, very low birth weight, prematurity
Outcomes: hospital admissions, ER visits and days hospitalised in first year and ages 1–5
Comparison group: renters
sample_size: 1,105,559 observations on 198,435 women (125,903 births)
sample: Women aged 20–44 who became first-time homeowners between 1993 and 2004, purchasing between ages 18 and 42.

definitions.definition: The public valuation of the home times the owner's share, multiplied by the mean ratio of sale price to public valuation among homes sold in the same year, municipality, housing type and valuation-quartile cluster (a SPAR-type index); woman's and partner's shares are summed. The value is fixed to the first house the woman is observed buying, and is in 100,000 DKK at 2006 prices (CPI-deflated).

One-year change in estimated home value, lagged one year relative to the fertility outcome. Public valuations were made in January of the prior year until end-2003 and in October of the prior year afterwards. Homes whose valuation rose by more than 50% in a year, and the 1st and 99th percentiles of the lagged change, are excluded.

Residential houses and apartments in clusters with at least five sales; only normal sales between individuals (no intra-family sales). Excluded: negative valuations or sale prices, multiple addresses at the same location, and sales above 300% or below 40% of the public valuation.

Women not homeowners at the beginning of 1992-1993 who became homeowners between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42; owning means the woman, her partner or both own the home. Women whose partner bought before the couple formed, who moved out of the new home within the year, or who have incomplete income or home data are dropped, leaving women aged 20-44 observed 1995-2006.

definitions.variable: Low / very low birth weight, prematurity
definitions.definition: From the Birth Registry for live births: low birth weight is below 2,500 grams, very low birth weight below 1,500 grams, and premature is gestational age under 37 completed weeks; birth weight is also used continuously.

definitions.variable: Hospital admissions, inpatient days and ER visits
definitions.definition: Indicators for any hospital admission and any ER visit in the first year of life and at ages 1-5, plus the number of days hospitalised and ER visits in the first five years. Inpatient days exclude the childbirth admission and the following four days.

Indicator for giving birth in the year, from the Birth Registry. In a robustness check, the conception date is computed from gestational length and birth date, the price change is scaled by the fraction of the year before conception, and non-mothers get randomly assigned birth months.
Household consumption imputed from income and year-to-year wealth changes following Browning and Leth-Petersen (2003).

authors: Marianne Simonsen, Lars Skipper, Niels Skipper and Anne Illemann Christensen
title: Spot Price Biases in Non-Linear Health Insurance Contracts
summary: The Danish prescription drug reimbursement scheme has coverage that rises with annual spending and resets each year. Consumers look forward-looking around the reset but react too strongly to current prices within the year, and liquidity constraints rather than plan literacy or cognitive decline explain the spot-price bias.
data: Population-wide individual data on prescription drug purchases and reimbursement under the Danish non-linear drug insurance scheme (registers not named in the abstract)
variables: Incentive: spot price of drugs as a non-linear function of year-to-date spending
Incentive: end-of-year reset of the coverage (deductible) year
Outcome: timing and amount of prescription drug purchases
Heterogeneity: liquidity constraints, plan literacy, cognitive decline
sample: Population-wide data on Danish consumers of prescription drugs covered by the non-linear reimbursement scheme (details not available from the abstract).

definitions.definition: The full history of prescription drug purchases from the Danish Prescription Drug Register (Laegemiddelstatistikregisteret), covering 1995-2014: date, shelf price, government coverage, type of coverage and type of drug. It is aggregated to daily (descriptive) or monthly (estimation) spending within coverage years. Outcomes include spending, number of pharmacy visits, and days until next purchase truncated at 365.

definitions.variable: Coverage year and synthetic pre-reform coverage year
definitions.definition: Post-reform coverage years start with the first purchase after the March 2000 reform and reset 365 days after the first purchase, with the next year starting at the next purchase. Synthetic pre-reform coverage years apply the same rule from the first observed purchase, keeping only years that end by December 1999.

Coinsurance rate at the start of coverage month m given year-to-date spending, taking values 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.15 or 0. Under the 2000 contract: a DKK 500 deductible, 50% coinsurance to DKK 1,200, 25% to DKK 2,800, 15% beyond, and a stop-loss at DKK 18,500 capping out-of-pocket costs at DKK 3,600. The spot price is 1 for the purchase that starts a coverage year.

Average realised end-of-year price within cells of 5 age groups x 6 sextiles of predicted health spending x 100 percentiles of year-to-date spending, for each coverage month. Pre-reform counterfactual prices for 1998 are imputed by matching percentiles to pooled coverage years starting in 2000-2001.

Following Handel (2013), year-t drug spending is regressed on year t-1 gender, age and age squared, number of GP office visits, fee-for-service payments to the physician, drug spending and its square, ATC level-3 drug-type indicators (88 categories), and hospital ICD-10 level-2 diagnosis indicators (215 categories). The model is then used to predict next year's spending; for coverage-reset analyses, covariates are measured in the 365 days before the coverage year starts.
definitions.codes: ATC level 3 (88 categories); ICD-10 level 2 (215 categories)

definitions.definition: Following Alpert (2016), a drug at ATC level 3 (pharmacological subgroup) is chronic if its median consumer buys it in at least three calendar months of a year (more than twice).

From the 2000 Danish National Health Interview Survey (DNHIS) question 'During the last 12 months, how often have you had trouble paying your bills'. Respondents answering at least 'some months' are coded as liquidity constrained (12%).

'Economic literates' are individuals with a master-level degree in economics or business (ISCED level 7); medical professionals hold a university degree in medicine or pharmacology (ISCED levels 7-8). Cognitive decline is proxied by age 65 and above versus below 65.
