authors: Katrine Jakobsen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: Identifying Behavioral Responses to Tax Reforms: New Insights and a New Approach
summary: Shows that standard estimates of taxable income elasticities from tax reforms are biased by mean reversion and diverging income trends across the distribution, and proposes an approach that exploits reform timing to separate behavioural responses from these trends, applied to Danish tax reforms.
data: Danish administrative registers for the full population since 1980 (labour market history, education, earnings, demographics)
Third-party reported income tax records
Simulated marginal tax rates from an extended Danish tax simulator (Kleven and Schultz 2014 model)
variables: Outcome: changes in taxable income (broad, personal, labour income) over four-year periods
Treatment: predicted change in log net-of-tax rate from the 2004 and 2009–10 Danish tax reforms
Income-bin dummies capturing trend differentials across the income distribution
Validation: income trends in parts of the distribution unaffected by the reform
period: Data since 1980; main analyses 1999–2012 (2004 reform: 1999–2003 pre-period, 2003–2007 reform period; 2009–10 reform: 2004–2008 pre-period, 2008–2012 reform period); 1987 and 1994 reforms in appendix
sample_size: over 2,000,000 individuals per period (2,240,332 and 2,295,922 for the 2004 reform pre-reform and reform periods; 2,097,862 and 2,240,833 for the 2009–10 reform)
sample: Individuals present in the tax data with positive income over each four-year period and initial personal income above DKK 200,000 (2004 reform) or DKK 250,000 (2009–10 reform), about half the Danish adult population.

definitions.definition: Salary, wages, honoraria, fees, bonuses, fringe benefits and business earnings, as defined in the Danish income tax system.
Labour market income plus transfers, certain pension payouts and received alimony; it equals personal income before deductions.

Broad income minus the labour market contribution and certain pension contributions (employer-administered annuity pension contributions were fully deductible until 2010, then capped at DKK 100,000 for expiring annuities). PI is the main outcome and initial-income concept, and responses are also shown with and without pension contributions.

Personal income plus capital income (interest, rental and business capital income minus interest on debt) minus itemized deductions (commuting, union fees, unemployment insurance contributions, other work expenses, charitable donations, paid alimony). Stock income is taxed separately.

definitions.variable: Simulated marginal tax rate / predicted change in log net-of-tax rate
definitions.definition: Marginal tax rates are imputed with an extension of the Kleven and Schultz (2014) Danish tax simulator, as the increase in total household taxes from an incremental increase in labour income. The predicted change compares rates under the period-t and t-1 tax systems, holding income and characteristics fixed at their t-k levels (k = 1 baseline).

Four-year periods: 2004-08 (pre) and 2008-12 (reform) for the 2009-10 reform; initial years 1999 and 2003 for the 2004 reform. Individuals present in tax data with positive income over the period, and initial personal income above DKK 250,000 (2009-10 reform) or DKK 200,000 (2004 reform) at 2019 levels deflated by tax-code wage indexes.

Fifty dummies for initial personal income measured at the start of each period (e.g. 2004 or 2008). The DKK 300,000 bin is omitted, so coefficients measure income-growth trend differentials relative to that bin.

authors: Mette Foged, Linea Hasager, Giovanni Peri, Jacob Nielsen Arendt and Iben Bolvig
title: Intergenerational Spillover Effects of Language Training for Refugees
summary: Follows the children of refugees affected by the 1999 Danish reform that improved language training. Children of treated parents achieve better educational outcomes, showing that the integration gains from language training carry over to the next generation.
data: Danish administrative registers from Statistics Denmark on refugees' asylum/admission dates and parent–child links
Lower secondary school completion and final exam records
Criminal conviction records (property, violent, narcotics crime)
Earnings, occupation (ISCO), disposable income, marriage and fertility registers for parents
variables: Running variable: parent's admission (asylum grant) date relative to 1 January 1999 (Integration Act language training reform)
Outcome: completing lower secondary school and taking final exams by age 18
Outcome: criminal convictions between ages 15 and 18
Parental outcomes: annual earnings, complex job, disposable income, convictions
period: Children born 1990–2001, followed up to 2019; parental outcomes 1999–2016
sample_size: 6,467 children; 5,197 adult parents
sample: Children born 1990–2001 with at least one parent granted asylum in Denmark within a four-year window around 1 January 1999, who arrived before or during primary school age.

definitions.variable: Treatment / running variable: parent's admission date
definitions.definition: A child is treated if the first parent was granted refugee status (admission date) on or after 1 January 1999, when the Integration Act's language training applied. The running variable is days between the admission date and the cutoff; specifications using the father's admission date are also reported.

Children born 1990-2001 with at least one parent granted asylum in Denmark within a four-year window around 1 January 1999. Children were born in the first three years after the reform or were of pre-school or primary-school age on arrival. They are followed to age 18, through 2019; 6,467 children with parents born 1948-1982.

definitions.variable: Lower secondary completion and final exam
definitions.definition: Two indicators: the child completed lower secondary (compulsory) school by age 18 (before turning 19), and the child took the final exams marking the end of lower secondary school. Exemption from the exams, e.g. for low language proficiency, is possible.
definitions.source_location: Section III, footnote 9; Section V, Table 3

definitions.definition: Indicator for any criminal conviction between ages 15 and 18, and separate indicators for property, violent and narcotics crime.

Indicator for working in an occupation from managers (ISCO 1) to services and sales workers (ISCO 5), jobs that require some schooling and technical knowledge, or literacy and good communication skills.
Annual gross earnings in year-2000 prices converted to USD at 6.6 DKK/USD. Disposable income includes public transfers net of taxes, deflated to year-2000 USD.
Indicator for marrying a Danish citizen, and total number of children born after admission.

authors: Sofie Cairo and Robert Mahlstedt
title: The Disparate Effects of Information Provision: A Field Experiment on the Work Incentives of Social Welfare
summary: A field experiment in Denmark informed welfare recipients about a minimum work requirement, either with personalised running counts of their hours or with generic rules. Personalised information raised employment among those below the required hours, while generic notices reduced labour supply among those at low near-term risk of sanctions.
data: Field experiment assignment and messaging data (Danish public employment service, jobnet.dk online tool)
Population registers (socio-demographic background)
Benefit payment records (DREAM)
Monthly income and employment records (eIndkomst/BFL)
Public employment service data on sanctions, exemptions, collected working hours, click data and registered job applications
variables: Treatment: random assignment to personalised online information tool about benefit-reduction risk under the work requirement (three arms)
Outcome: employment and earnings
Outcome: welfare benefit receipt and exit to alternative income support
Outcome: working hours collected toward the requirement and job applications
Heterogeneity: job search activity and sanction risk
period: Intervention from 15 August 2018 with up to five monthly reminders
sample_size: 47,294 individuals
sample: All Danish welfare benefit recipients on 15 August 2018 subject to the 225-hour work requirement who had received the official notification letter.

definitions.definition: After 12 months on welfare benefits within the last three years, recipients keep the full benefit only if they worked at least 225 hours in regular non-subsidised jobs in the previous 12 months. Otherwise the benefit is reduced by about DKK 500-1,000 per month depending on family status; after a sanction the hour count resets to zero. Caseworkers may grant exemptions to those unable to work at least five hours a week.
registers: Public employment service data (sanctions, exemptions, collected hours)

definitions.definition: All welfare benefit recipients in stock on 15 August 2018 who were subject to the work requirement and had received the official notification letter (N = 47,294), randomised into three arms. Treated: up to six monthly messages plus access to the personalised online tool on jobnet.dk. Control I: general reminders only. Control II: neither.

definitions.variable: Cumulated job finding rate, hours and earnings
definitions.definition: Cumulated job finding rates by month since the intervention (extensive margin), and total working hours and labour earnings accumulated over the first 12 months after the start (intensive margin), from monthly income and employment records.
Full-time jobs have average weekly working hours at or above 90% of the full-time equivalent (37 hours per week); part-time jobs are below that.
Indicator that the individual receives any other benefit not subject to the work requirement, such as educational support, sickness or disability benefits.

Active job seekers have a positive number of collected working hours at the onset of the intervention, or at least one job application registered in the public employment service portal in the last four weeks; all others are inactive.
registers: Public employment service data (collected hours, job applications)

definitions.definition: Average number of caseworker meetings per recipient in the municipality in the six months before the intervention, split at the median. A residualised version conditions on observable characteristics.

authors: Hans Schytte Sigaard
title: Estimating Labor Supply Responses to Danish Tax Reforms
summary: Applies taxable income elasticity methods to register data on hours actually worked. The intensive-margin labour supply elasticity is about 0.08, close to the labour income and taxable income elasticities, and it comes from changes in contract hours, paid absence and switches between main and secondary jobs.
data: Wage Statistics Register (Lønstatistikken, LON) for performed hours of work
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDAN) for workplace controls
Income registers (IND, INDK, INPI) for marginal tax rate simulation
Population register (BEF) and family income register (FAIN)
Family register (FAMILIE)
Education register (UDDA)
Danish tax simulation programs (Kleven and Schultz 2014, extended by the Ministry of Finance)
variables: Outcome: three-year log change in annual performed hours of work
Treatment: three-year log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate on labour income
Instrument: mechanical (simulated) change in marginal tax rate from tax reforms, using lagged income
Secondary outcomes: labour income and taxable income
Controls: income splines, socio-economic and municipality controls
sample_size: 10,755,733 observations
sample: Employed wage earners aged 25–65 covered by the Wage Statistics Register with positive hours in both years of each three-year difference and base-year labour income above DKK 250,000.

definitions.definition: Contract hours plus paid overtime, minus paid absence, vacation and weekday holiday hours, summed over all employments in a year per individual (including secondary jobs). Contract hours are available from 2002, so the sample covers 2002-2016. LON covers all public firms and private firms with 100+ employees, plus a sample of private firms with 10-99 employees (about 50% of main employments).

definitions.variable: Three-year log change in performed hours
definitions.definition: Main outcome: log change in annual performed hours between base year t and t+3. Strictly positive hours are required in both years. Decompositions condition on staying in the same job versus switching jobs between t and t+3.

definitions.variable: Marginal tax rate on labour income
definitions.definition: Simulated using tax programs from Kleven and Schultz (2014), extended by the Danish Ministry of Finance (available 1984-2016), as [T_t(z+100) - T_t(z)]/100, with income information mainly from IND, INDK and INPI. The treatment is the three-year log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate.

definitions.variable: Predicted (mechanical) change in net-of-tax rate instrument
definitions.definition: ln(1 - T'_{t+s}(z_{i,t-k})) - ln(1 - T'_t(z_{i,t-k})): marginal rates under the period t+s and t tax systems evaluated at income lagged k periods, following Weber (2014). The main specification uses k = 2, with lags 2-4 used for overidentification tests.
Ten-piece spline with breakpoints at the deciles of log labour income lagged twice, to control for mean reversion and heterogeneous income trends.

Individuals aged 25-65 with all information needed to simulate marginal taxes, who are neither jobless nor outside the labour force as primary occupation at end of November in year t, and have strictly positive hours at t and t+3. Base-year labour income must exceed DKK 250,000 (2015 prices, CPI-deflated) and all controls must be non-missing.
Workplace controls from IDAN, socioeconomic and municipal controls from BEF and FAIN, children from FAMILIE, and education from UDDA; industry groups follow Statistics Denmark's standard groupings.

authors: Esteban García-Miralles and Jonathan M. Leganza
title: Joint Retirement of Couples: Evidence from Discontinuities in Denmark
summary: Uses age discontinuities in eligibility for Danish early retirement and public pensions to show that when one spouse becomes eligible and retires, the other spouse is substantially more likely to retire as well, quantifying spillovers that matter for evaluating retirement reforms.
data: Danish administrative registers for the full population 1986–2014 (labour market outcomes, pension benefits, socio-demographics, family/couple links)
Annual taxable earnings registers
Monthly earnings records for all employees (eIndkomst/BFL) and monthly pension benefit records, from 2008
Voluntary early retirement pension (VERP) contribution records
variables: Outcome: spouse's retirement (ceasing to earn labour income)
Outcome: pension claiming (VERP or OAP) and annual labour earnings
Running variable (age-based design): reference individual's age relative to early pension eligibility age 60
Running variable (reform-based design): birth date relative to 1 January 1954 cutoff of the 2011 reform raising VERP eligibility age by 6 months
sample_size: 367,585 couples and 2,206,044 couple-year observations (age-based sample); 10,321 couples and 73,395 couple-year observations (reform-based sample)
sample: Dual-earner Danish couples (married, registered partners or cohabiting) up to 8 years apart in age, with the reference individual aged 57–60, excluding self-employed and disability recipients.

definitions.definition: Retirement is ceasing to earn labour market income: the year in which the individual earned labour income for the last time, treated as an absorbing state (1 thereafter). Small positive income up to the equivalent of one month of average earnings is allowed after retirement (holiday pay, delayed wages). A flow definition allowing multiple retirements is used as robustness.
Using monthly earnings records (eIncome, from 2008), a dummy equal to one if the individual works past the first half of the year (past July 1) in a given year.

Receiving pension income, either voluntary early retirement pension (VERP) or old-age pension (OAP): annual indicator for any pension income in the year (age-based design), or indicator for receiving pension income before July 1 using monthly pension benefit records (reform-based design).
Taxable annual labour market earnings from the annual registers, winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles, deflated to 2010 prices and converted at 1 USD = 5.56 DKK.

Married, registered-partnership or cohabiting couples residing in Denmark 1991-2014, identified when both partners are below age 60 and followed while they remain together; age difference within couple at most 8 years.

Reference individual (partner reaching own eligibility age) earned labour income at least once at ages 55-59 and was never self-employed or on disability benefits at ages 50-59; spouse earned labour income at least once at ages 50-59. Age-based sample: 1991-2013, reference individual aged 57-60 (eligibility age 60). Reform-based sample: 2008-2014, reference individuals with qualifying VERP contributions at least once at ages 50-59, born within 3 months either side of 1 January 1954, balanced panel.

authors: Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen and Jack Blundell
title: Income Effects and Labour Supply: Evidence from a Child Benefits Reform
summary: A 2011 Danish cap on child benefits cut payments to families with several young children and left smaller families unaffected. Mothers' labour supply rises substantially after the cut, mainly on the extensive margin, and sterilisation records are used to control for differences in preferences for more children.
data: Population register (BEF) for family composition, marital status and cohabitation
Monthly payroll records with hours worked (BFL/eIndkomst)
Child benefit payment records (BOBO/BOTI)
Register OF (monthly demographics and parental leave status)
Sterilisation consultations from the National Patient Register (LPRADM) and health insurance service registers (SYSI, SSSY)
Annual income register (IND) for self-employment robustness
variables: Treatment: 2011 cap on child benefits (DKK 35,000) reducing unearned income for larger families with young children
Outcome: monthly hours worked (intensive and extensive margins)
Outcome: annual earnings (robustness incl. self-employed)
Control/restriction: family sterilisation consultation before the reform
Design: difference-in-differences, treated vs unaffected families
sample_size: 28,968 treated women and 22,477 treated men
sample: Native Danish married or cohabiting parents aged 25–59 over the window with 2–4 children (at least two under 18) in January 2011, not self-employed, observed in a balanced monthly panel.

definitions.definition: Total hours worked per month from employer reports to the tax authorities (BFL, from 2008), summed over all jobs held in the month; for employees on parental leave with fixed contractual hours not adjusted in BFL, hours are adjusted using observed days of leave.
Indicator for working non-zero hours in the month in BFL.
definitions.source_location: Fig. 10 and Table notes (employment indicator), Section 6

definitions.definition: Family experienced a strictly positive reduction in child benefits due to the DKK 35,000 cap in the first and/or second quarter of 2011 (benefits based on number and ages of children in the previous quarter; simulated from population registers and validated with Q4 BOBO/BOTI payments); control group = families not affected in Q1-Q2 2011. Continuous treatment = reduction in child benefits in 2011 in thousand DKK for treated families, zero otherwise.

Monthly indicator equal to one if the individual has ever (from 1994 onwards) consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation; a family-level version equals one if either partner in the couple has done so.

Balanced monthly panel September 2008-December 2014 of individuals aged at least 25 in September 2008 and under 60 in December 2014; excludes immigrants and children of immigrants, parents of children with irregular child benefit payments, and (main analysis) anyone self-employed at any point; in January 2011 must have at least 2 children under 18, no more than 4 children in total, and be married or cohabiting.
Annual income measures from the income register IND, used in a robustness check that includes the self-employed because self-employment income is not measured monthly.

authors: Linea Hasager
title: Does Granting Refugee Status to Family-Reunified Women Improve Their Integration?
summary: Women who enter Denmark through family reunification usually hold permits that depend on staying married. Granting them independent refugee status improves their economic integration, raises divorce rates and lowers the risk of violence against them, consistent with reduced residency uncertainty and greater bargaining power.
data: Admission register on immigrant status and residence permit application/approval dates (Danish Immigration Service data via Statistics Denmark)
Labour market data from the Danish tax authorities (employment; hours and earnings from 2008)
Police registers on victimisation and criminal convictions
Hospital admissions data (National Patient Register) for assault injuries
Central population register (BEF) for demographics, spouse links and divorce
variables: Treatment: family-reunified woman granted her own refugee status (asylum), staggered timing
Outcome: quarterly employment, hours of work and earnings
Outcome: victimisation of violence (police records or assault-related hospitalisation)
Outcome: divorce
Design: staggered difference-in-differences with not-yet-treated women as controls
sample_size: 1,349 adult women
sample: Women aged 18+ who were family-reunified to a refugee spouse in Denmark between 2001 and 2017 and later applied for and obtained their own refugee status.

definitions.variable: Treatment: change from family reunification to own refugee status
definitions.definition: Adult women (18+) admitted 2001-2017 as family-reunified to a refugee spouse who later apply for and obtain their own asylum (UN Convention, de facto/B-status or temporary protection), identified from application and approval dates of residence permits in the admission register; event time is the quarter of asylum recognition. Controls are not-yet-treated women recognized at most three years later; women followed from 3 years before to 1.5 years after recognition.
registers: Admission register (Danish Immigration Service, via Statistics Denmark)

definitions.definition: Quarterly indicator equal to one if police records show the woman was a victim of violence or sexual assault, or if she was hospitalized due to assault based on physician classification of injury (following Aizer 2010); captures mainly severe cases and also non-partner violence.

Quarterly employment indicator (available 2001-2019) and quarterly hours of work and earnings (from 2008) from tax-authority labour market data; earnings CPI-deflated to 2015 and converted to 1,000 USD at the 27 March 2019 exchange rate.
registers: Labour market data from Danish tax authorities

definitions.definition: Indicator equal to one if the woman is divorced (quarterly), from the central population register with spouse links.

authors: Thomas Høgholm Jørgensen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard
title: The Division of Parental Leave: Empirical Evidence and Policy Design
summary: Uses sharp incentives in the Danish parental leave benefit system for about 190,000 births to estimate parents' willingness to pay for leave. Parents bunch at kinks and are willing to pay for a traditional split with little leave for fathers, and simulations show that earmarked leave works much better when combined with high replacement rates.
data: Parental leave benefit spell data (parents of children born 2008–2015), incl. benefits paid to parent or employer
Monthly earnings records for all employees (BFL/eIndkomst), from 2008
Danish administrative registers on demographics, family links and firm links (population and labour market registers)
variables: Outcome: weeks of parental leave taken by mother and father within three years of birth
Incentive: individual benefit replacement rates and benefit cap creating kinks in the household budget set
Incentive: employer-provided full wage compensation (from benefits paid to employer)
Policy: earmarked (father quota) leave and replacement rate counterfactuals in a structural model
sample_size: 189,974 births
sample: Births 2008–2015 to parents in stable employment and not on non-birth public benefits in the three months before birth, excluding births followed by another child within 15 months.

definitions.definition: Total number of parental leave weeks computed from start and end dates of benefit spells in the parental leave spell data (children born 2008-2015); includes all full-time leave taken at most three years after childbirth, separately for mother and father.

Computed from total parental leave benefits paid out per parent-child spell relative to weeks of leave; statutory benefits replace 100% of pre-birth earnings for a full-time (37 hours/week) employee up to a cap of EUR 580 per week (2019 level), scaled down proportionally for part-time.

Weeks of leave with employer-provided full wage compensation, computed from the amount of parental leave benefits paid to the employer (benefits are paid to the employer as reimbursement when it pays full wage) using the individual replacement rate.

definitions.variable: Imputed individual right to wage compensation
definitions.definition: Public sector: imputed from collective-agreement rules (6-6-6 model, Apr 2008-Apr 2015: 6 weeks each parent plus 6 shared weeks if both parents work in the same public sub-sector, otherwise the shared 6 accrue to the public-sector parent) using both parents' employment sector. Private sector: equals observed compensated weeks for parents who also take uncompensated leave (exhausters); otherwise the mode of compensated weeks among exhausting co-workers with weakly higher compensation, with co-worker groups defined as firm-year cells, or 6-digit then 5-digit industry-year cells when fewer than two exhausting co-workers exist.

Births 2008-2015; parents must be continuously employed in the same firm in the 3 months before birth and not on non-birth-related public benefits during those 3 months; births are excluded if parents have a subsequent child within 15 months; parents must appear in the parental leave data (final sample 189,974 births).

authors: Linea Hasager and Mia Jørgensen
title: Sick of Your Poor Neighborhood? Quasi-Experimental Evidence on Neighborhood Effects on Health
summary: Uses the quasi-random dispersal of refugees across Danish neighbourhoods from 1986 to 1998. Refugees placed in low-income neighbourhoods had a 12 percent higher risk of developing a lifestyle-related disease 8 to 15 years later, driven by neighbours and the local environment rather than health care access, ethnic networks or labour market outcomes.
data: National Patient Register (LPR)
Health Insurance Register (SYSI, SSSY)
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Income register (IND)
Population register (BEF) and address/mobility registers (BEFBOP, BEFADR)
Migration register (VNDS)
Criminal convictions register (KRAF)
O*NET occupational data merged via occupation codes
variables: Treatment: assignment to a bottom- vs top-income-third parish (neighbourhood median household disposable income) under the 1986–1998 Refugee Spatial Dispersal Policy
Outcome: lifestyle-related disease diagnosis (circulatory, nutritional/metabolic, COPD, hip arthrosis, alcohol-related) 2–15 and 8–15 years after immigration
Outcome: mental disorder diagnoses
Mechanisms: health care access, employment and earnings, neighbour characteristics
sample_size: 21,965 refugees
sample: Refugees aged 18–64 at arrival from nine refugee-sending countries who arrived in Denmark in 1986–1998 and were assigned a municipality under the dispersal policy (excluding family-reunified spouses).

definitions.definition: Indicator for any primary or secondary hospital diagnosis (inpatient or outpatient, National Patient Register; ICD-8 before 1994, ICD-10 after) within 2-15 years, or within 8-15 years, after immigration in one of: circulatory diseases (hypertension, ischaemic heart diseases, pulmonary diseases, other heart disease, cerebrovascular and arterial diseases), nutritional/endocrine/metabolic diseases (diabetes type I and II, obesity, elevated cholesterol), COPD, hip arthrosis, and alcohol-related diseases. Exact code grouping is in Online Appendix Section B (not accessed).

Indicator for a hospital diagnosis 2-15 or 8-15 years after immigration of mental and behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance use; schizophrenia, schizotypal and delusional disorders; mood (affective) disorders; neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders; behavioural syndromes associated with physiological disturbances; and disorders of adult personality and behaviour.

Neighbourhood = parish (alternatives: municipality, apartment building). Each year, neighbourhoods are ranked by median household disposable income per adult household member (Income Register, CPI-deflated to 2000) and split into thirds: bottom (below 33rd percentile), middle (34th-66th), top (67th-100th); groups are recomputed every year for all neighbourhoods.
Neighbourhood of the refugee's address on 1 January in the year after immigration, to capture permanent resettlement rather than temporary accommodation.

Immigrants arriving 1986-1998 from Afghanistan, Ethiopia, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Palestine (stateless), Sri Lanka and Vietnam (1986-1998) or Somalia (1989-1998), aged 18-64 at arrival; former Yugoslavs excluded; excludes those married at arrival to a non-refugee partner or to a refugee partner who arrived earlier (family reunification).

definitions.variable: Employment as fraction of full working year
definitions.definition: Fraction of a full-time working year employed: 1 if full-time employee during the whole year, less than one for part-time or part-year employment.
Annual gross earnings from tax returns in the Income Register, CPI-deflated to 2000 and converted to USD at the 27 March 2020 exchange rate.
Ratio of communication and cognitive tasks to manual tasks from O*NET, merged via ISCO occupation codes, for those employed at the end of November each year.
Number of visits to general practitioners and psychologists (no diagnosis codes available in these data).
